Genesis 1.overview: God creates the heavens and the earth, orders light, sky, land, seas, vegetation, and the lights of the sky across the first four days. He creates sea creatures and birds on the fifth day, then land animals and humanity in God’s image on the sixth, blessing them and giving them food and rule over the earth before declaring all he made very good.

Genesis 2.overview: God completes creation, rests on the seventh day, and sets it apart. The LORD God forms Adam, places him in Eden with a command concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and makes a woman as his companion.

sections.heading: Creation completed and the seventh day set apart
The LORD God forms Adam and plants Eden
Adam’s work and the command about the tree
The woman is made and brought to Adam

Genesis 3.overview: The serpent persuades the woman to eat from the forbidden tree, and she gives its fruit to Adam; they recognize their nakedness and hide from the LORD God. After questioning them and pronouncing consequences for the serpent, the woman, and Adam, God clothes the couple and drives them from Eden, guarding the way to the tree of life.

sections.heading: The Serpent and the Forbidden Fruit
God Questions the Man and Woman
Consequences for the Serpent and Humanity

Genesis 4.overview: Eve bears Cain and Abel, whose offerings receive different responses from the LORD; Cain kills Abel and is sentenced to wander, but the LORD marks him for protection. Cain settles in Nod and his descendants include Lamech and the founders of several crafts, while Adam and Eve have Seth, whose son is Enosh as people begin to call on the LORD.

sections.heading: Cain kills Abel and is judged

Genesis 5.overview: The chapter traces Adam’s line through Seth, listing each descendant’s age at fatherhood, years lived, and death, while Enoch walks with God and is taken away. Lamech names his son Noah in hope of comfort from the cursed ground, and Noah becomes the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

Genesis 6.overview: The sons of God take wives from among human women, and the Nephilim and mighty men arise as the LORD sees widespread human wickedness and resolves to blot out life, while Noah finds favor. God identifies Noah as righteous, announces the coming flood, gives him instructions for building the ark and preserving his family and animals, and establishes a covenant with him; Noah does everything commanded.

Genesis 7.overview: The LORD commands Noah to enter the ark with his family and specified pairs of animals, and Noah obeys as the flood begins. The waters rise over the earth, destroy every living thing on dry land, and prevail for 150 days, while Noah and those with him remain in the ark.

sections.heading: The Flood Begins and the Ark Is Sealed

Genesis 8.overview: God sends a wind, the floodwaters recede, and Noah tests the ground with birds before leaving the ark with his family and the animals. Noah offers sacrifices, and the LORD declares that he will not again destroy all living creatures by flood and that the earth’s seasons will continue.

Genesis 9.overview: God blesses Noah and his sons, permits animals as food while forbidding blood, and requires an accounting for human bloodshed. God establishes a covenant never again to destroy all life by flood, marked by the rainbow; Noah’s drunkenness leads to a curse on Canaan and blessings concerning Shem and Japheth, before Noah’s death at 950 years.

Genesis 10.overview: The chapter lists the descendants of Japheth, Ham, and Shem, tracing their clans, lands, languages, and nations. It records Nimrod’s kingdoms and cities, the borders of Canaan, and the spread of the nations across the earth after the flood.

sections.heading: Descendants of Shem and the Nations

Genesis 11.overview: The people of Shinar build a city and tower at Babel, but the LORD confuses their language and scatters them across the earth. Shem’s genealogy leads to Terah, whose family includes Abram, Nahor, Haran, and Lot; Terah leaves Ur for Canaan but settles in Haran, where he dies.

Genesis 12.overview: The LORD calls Abram to leave Haran, promises to make him a great nation and bless all families of the earth through him, and promises Canaan to his offspring. During a famine Abram goes to Egypt, presents Sarai as his sister, and leaves after the LORD afflicts Pharaoh’s household and Pharaoh sends them away.

Genesis 13.overview: Abram returns from Egypt to Bethel, where conflict between his and Lot’s herdsmen leads them to separate; Lot chooses the Jordan plain and settles near Sodom. The LORD promises Abram the land and numerous offspring, and Abram settles near Hebron and builds an altar.

Genesis 14.overview: Chedorlaomer and his allied kings defeat the rebellious kings of the Valley of Siddim, capture Lot, and lose their prisoners and plunder when Abram pursues and routs them. Melchizedek blesses Abram and receives a tenth, while Abram refuses the king of Sodom’s goods and allows his allies their share.

Genesis 15.overview: The LORD promises Abram an heir from his own body and offspring as numerous as the stars, and Abram believes Him. The LORD confirms His land promise through a covenant ceremony, foretelling Abram’s descendants’ enslavement and return before naming the land’s boundaries and peoples.

Genesis 16.overview: Sarai gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram after years without children; Hagar conceives, despises Sarai, and flees after Sarai mistreats her. The angel of the LORD finds Hagar, directs her to return, and promises many descendants and a son named Ishmael; Hagar names the LORD as the God who sees her, and she bears Ishmael to Abram.

Genesis 17.overview: God renews the covenant with Abram, renames him Abraham, promises nations and Canaan to his descendants, and commands circumcision as its sign. God renames Sarai Sarah and promises a son, Isaac, as the covenant heir while also promising to bless Ishmael; Abraham circumcises the males of his household.

Genesis 18.overview: The LORD visits Abraham at Mamre with two other men, announces that Sarah will have a son within a year, and tells Abraham that the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah has reached him. Abraham questions whether the righteous will be swept away with the wicked and secures the LORD’s agreement to spare Sodom if ten righteous people are found there.

Genesis 19.overview: Two angels visit Lot in Sodom, where the men of the city threaten them; the angels rescue Lot and his family and announce the city’s destruction. Lot reaches Zoar as the LORD destroys Sodom and Gomorrah, and the chapter ends with Lot’s daughters bearing Moab and Ben-ammi.

sections.heading: Lot and the Men of Sodom
Lot Is Led Out of Sodom

Genesis 20.overview: Abraham tells Abimelech, king of Gerar, that Sarah is his sister, and God warns Abimelech in a dream that Sarah is married and commands him to restore her. Abimelech confronts Abraham, then returns Sarah with gifts and land, and Abraham prays as God heals Abimelech’s household and restores its fertility.

Genesis 21.overview: The LORD fulfills his promise to Sarah, and Isaac is born and circumcised; after Sarah demands that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away, God promises to make Ishmael a nation and provides for them in the wilderness. Abraham and Abimelech make a covenant at Beersheba over a well, and Abraham settles in the land of the Philistines.

Genesis 22.overview: God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac at Moriah, but the angel of the LORD stops him and Abraham offers a ram instead. The LORD renews promises of descendants and blessing, Abraham returns to Beersheba, and the chapter lists Nahor’s descendants, including Rebekah.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Promise and Abraham’s Return

Genesis 23.overview: Sarah dies at age 127 in Hebron, and Abraham mourns her before asking the Hittites for a burial place. Abraham purchases Ephron’s field and cave at Machpelah, and the Hittites deed the property to him before he buries Sarah there.

Genesis 24.overview: Abraham sends his chief servant to his homeland to find a wife for Isaac, and the servant asks the LORD to guide him to the right woman. Rebekah answers the sign at the well, agrees to leave with the servant, and becomes Isaac’s wife in the Negev.

sections.heading: The Servant’s Account and Rebekah’s Betrothal

Genesis 25.overview: Abraham’s descendants through Keturah and Ishmael are recorded, and Abraham dies and is buried by Isaac and Ishmael at Machpelah; God blesses Isaac. Rebekah bears Esau and Jacob after Isaac prays, and Jacob obtains Esau’s birthright in exchange for food.

Genesis 26.overview: During a famine, the LORD renews Abraham’s promises to Isaac, who settles in Gerar and conceals Rebekah’s identity until Abimelech discovers the truth. Isaac prospers, faces disputes with the Philistines over wells, makes a covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba, and Esau’s Hittite wives bring grief to Isaac and Rebekah.

Genesis 27.overview: Isaac prepares to bless Esau, but Rebekah arranges for Jacob to pose as his brother and bring Isaac food. Isaac gives Jacob the blessing intended for Esau; Esau receives a lesser blessing and plots to kill Jacob, so Rebekah sends Jacob to Laban in Haran and raises her concern about Hittite wives.

sections.heading: Rebekah prepares Jacob to deceive Isaac

Genesis 28.overview: Isaac blesses Jacob, sends him to Paddan-aram to marry within Rebekah’s family, and repeats the promise of descendants and land; Esau responds by marrying Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael. On the way to Haran, Jacob dreams of a ladder between earth and heaven, receives the LORD’s promises of land, descendants, presence, and return, then names the place Bethel and vows to worship God and give a tenth.

sections.heading: Jacob’s Dream and the LORD’s Promise

Genesis 29.overview: Jacob arrives near Haran, meets Rachel at a well, and is welcomed by her father Laban, agreeing to serve seven years to marry her. Laban gives Jacob Leah instead of Rachel, then gives him Rachel after another agreement for seven years of service; Leah bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah while Rachel remains barren.

sections.heading: Laban Gives Jacob Leah and Rachel

Genesis 30.overview: Rachel and Leah compete for children through their servants Bilhah and Zilpah, while Leah bears Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah and Rachel bears Joseph. After Joseph’s birth, Jacob negotiates wages with Laban and uses a selective breeding strategy that leaves him with the stronger flocks and growing wealth.

Genesis 31.overview: Jacob, urged by God and supported by Rachel and Leah, leaves Laban with his family and possessions; Rachel takes Laban’s household idols, and Laban pursues them to Gilead. After Laban fails to find the idols, Jacob recounts his service and God’s protection, and the two establish a covenant marked by a mound and pillar before Laban returns home.

sections.heading: The search for the idols and Jacob’s defense
The covenant at Gilead and farewell

Genesis 32.overview: Jacob encounters God’s angels at Mahanaim, learns that Esau is approaching with four hundred men, prays for deliverance, and sends gifts ahead to seek Esau’s favor. At the Jabbok, Jacob wrestles with a man until daybreak, receives the name Israel and a blessing, and names the place Peniel after seeing God face to face; his injured hip becomes the basis for an Israelite food custom.

Genesis 33.overview: Jacob arranges his family before approaching Esau, and the brothers embrace and weep; Esau accepts Jacob’s gift. Esau returns toward Seir while Jacob travels to Succoth and then Shechem, where he buys land and builds an altar called El-Elohe-Israel.

sections.heading: Separate Journeys to Seir and Succoth

Genesis 34.overview: Shechem son of Hamor forces himself on Dinah, and Hamor and Shechem seek her marriage while offering intermarriage and settlement to Jacob’s family. Jacob’s sons deceitfully secure the circumcision of the city’s men, then Simeon and Levi kill the males and the other brothers plunder the city; Jacob objects to the danger, and they defend their response to the assault on Dinah.

sections.heading: Simeon and Levi attack the city

Genesis 35.overview: God directs Jacob to Bethel, where Jacob purifies his household, builds an altar, and receives a renewed name and promises from God. On the journey south Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, Reuben sleeps with Bilhah, Jacob’s twelve sons are listed, and Esau and Jacob bury Isaac at Hebron.

Genesis 36.overview: Esau’s wives and sons are named, and he settles in Mount Seir as his household and possessions separate from Jacob. The chapter lists Esau’s descendants and chiefs, the Horite clans of Seir, and the kings who reign in Edom before Israel has a king.

Genesis 37.overview: Joseph’s favored status and two dreams deepen his brothers’ hatred, and Jacob sends him from Hebron to find them near Shechem and Dothan. His brothers sell him to traders bound for Egypt, deceive Jacob with Joseph’s bloodied robe, and Joseph is sold to Potiphar.

sections.heading: Joseph Sent to Find His Brothers

Genesis 38.overview: Judah fathers Er, Onan, and Shelah, but the LORD puts Er and Onan to death, and Tamar remains a widow without being given to Shelah. Tamar disguises herself and conceives by Judah; when she reveals his seal, cord, and staff, Judah acknowledges his failure, and she gives birth to the twins Perez and Zerah.

sections.heading: The Birth of Perez and Zerah

Genesis 39.overview: Joseph prospers in Potiphar’s household, and Potiphar entrusts him with all he owns. After Potiphar’s wife falsely accuses Joseph, Potiphar sends him to prison, where the LORD remains with him and the warden places the prisoners in his care.

Genesis 40.overview: Pharaoh imprisons his cupbearer and chief baker alongside Joseph, and Joseph interprets their dreams as predicting their outcomes in three days. Pharaoh restores the cupbearer and executes the baker as Joseph foretells, but the cupbearer forgets Joseph.

sections.heading: The Baker’s Dream and Its Fulfillment

Genesis 41.overview: Pharaoh dreams of seven healthy cows and grain heads consumed by seven lean ones, and Joseph interprets the dreams as seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh appoints Joseph to oversee Egypt, Joseph stores grain during the abundant years, and when famine comes he sells grain to Egypt and the surrounding nations.

sections.heading: Pharaoh’s Dreams and the Cupbearer’s Reminder
Joseph Interprets the Dreams and Advises Pharaoh

Genesis 42.overview: During the famine, Jacob sends ten sons to Egypt for grain but keeps Benjamin at home. Joseph recognizes his brothers, accuses them of spying, demands that they bring Benjamin, detains Simeon, and secretly returns their silver; when they report this to Jacob, he refuses to send Benjamin.

Genesis 43.overview: As famine persists, Judah persuades Jacob to send Benjamin with his brothers to Egypt, and Jacob sends gifts and double silver with them. Joseph welcomes the brothers, reunites them with Simeon, conceals his identity as he questions them and weeps over Benjamin, then hosts them at a meal where they are seated by age and Benjamin receives five times the portion.

Genesis 44.overview: Joseph has his silver cup planted in Benjamin’s sack, then sends his steward after the brothers and brings them back to his house when the cup is found. Judah acknowledges that God has exposed their guilt and pleads for Benjamin’s release, offering to remain Joseph’s slave in his place so their father, Jacob, will not die of grief.

Genesis 45.overview: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers, explains that God sent him ahead to preserve life during the famine, and reconciles with them. Pharaoh offers land and provisions for Jacob’s household, and the brothers return to Canaan with the news, prompting Jacob to go to Egypt.

sections.heading: Joseph Reveals Himself to His Brothers

Genesis 46.overview: At Beersheba, God tells Jacob not to fear going to Egypt and promises to make his descendants a great nation there, accompany him, and bring him back; Jacob’s family and possessions travel from Canaan to Egypt, and the chapter lists his descendants and totals the family at seventy. In Goshen, Jacob reunites with Joseph, and Joseph instructs his family to tell Pharaoh that they raise livestock so they can settle there.

Genesis 47.overview: Joseph presents five of his brothers and Jacob to Pharaoh, who grants the family land in Goshen, while Joseph provides for them during the famine. Joseph gathers Egypt’s money, livestock, and land for Pharaoh in exchange for food and establishes a fifth of the harvest as Pharaoh’s share; Israel prospers in Goshen, and Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers.

Genesis 48.overview: As Jacob lies ill, he recalls God's promise at Luz, claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own, and recalls Rachel's burial near Ephrath. He blesses the boys with crossed hands, placing Ephraim before Manasseh, and gives Joseph a ridge of land while declaring that God will bring him back to the land of his fathers.

Genesis 49.overview: Jacob gathers his sons and speaks over them, describing Reuben, Simeon, and Levi’s losses, Judah’s rule, and the distinct fortunes of the remaining tribes, with special blessings for Joseph and a warrior’s image for Benjamin. He instructs his sons to bury him in the cave at Machpelah in Canaan, where his ancestors and Leah are buried, and then dies.

Genesis 50.overview: Joseph mourns Jacob, leads a large procession to bury him at Machpelah, and returns to Egypt. When his brothers fear his revenge, Joseph reassures them that God turns their evil intent toward preserving lives, and before Joseph dies in Egypt, he makes Israel’s sons swear to carry his bones to the promised land.

Exodus 1.overview: The descendants of Jacob, who entered Egypt as seventy people, multiply after Joseph and his generation die, and a new king enslaves them out of fear of their numbers. Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill newborn boys, but they let them live, and Pharaoh then commands all Egyptians to throw Hebrew sons into the Nile.

Exodus 2.overview: Moses is born to a Levite woman, rescued from the Nile by Pharaoh’s daughter, and raised as her son. After killing an Egyptian, he flees to Midian, marries Zipporah, and becomes a father, while Israel’s cries reach God, who remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Exodus 3.overview: At Horeb, the LORD appears to Moses in a burning bush, identifies himself as the God of the patriarchs, and commissions Moses to lead Israel out of Egypt. God reveals the name I AM, directs Moses to approach Israel’s elders and Pharaoh, and promises deliverance, a journey to Canaan, and Egyptian goods.

sections.heading: God’s Name and Instructions to Moses

Exodus 4.overview: The LORD gives Moses signs to answer Israel’s doubts, promises help with his speech, appoints Aaron as his spokesman, and warns that Pharaoh’s refusal to release Israel will bring the death of his firstborn. Moses returns toward Egypt with his family, Zipporah circumcises their son at a lodging place, and Aaron joins Moses to present the LORD’s words and signs to Israel’s elders, who believe and worship.

Exodus 5.overview: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go into the wilderness to worship the LORD, but Pharaoh refuses and increases the Israelites’ brickmaking burden by withholding straw. The Israelite foremen appeal to Pharaoh, then blame Moses and Aaron for their worsening plight, and Moses asks the LORD why he has sent him when Israel remains oppressed.

sections.heading: Straw Withheld and Brick Quotas Enforced
Foremen Appeal to Pharaoh and Confront Moses

Exodus 6.overview: The LORD promises to free Israel from Egyptian bondage, make the Israelites his people, and bring them into the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; they do not listen to Moses, and Moses questions whether Pharaoh will hear him. The LORD charges Moses and Aaron to bring Israel out, and a genealogy traces the families of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, identifying Aaron and Moses before the LORD repeats his command to Moses.

sections.heading: The families of Israel and Levi

Exodus 7.overview: The LORD commissions Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh, predicts Pharaoh’s resistance, and says Egypt will know that he is the LORD when he brings Israel out. Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent before Pharaoh, and Aaron then strikes the Nile, turning Egypt’s waters to blood; Pharaoh remains unmoved as the Egyptians seek drinking water and seven days pass.

Exodus 8.overview: The LORD sends frogs, gnats, and swarms of flies over Egypt through Moses and Aaron, while Pharaoh repeatedly hardens his heart and refuses to release Israel. Pharaoh asks for relief and offers limited permission to sacrifice, but the LORD distinguishes Goshen from Egypt during the fly plague and Pharaoh again breaks his promise.

sections.heading: The Plague of Flies and Pharaoh’s Refusal

Exodus 9.overview: The LORD sends a livestock plague and boils on Egypt, while distinguishing Israel from Egypt, but Pharaoh refuses to release the Israelites. The LORD sends devastating hail after warning Pharaoh’s officials; Pharaoh admits his wrongdoing and promises release, but hardens his heart again when the storm ends.

Exodus 10.overview: Moses and Aaron warn Pharaoh of a locust plague, while Pharaoh’s officials urge him to release Israel and Pharaoh offers to let only the men go. The locusts devastate Egypt and are removed after Pharaoh seeks relief, but he again refuses release; darkness then covers Egypt, and Pharaoh orders Moses away after demanding Israel leave its livestock behind.

sections.heading: Warning of Locusts and Pharaoh’s Offer

Exodus 11.overview: The LORD tells Moses that one final plague will lead Pharaoh to drive Israel out, and instructs the people to ask the Egyptians for silver and gold as Moses gains their favor. Moses announces the death of Egypt’s firstborn and the distinction between Egypt and Israel, while the LORD says Pharaoh will not listen and hardens his heart against releasing Israel.

sections.heading: The Final Plague and Egyptian Favor

Exodus 12.overview: The LORD gives Moses and Aaron instructions for the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and Moses relays them to Israel. After the LORD strikes Egypt’s firstborn, Pharaoh sends Israel away; the people depart with possessions and a mixed multitude, and the chapter sets out further Passover regulations as the LORD brings Israel out of Egypt.

sections.heading: The Firstborn Struck and Israel Departs

Exodus 13.overview: The LORD commands the consecration of Israel’s firstborn, and Moses instructs the people to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread and redeem their firstborn sons as memorials of the exodus from Egypt. God leads Israel away from the Philistine road toward the Red Sea, Moses carries Joseph’s bones, and pillars of cloud and fire guide the people.

sections.heading: Israel’s Route and the Guiding Pillars

Exodus 14.overview: The LORD directs Israel to camp by the sea, hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and sends the Egyptian army in pursuit; Moses tells the terrified Israelites that the LORD will fight for them. The LORD parts the sea so Israel crosses on dry ground, then returns the waters over Pharaoh’s army, and Israel sees the LORD’s power and believes in Him and Moses.

Exodus 15.overview: Moses and the Israelites sing of the LORD’s victory over Pharaoh’s army, and Miriam leads the women in a song celebrating the same deliverance. At Marah the LORD sweetens bitter water and gives Israel a statute and test, and the people then camp at Elim, where water and palm trees are plentiful.

sections.heading: Moses’ Song of the LORD’s Victory

Exodus 16.overview: Israel grumbles in the Desert of Sin over food, and the LORD promises quail and daily bread, with a double portion on the sixth day. Quail and manna arrive, the people receive instructions for gathering and Sabbath rest, and an omer of manna is preserved as the food sustains Israel until the border of Canaan.

sections.heading: Israel Grumbles and the LORD Promises Food
Quail and Manna in the Camp
The Sixth-Day Provision and Sabbath Rest

Exodus 17.overview: At Rephidim, Israel quarrels with Moses over the lack of water, and the LORD provides water from a rock at Horeb; Moses names the place Massah and Meribah. When Amalek attacks, Joshua leads Israel’s fight as Aaron and Hur support Moses, and the LORD commands a written reminder before Moses builds an altar and declares the LORD’s continuing war against Amalek.

sections.heading: Water from the Rock at Horeb

Exodus 18.overview: Jethro visits Moses in the wilderness with Zipporah and their sons, hears how the LORD delivered Israel from Egypt, and praises the LORD. Seeing Moses judge the people alone, Jethro advises him to appoint capable leaders to handle routine cases, and Moses adopts the arrangement before Jethro returns home.

sections.heading: Jethro Visits and Praises the LORD

Exodus 19.overview: Israel arrives at Mount Sinai, where the LORD offers the people a covenant calling them his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation, and they agree to obey. The LORD prepares to descend before the people amid thunder, fire, and a trembling mountain, while Moses receives repeated warnings to keep them from approaching the mountain.

sections.heading: Israel Arrives at Sinai and Accepts the Covenant
The LORD Descends and Sets Boundaries

Exodus 20.overview: The LORD identifies himself as Israel’s deliverer from Egypt and gives commandments concerning worship, the Sabbath, family, and conduct toward others. The Israelites fear the signs at Mount Sinai and ask Moses to speak for them, after which the LORD gives instructions for altars and offerings.

Exodus 21.overview: The ordinances address the release and treatment of Hebrew servants, penalties for violence and injury, and restitution for harm caused by animals or uncovered pits. They distinguish between intentional and accidental harm and set compensation or penalties for cases involving death, bodily injury, and property loss.

sections.heading: Restitution for Animal and Property Damage

Exodus 22.overview: The chapter sets out restitution and liability rules for theft, property damage, safekeeping, borrowed animals, and seduction, then prescribes penalties for sorcery, bestiality, and sacrifice to other gods. It gives commands concerning foreigners, widows, orphans, poor borrowers, pledges, offerings, firstborn, and the conduct expected of Israel as the LORD’s holy people.

Exodus 23.overview: The chapter sets out laws on truthful testimony, impartial justice, care for others, the land’s rest, the Sabbath, and the annual feasts. The LORD promises an angel’s guidance, protection, and blessing as Israel enters the land, while warning against its gods and covenants with its inhabitants.

sections.heading: The angel and the LORD’s promises
Conquest and boundaries of the land

Exodus 24.overview: Moses presents the LORD’s words to Israel, records the covenant, and seals it with offerings and blood after the people pledge obedience. Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and Israel’s elders see God, and Moses then ascends Mount Sinai to receive the stone tablets and remains there forty days and nights.

Exodus 25.overview: The LORD tells Moses to collect offerings from the Israelites and directs them to build a sanctuary according to the pattern shown on the mountain. He specifies the ark and mercy seat, the table for the Bread of the Presence, and the gold lampstand and its utensils.

sections.heading: The Table and Bread of the Presence

Exodus 26.overview: The instructions specify the tabernacle’s linen and goat-hair curtains, outer coverings, acacia frames, silver bases, and gold crossbars. They describe the inner veil separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, the placement of the ark, mercy seat, table, and lampstand, and the entrance curtain and its posts.

Exodus 27.overview: The chapter gives instructions for a bronze altar, including its utensils, grate, and carrying poles, and sets out the dimensions and materials of the tabernacle courtyard. It also directs the Israelites to provide pure olive oil and assigns Aaron and his sons to tend the lamps in the Tent of Meeting from evening until morning.

Exodus 28.overview: The LORD directs Moses to appoint Aaron and his sons as priests and to have skilled craftsmen make their holy garments. The instructions describe the ephod and breastpiece bearing Israel’s tribal names, the robe and headpiece marked “HOLY TO THE LORD,” and garments for Aaron’s sons, along with requirements for consecration and service.

sections.heading: Aaron and His Sons as Priests

Exodus 29.overview: The LORD instructs Moses to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests through washing, vesting, anointing, and a seven-day sequence of sacrifices and offerings. He establishes daily offerings at the Tent of Meeting and promises to meet Israel there, consecrate the sanctuary and priests, and dwell among the people as their God.

Exodus 30.overview: The LORD instructs Moses to make the incense altar and establish its daily use and annual atonement, require a half-shekel ransom from counted Israelites, and provide a bronze basin for priestly washing. He gives the formula and restrictions for the sacred anointing oil and incense, and directs that the Tabernacle furnishings and Aaron and his sons be consecrated.

Exodus 31.overview: The LORD appoints Bezalel and Oholiab and equips them and the other craftsmen to make the sanctuary, its furnishings, priestly garments, anointing oil, and incense. He commands Israel to keep the Sabbath as a permanent covenant sign, then gives Moses the stone tablets of the Testimony on Mount Sinai.

sections.heading: The Sabbath as a Covenant Sign

Exodus 32.overview: While Moses is on the mountain, the Israelites make and worship a golden calf, and the LORD tells Moses that the people have corrupted themselves. Moses intercedes for them, breaks the tablets when he reaches the camp, directs the Levites to kill about three thousand people, and later pleads for forgiveness as the LORD promises judgment and sends a plague.

Exodus 33.overview: The LORD tells Moses to lead Israel toward the promised land, but says his presence will not go with the stiff-necked people; Israel mourns, and Moses meets the LORD at the Tent of Meeting outside the camp. Moses asks for the LORD’s presence and glory, and the LORD promises to go with him, proclaim his name and goodness, and shield Moses in a cleft of rock so he sees only the LORD’s back.

sections.heading: Moses Asks to See the LORD’s Glory

Exodus 34.overview: The LORD tells Moses to prepare new stone tablets, reveals his compassionate and just character on Mount Sinai, and renews the covenant with Israel through commands and festivals. After Moses spends forty days with the LORD and receives the covenant words, he descends with a radiant face and veils it when he is not speaking with the LORD.

sections.heading: New Tablets and the LORD’s Character

Exodus 35.overview: Moses instructs Israel to observe the Sabbath and bring willing offerings and skilled labor for the tabernacle, its furnishings, and priestly garments. The Israelites contribute materials, and Moses identifies Bezalel and Oholiab, whom the LORD equips with skill and ability to teach others.

Exodus 36.overview: Moses commissions Bezalel, Oholiab, and the skilled workers, who receive more offerings than the sanctuary work requires, so Moses stops further contributions. The workers make the tabernacle curtains and coverings, its acacia frames and crossbars, the inner veil, and the entrance curtain with their supports.

Exodus 37.overview: Bezalel constructs the ark and mercy seat, the gold-covered table and its utensils, and the hammered-gold lampstand with its lamps. He makes the gold-covered altar of incense and its carrying poles, along with the sacred anointing oil and fragrant incense.

Exodus 38.overview: Bezalel makes the bronze altar and basin, then constructs the courtyard and its embroidered entrance. The chapter records the tabernacle inventory under Ithamar’s direction, names Bezalel and Oholiab as craftsmen, and accounts for the gold, silver, and bronze used in the work.

Exodus 39.overview: Bezalel and the Israelites make Aaron’s ephod, breastpiece, robe, and other priestly garments with the materials and details commanded by the LORD. They complete the tabernacle work, bring its furnishings and garments to Moses, and he inspects the work and blesses them.

Exodus 40.overview: The LORD instructs Moses to set up and consecrate the tabernacle, its furnishings, and Aaron and his sons for priestly service, and Moses carries out the commands. The cloud covers the Tent of Meeting and the LORD’s glory fills the tabernacle, while the cloud and fire guide Israel’s journeys.

sections.heading: Instructions for the Tabernacle and Priests
The LORD’s Glory and Israel’s Guidance

Leviticus 1.overview: The LORD speaks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and instructs the Israelites on presenting burnt offerings from the herd, flock, or birds. The chapter describes how the offerer and priests prepare each animal and burn it on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.

Leviticus 2.overview: The chapter prescribes grain offerings of fine flour and baked preparations, with the priests burning a memorial portion and giving the remainder to Aaron and his sons. It prohibits leaven and honey on the altar, requires salt in every grain offering, and specifies the offering of firstfruits.

Leviticus 3.overview: The chapter prescribes peace offerings from the herd, flock, and goats, detailing the animal’s presentation, slaughter, blood, and fat portions burned on the altar. It declares all fat to belong to the LORD and forbids eating fat or blood as a lasting statute.

sections.heading: Goat Offering and Prohibition on Fat and Blood

Leviticus 4.overview: The LORD instructs Moses on offerings for unintentional sins, prescribing a bull and detailed blood and fat rites when the anointed priest sins or the whole congregation incurs guilt. A leader brings a male goat, while a common person brings a female goat or lamb; the priest makes atonement, and the sinner is forgiven.

Leviticus 5.overview: The chapter addresses guilt from withholding testimony, contact with uncleanness, and rash oaths, prescribing confession and offerings scaled to a person’s means. It then requires restitution and a ram as a guilt offering for unintentional offenses against the LORD’s holy things or commandments.

sections.heading: Guilt and offerings scaled to means

Leviticus 6.overview: The LORD requires a person who defrauds a neighbor to make full restitution, add a fifth, and bring a guilt offering for atonement and forgiveness. He gives Moses instructions for the burnt offering, the grain offerings of Aaron and his sons, and the handling of the sin offering, including when it must be burned rather than eaten.

Leviticus 7.overview: The chapter gives the laws for guilt offerings and peace offerings, including their preparation, consumption, and distribution among the priests. The LORD prohibits eating animal fat and blood, assigns portions of peace offerings to Aaron and his sons, and identifies these instructions as given to Moses at Sinai.

sections.heading: Prohibitions Against Eating Fat and Blood
Priestly Portions and Summary of Offering Laws

Leviticus 8.overview: At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, Moses washes and clothes Aaron and his sons, anoints them and the tabernacle, and performs the sin, burnt, and ordination offerings as the LORD commands. Moses consecrates the priests, instructs them to eat the ordination offering and remain at the Tent for seven days, and Aaron and his sons do everything commanded through Moses.

sections.heading: Aaron and his sons are consecrated
Seven days at the Tent of Meeting

Leviticus 9.overview: On the eighth day, Moses directs Aaron and the Israelites to present offerings so the LORD’s glory will appear, and Aaron performs the prescribed sacrifices for himself and the people. Moses and Aaron bless the people, the LORD’s glory appears, and fire consumes the altar offerings as the people shout and fall facedown.

Leviticus 10.overview: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD and die, while Moses directs Aaron and his remaining sons on mourning and their duties at the Tent of Meeting. The LORD instructs Aaron on drink, discernment, and teaching, and Moses later accepts Aaron’s explanation for not eating the sin offering.

sections.heading: Aaron Explains the Un eaten Offering

Leviticus 11.overview: The LORD gives Moses and Aaron rules for distinguishing clean and unclean animals, identifying permitted and forbidden creatures on land, in water, among birds, and among insects. He also sets out how contact with carcasses causes uncleanness and grounds Israel’s holiness in his own holiness and deliverance from Egypt.

sections.heading: Holiness and Distinguishing Clean from Unclean

Leviticus 12.overview: The LORD instructs Moses that a woman who gives birth is unclean for a prescribed period, with different purification periods after the birth of a son and a daughter. After purification, she brings offerings to the priest at the Tent of Meeting for atonement and cleansing, with birds permitted in place of a lamb if she cannot afford one.

Leviticus 13.overview: The LORD gives Moses and Aaron procedures for priests to examine skin conditions, using signs and periods of isolation to pronounce people clean or unclean. The chapter also sets rules for mildew in fabrics and leather, including isolation, washing, removal, or burning, and concludes with the law for declaring such articles clean or unclean.

Leviticus 14.overview: The LORD gives Moses the procedures for cleansing a person healed of a skin disease, including a reduced offering for someone who is poor. He also gives Moses and Aaron rules for inspecting, repairing, or removing a house with mildew, its cleansing ritual, and the concluding laws for distinguishing clean from unclean conditions.

Leviticus 15.overview: The LORD instructs Moses and Aaron on uncleanness caused by male discharges, semen, menstruation, and prolonged female bleeding, including its effects on people and objects. The chapter prescribes washing, waiting periods, and offerings for purification, and warns Israel to guard the tabernacle from defilement.

Leviticus 16.overview: The LORD instructs Moses on Aaron’s restricted entry into the Most Holy Place and the offerings, blood rites, and live scapegoat used to make atonement for himself, his household, Israel, and the sanctuary. The chapter establishes the annual Day of Atonement, including the people’s rest and the high priest’s duties, as a permanent statute.

Leviticus 17.overview: The LORD commands Israelites to bring animal sacrifices to the Tent of Meeting, where priests offer them to the LORD, and forbids sacrifices to goat demons. He prohibits eating blood because life is in the blood and it makes atonement, and prescribes purification for anyone who eats an animal found dead or mauled.

sections.heading: Sacrifices at the Tent of Meeting

Leviticus 18.overview: The LORD tells Moses to instruct Israel to reject the customs of Egypt and Canaan and to keep the LORD’s statutes. He prohibits specified sexual relations, child sacrifice to Molech, and bestiality, then warns that these practices defile the land and bring expulsion and punishment.

sections.heading: Israel’s Call to Keep the LORD’s Laws

Leviticus 19.overview: The LORD tells Moses to command Israel to be holy, setting out rules for worship, harvest gleanings, honest dealings, justice, and love of neighbor. Further statutes address mixed kinds, a guilt offering, fruit trees, prohibited practices, reverence for the sanctuary and elders, treatment of foreigners, and honest measures.

sections.heading: Honesty, Justice, and Love of Neighbor
Mixed Kinds, Guilt Offering, and Fruit Trees

Leviticus 20.overview: The LORD commands Israel to put to death those who give children to Molech, consult mediums or spiritists, curse parents, or commit specified sexual offenses, and warns that neglecting these laws brings judgment. He calls Israel to keep his statutes, distinguish clean from unclean, and remain holy as he sets the people apart to inherit the land.

Leviticus 21.overview: The LORD gives Moses rules for the priests’ mourning, bodily practices, marriages, and holiness, with stricter requirements for the high priest and his family. He bars Aaron’s descendants with physical defects from offering sacrifices or approaching the altar and veil, while allowing them to eat the holy food; Moses relays the rules to Aaron, his sons, and Israel.

Leviticus 22.overview: The LORD instructs Moses on priests’ fitness to eat sacred offerings, who may share them, and how accidental consumption is to be made good. He then sets requirements for acceptable animal offerings, including rules for young animals and thank offerings, and calls Israel to keep his commands and honor his holy name.

Leviticus 23.overview: The LORD gives Moses Israel’s appointed times, including the weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, firstfruits and the Feast of Weeks, the trumpet assembly, and the Day of Atonement. He sets out the Feast of Tabernacles and its offerings, rest, rejoicing, and booths, directs that harvest gleanings be left for the poor and foreign resident, and Moses announces the feasts to Israel.

sections.heading: Trumpet Assembly and Day of Atonement
Feast of Tabernacles and Final Announcement

Leviticus 24.overview: The LORD instructs Moses on the continual tending of the lamps and the Sabbath presentation of twelve loaves for Aaron and his sons. After a man who blasphemes the Name is held in custody, the LORD gives Moses laws on blasphemy, killing, restitution, and equal justice, and the Israelites stone the man as commanded.

Leviticus 25.overview: The LORD instructs Moses on Mount Sinai to establish sabbatical years and the Jubilee, when liberty is proclaimed, property returns to its original clan, and land prices reflect the years remaining until Jubilee. He sets rules for redeeming land and houses and for supporting impoverished Israelites, including limits on debt, servitude, and harsh treatment, because the Israelites are his servants.

Leviticus 26.overview: The LORD warns Israel against idols and commands Sabbath observance, then promises rain, safety, victory, abundance, and his presence if the people keep his statutes. He describes escalating covenant punishments for disobedience, but promises to remember his covenants with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob if the exiles confess their iniquity, and concludes by identifying these laws as those given through Moses at Mount Sinai.

Leviticus 27.overview: The LORD instructs Moses on valuations for persons, animals, houses, and fields dedicated by vow, including redemption payments and rules for land at the Jubilee. He sets rules for firstborn animals, irrevocably devoted things, and tithes, then identifies these commands as given to Moses for Israel at Mount Sinai.

Numbers 1.overview: At the LORD’s command in the Wilderness of Sinai, Moses and Aaron count Israel’s men aged twenty and older who can serve in the army, with twelve tribal leaders assisting; the total is 603,550. The Levites are excluded from the census and assigned to carry, maintain, and guard the tabernacle, while the other Israelites camp by their divisions, and the people carry out the LORD’s commands.

Numbers 2.overview: The LORD instructs Moses and Aaron to arrange Israel’s tribes around the Tent of Meeting under four standards, with Judah’s camp to the east, Reuben’s to the south, Ephraim’s to the west, and Dan’s to the north. The chapter gives each camp’s tribal leaders and numbers, sets their order of travel with the Levites and Tent of Meeting in the center, and reports that the Israelites follow the arrangement while the Levites remain uncounted among them.

sections.heading: Dan’s camp on the north and Israel’s order

Numbers 3.overview: The chapter names Aaron’s sons and assigns the Levites to assist the priests, replacing Israel’s firstborn because the firstborn belong to the LORD. Moses counts the Levite clans and their tabernacle duties, then counts Israel’s firstborn and collects redemption money for the 273 who exceed the Levites.

sections.heading: Aaron’s Sons and the Levites’ Appointment

Numbers 4.overview: The LORD directs Moses and Aaron to count the Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites aged thirty to fifty who serve at the Tent of Meeting, and assigns each clan its transport duties under priestly oversight. Moses, Aaron, and Israel’s leaders count 8,580 Levites and assign each man his work and burden as the LORD commands.

sections.heading: Census and Assignment of the Levites

Numbers 5.overview: The LORD commands Israel to remove people with specified impurities from the camp and sets rules for confession, restitution, and sacred gifts. He establishes a priestly procedure for a husband’s suspicion of his wife’s adultery, including an oath and bitter water whose effects distinguish guilt from innocence.

sections.heading: The Bitter Water and Its Outcomes

Numbers 6.overview: The LORD gives Moses the regulations for a Nazirite vow, including its restrictions, cleansing after accidental defilement, and offerings and rites at the vow’s completion. He then instructs Moses to have Aaron and his sons bless Israel, promising to place his name on the people and bless them.

sections.heading: Defilement and Completion of the Vow

Numbers 7.overview: After the tabernacle and altar are consecrated, Israel’s leaders provide six carts and twelve oxen for the Levites’ work, with none assigned to the Kohathites. Over twelve days, each tribal leader presents an identical dedication offering for the altar, whose offerings are totaled, and Moses hears the LORD’s voice from above the ark’s mercy seat.

sections.heading: Offering Totals and the LORD’s Voice

Numbers 8.overview: The LORD directs Aaron to arrange the lampstand’s seven lamps, then instructs Moses on cleansing and presenting the Levites for service in place of Israel’s firstborn. Moses, Aaron, and Israel carry out the instructions, and the LORD sets the Levites’ service ages and retirement duties.

sections.heading: Cleansing and Presentation of the Levites

Numbers 9.overview: In the Wilderness of Sinai, the Israelites observe Passover at the appointed time, and the LORD provides a second-month observance for those unclean from a dead body or away on a journey, while requiring the same statutes for foreigners and native Israelites. The cloud covers the tabernacle and appears like fire at night, directing when Israel camps and sets out at the LORD’s command through Moses.

Numbers 10.overview: The LORD instructs Moses to make silver trumpets for assembling Israel, signaling the camps to march, and marking battles and occasions of worship. As the cloud lifts, Israel follows its ordered divisions from Sinai toward Paran; Moses invites Hobab to join them, and he speaks when the ark sets out and comes to rest.

Numbers 11.overview: After the people complain about hardship and crave meat, the LORD sends fire and later promises meat, while Moses protests the burden of leading Israel. The LORD appoints seventy elders to share Moses’ burden, gives them the Spirit, sends quail, and strikes the people with a plague at Kibroth-hattaavah before Israel moves to Hazeroth.

sections.heading: The people crave meat and Moses protests

Numbers 12.overview: Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses over his Cushite wife and question whether the LORD speaks only through him. The LORD affirms Moses’ unique role, afflicts Miriam with leprosy, orders her confinement for seven days, and the people then travel from Hazeroth to the Wilderness of Paran.

Numbers 13.overview: The LORD commands Moses to send twelve tribal leaders from Kadesh to scout Canaan, and Moses gives Hoshea the name Joshua. After forty days, the scouts return with fruit and report that the land is fertile but its fortified cities and powerful inhabitants make conquest seem impossible, while Caleb urges the people to take possession of it.

sections.heading: The Scouts Report on the Land
Caleb’s Challenge and the Bad Report

Numbers 14.overview: The Israelites reject Joshua and Caleb’s report, grumble against Moses and Aaron, and threaten to stone the two spies, prompting the LORD to announce judgment. Moses intercedes, and the LORD pardons the people but decrees that the adult generation will die in the wilderness while Caleb, Joshua, and the children will enter the land; after the scouts are struck by a plague, the Israelites attempt to advance without the LORD and are routed at Hormah.

sections.heading: The people reject Joshua and Caleb
Moses intercedes and the LORD responds
The wilderness judgment and the scouts’ fate
The failed advance into the hill country

Numbers 15.overview: The LORD gives Moses regulations for grain and drink offerings in the land, including equal requirements for native Israelites and resident foreigners, and instructions for offerings when the community or an individual sins unintentionally. He distinguishes defiant sin, commands the execution of a man who gathers wood on the Sabbath, and orders Israel to wear tassels as reminders of his commandments.

Numbers 16.overview: Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and 250 leaders challenge Moses and Aaron’s authority, and Moses proposes a test before the LORD while Dathan and Abiram refuse his summons. The earth swallows the rebels, fire consumes the incense offerers, their censers become an altar covering, and Aaron’s incense halts a plague after 14,700 people die.

sections.heading: Korah’s Challenge to Moses and Aaron
Dathan and Abiram Refuse; Judgment Falls

Numbers 17.overview: The LORD tells Moses to collect twelve tribal staffs and place them before the Testimony, declaring that the chosen man’s staff will sprout. Aaron’s staff sprouts and bears almonds, the LORD commands it to be kept as a sign against grumbling, and the Israelites fear that anyone approaching the tabernacle will die.

Numbers 18.overview: The LORD assigns Aaron and his sons responsibility for the priesthood and sanctuary, with the Levites assisting in the Tent of Meeting under defined limits. He gives Aaron’s household portions of Israel’s offerings, assigns the Levites Israel’s tithes instead of land inheritance, and requires them to offer a tenth of those tithes to the LORD for Aaron.

Numbers 19.overview: The LORD instructs Moses and Aaron on preparing and keeping the ashes of an unblemished red heifer as water for purification, including the duties and temporary uncleanness of those involved. The chapter sets out how people and objects made unclean by contact with a corpse are purified on the third and seventh days, and the consequences of failing to be purified.

sections.heading: The Red Heifer and Its Ashes
Uncleanness from Contact with the Dead

Numbers 20.overview: At Kadesh, Miriam dies, and Israel complains over the lack of water; Moses strikes the rock, water flows, and the LORD says Moses and Aaron will not lead Israel into the land. Edom refuses Israel passage through its territory, and at Mount Hor Aaron transfers his priestly garments to Eleazar, dies, and is mourned by Israel for thirty days.

sections.heading: Water from the Rock at Meribah

Numbers 21.overview: Israel defeats the Canaanite king of Arad, then complains during the journey from Mount Hor and survives the venomous snakes by looking at Moses’ bronze serpent; the Israelites travel through the wilderness and sing at the well God provides. Israel defeats Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, takes their territories, and occupies the land from the Arnon to Bashan.

Numbers 22.overview: Balak, king of Moab, summons Balaam to curse Israel, but God first forbids him and then permits him to go only with strict instructions. On the journey the angel of the LORD confronts Balaam, who reaches Moab and tells Balak he can speak only what God puts in his mouth.

Numbers 23.overview: At Balak’s direction, Balaam offers sacrifices and delivers an oracle declaring that he cannot curse Israel, whom God has not cursed. After a second set of sacrifices, Balaam proclaims God’s unchangeable blessing and Israel’s strength, while Balak takes him to Peor for another attempt.

Numbers 24.overview: Balaam sees Israel encamped and, moved by the Spirit of God, blesses Israel in an oracle describing its prosperity and strength; Balak angrily dismisses him, and Balaam insists that he can speak only what the LORD commands. Balaam then foretells a ruler from Israel who will strike Moab and Edom, pronounces further oracles against Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur, and Eber, and returns home as Balak departs.

Numbers 25.overview: At Shittim, Israel joins Moabite worship of Baal of Peor, and the LORD commands judgment as a plague strikes the people. Phinehas kills Zimri and Cozbi, halting the plague, and the LORD grants him a covenant of peace and permanent priesthood while commanding Israel to attack Midian.

sections.heading: The Victims Named and Midian Targeted

Numbers 26.overview: After the plague, the LORD directs Moses and Eleazar to count Israel’s military-age men by tribe on the plains of Moab, recording 601,730 and noting the clans of the Levites separately. The LORD assigns tribal inheritances according to population and by lot, while the chapter states that none counted in the earlier wilderness census remains except Caleb and Joshua.

Numbers 27.overview: The daughters of Zelophehad ask for an inheritance, and the LORD rules that they may inherit and establishes an order of succession for cases without sons. The LORD tells Moses he will die before entering the land, and Moses commissions Joshua as Israel’s leader.

sections.heading: Moses’s Death and Request for a Successor

Numbers 28.overview: The LORD prescribes daily, Sabbath, and monthly burnt offerings, including their grain and drink offerings and a goat for the monthly sin offering. He also specifies the offerings and sacred assemblies for Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread and for the Feast of Weeks and its firstfruits.

Numbers 29.overview: The LORD prescribes offerings for the seventh month: the trumpet day on the first, the day of atonement on the tenth, and the seven-day Feast of Tabernacles beginning on the fifteenth, with the number of bulls decreasing each day. He sets out the offerings for the solemn assembly on the eighth day, and Moses conveys all the instructions to Israel.

sections.heading: Offerings for the Day of Atonement
Offerings for the Feast of Tabernacles

Numbers 30.overview: Moses gives Israel’s tribal heads rules requiring a man to fulfill his vows and describing when a father or husband may nullify a woman’s vow. Vows made by widows and divorced women remain binding, while a husband’s silence confirms his wife’s vow and delayed nullification makes him bear her iniquity.

sections.heading: Vows of Widows and Married Women

Numbers 31.overview: At the LORD’s command, Israel’s forces led by Phinehas defeat Midian, kill its kings and Balaam, and bring captives and plunder to the camp in Moab. Moses orders the captives and goods purified and apportioned, with tributes for Eleazar and the Levites, and receives the officers’ gold offering for the Tent of Meeting.

sections.heading: Division of the Captives and Plunder

Numbers 32.overview: The Reubenites and Gadites ask Moses, Eleazar, and Israel’s leaders to possess the livestock-suitable land east of the Jordan, and Moses warns that their withdrawal could discourage Israel as their fathers did. They pledge to fight alongside the other tribes before settling their families east of the Jordan; Moses assigns land to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, and the tribes build cities and capture territory in Gilead and Bashan.

Numbers 33.overview: Moses records Israel’s journey from Rameses through successive wilderness camps to the plains of Moab, including Aaron’s death on Mount Hor. There the LORD commands Israel to drive out Canaan’s inhabitants, destroy their idols, take and divide the land, and warns of the consequences if they leave the inhabitants in place.

sections.heading: Aaron’s Death and Arrival in Moab

Numbers 34.overview: The LORD defines Canaan’s southern, western, northern, and eastern boundaries as the inheritance of Israel’s nine and a half tribes, noting that Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh already receive land east of the Jordan. The LORD names Eleazar, Joshua, and one leader from each tribe to apportion the inheritance.

Numbers 35.overview: The LORD commands Israel to give the Levites forty-eight cities with pasturelands, including six cities of refuge. He establishes rules distinguishing murder from accidental killing, governing refuge and judgment, and forbidding ransom for murderers or premature release from refuge, because bloodshed pollutes the land where the LORD dwells.

Numbers 36.overview: The clan heads of Gilead raise the concern that Zelophehad’s daughters’ inheritance could pass to another tribe if they marry outside their father’s tribe. Moses rules that women who inherit land must marry within their father’s tribe, and Zelophehad’s daughters marry within Manasseh so their inheritance remains there; the chapter closes with a notice of the commandments given on the plains of Moab.

sections.heading: Moses’ Ruling on Marriage and Inheritance

Deuteronomy 1.overview: Moses addresses Israel in Moab after defeating Sihon and Og, recalls the LORD’s command to leave Horeb, and explains the appointment of tribal leaders and judges. He recounts Israel’s refusal to enter the land after the spies’ report, the LORD’s judgment on that generation, and the failed attack that leaves Israel at Kadesh.

sections.heading: Departure from Horeb and Appointed Leaders

Deuteronomy 2.overview: Moses recounts Israel’s journey past Seir, Moab, and Ammon, where the LORD forbids taking the lands given to Esau’s and Lot’s descendants and marks the passing of the wilderness generation. The LORD gives Sihon king of Heshbon and his land to Israel after Sihon refuses passage, and Israel defeats him while avoiding the forbidden territory of Ammon.

sections.heading: Moab, Ammon, and the Nations Before Them

Deuteronomy 3.overview: Moses recounts Israel’s defeat of Og, king of Bashan, and the division of the conquered territory among Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. He recalls commanding the eastern tribes to aid Israel’s campaign, commissioning Joshua, and asking the LORD to cross the Jordan, a request the LORD denies while directing Moses to view the land and strengthen Joshua.

sections.heading: Defeat of Og and Conquest of Bashan
Moses’ Request and the LORD’s Response

Deuteronomy 4.overview: Moses urges Israel to keep the LORD’s commandments, recalls the covenant and the LORD’s revelation at Horeb, and warns against making idols. He describes the consequences of apostasy and the hope of return, affirms that the LORD alone is God, sets apart three cities of refuge, and identifies the land and setting of his instruction.

sections.heading: Commandments and the Covenant at Horeb

Deuteronomy 5.overview: Moses recalls the covenant made with Israel at Horeb and restates the commandments given there. After Israel asks Moses to mediate because of the fire and God’s voice, the LORD directs him to teach the people and commands Israel to follow his ways in the land.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Instructions to Moses and Israel

Deuteronomy 6.overview: Moses instructs Israel to hear and keep the LORD’s commandments, declaring that the LORD is one and calling Israel to love him wholly and teach his words to their children. He warns Israel not to forget the LORD or follow other gods in the promised land, and directs parents to explain the commandments through the account of Israel’s deliverance from Egypt.

Deuteronomy 7.overview: Moses instructs Israel to destroy the nations in the land, avoid treaties and intermarriage, and remove their altars and idols. He grounds Israel’s status in the LORD’s love and covenant, promises blessing for obedience, and assures Israel that the LORD will drive out its enemies while warning against fear and idolatry.

sections.heading: Israel’s Election and the LORD’s Covenant
Blessings and the Removal of the Nations
Assurance of Victory and Warning Against Idols

Deuteronomy 8.overview: Moses recalls how the LORD humbled and tested Israel in the wilderness, sustained them, and led them toward the promised land. He warns Israel to keep the LORD’s commands, remember the source of its prosperity, and avoid idolatry, which would bring destruction.

Deuteronomy 9.overview: Moses warns Israel not to credit its righteousness for possessing the land, since the LORD drives out its wicked nations and keeps his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He recounts Israel’s rebellion at Horeb and elsewhere, the making and destruction of the golden calf, and his intercession for Israel and Aaron, appealing to God’s covenant and reputation among the nations.

sections.heading: The LORD drives out the nations

Deuteronomy 10.overview: Moses recounts the replacement tablets and their placement in the ark, the Israelites’ journey and Aaron’s death, Levi’s duties, and the LORD’s decision not to destroy Israel. He calls Israel to love and serve the LORD, keep his commands, love the foreigner, and remember the LORD’s justice, choice of Israel, wonders, and growth from seventy people in Egypt.

Deuteronomy 11.overview: Moses recalls the LORD’s mighty acts for Israel and contrasts Egypt’s irrigation with the land of Canaan, which depends on rain and receives the LORD’s care. He sets out the blessings of obedience and the consequences of turning to other gods, commands Israel to proclaim blessing and curse on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and urges the people to keep the LORD’s statutes and ordinances.

sections.heading: The LORD’s mighty acts for Israel
The land and the conditions of blessing
Remembering the commands and possessing the land

Deuteronomy 12.overview: Moses commands Israel to destroy Canaanite worship sites and bring offerings to the place the LORD chooses for His Name. He distinguishes ordinary meat from sacred offerings, forbids consuming blood, and warns Israel against adopting the nations’ worship practices or altering his commands.

Deuteronomy 13.overview: Moses warns Israel against prophets who promote worship of other gods and prescribes their execution, then addresses enticement to idolatry by a close relative or friend and prescribes communal stoning. He requires thorough investigation before a city that turns to other gods is destroyed, with its plunder burned, and links Israel’s obedience to the LORD’s mercy and compassion.

sections.heading: Enticement by a Relative or Friend
Cities That Turn to Other Gods

Deuteronomy 14.overview: Moses identifies Israel as the LORD’s holy, chosen people and gives rules for mourning and clean and unclean foods. He commands annual tithes for worship at the chosen place and a tithe every third year for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow.

sections.heading: Israel as the LORD’s chosen people

Deuteronomy 15.overview: Moses commands Israel to cancel debts every seventh year, lend generously to the poor, and release Hebrew servants after six years with provisions, recalling the LORD’s redemption of Israel from Egypt and promising blessing. He also requires Israel to set apart firstborn male livestock for the LORD, eat it yearly at the chosen place, and exclude defective animals from sacrifice and blood from food.

Deuteronomy 16.overview: Moses gives Israel instructions for Passover, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles, including their appointed place, offerings, and participation. He also commands the appointment of impartial judges and forbids Asherah poles and sacred pillars beside the LORD’s altar.

Deuteronomy 17.overview: The chapter forbids defective offerings and sets procedures for investigating and punishing idolatry, requiring multiple witnesses and the participation of the people. It directs difficult cases to the Levitical priests and judge, then limits a king’s power and requires him to keep and obey the law.

sections.heading: Limits and Duties of the King

Deuteronomy 18.overview: Moses specifies the Levites’ provisions and equal standing in service, and prohibits Israel from adopting the divination and occult practices of the nations. He recounts Israel’s request at Horeb for a prophet like himself, then states that God will hold hearers accountable and that a prophet whose prediction fails has not spoken for the LORD.

Deuteronomy 19.overview: The chapter establishes refuge cities for accidental manslayers, distinguishes them from intentional killers, and provides for three additional cities if Israel’s territory expands. It prohibits moving boundary markers and requires multiple witnesses, thorough investigation of false testimony, and punishment matching the harm intended.

Deuteronomy 20.overview: The chapter directs Israel’s priest and officers to encourage the army, excuse men with unfinished domestic commitments or fear, and appoint commanders. It distinguishes the treatment of distant cities from the nations of Canaan and limits the use of fruit trees during a siege.

sections.heading: Encouragement and exemptions for the army

Deuteronomy 21.overview: The chapter prescribes an atonement rite for an unsolved killing and rules for a captive woman taken as a wife, inheritance rights for a firstborn son, and a rebellious son. It also requires the burial that same day of anyone executed and hung on a tree, so the land is not defiled.

sections.heading: A Captive Woman Taken as a Wife
The Firstborn’s Rights and a Rebellious Son

Deuteronomy 22.overview: Moses gives laws concerning lost property and fallen animals, clothing, bird nests, house safety, mixed seeds and materials, and garment tassels. He sets out legal outcomes for accusations about a wife’s virginity, adultery, sexual encounters involving betrothed women, and a man’s marriage to his father’s wife.

Deuteronomy 23.overview: Moses sets rules for entry into the assembly of the LORD, distinguishing among excluded groups, Ammonites and Moabites, and Edomites and Egyptians. He gives laws for camp purity, protected fugitives, worship and lending, vows, and taking food from a neighbor’s field.

Deuteronomy 24.overview: Moses sets out laws concerning divorce and remarriage, a newly married man’s exemption from duty, security for debt, kidnapping, skin disease, lending, wages, and individual responsibility. He also commands justice for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, including leaving part of the harvest for them, recalling Israel’s slavery in Egypt as the basis for these laws.

Deuteronomy 25.overview: The chapter sets limits on flogging, protects an ox at work, establishes a brother’s duty to preserve a dead man’s name, prescribes punishment for a woman who intervenes in a fight, and requires honest weights and measures. It recalls Amalek’s attack on Israel’s stragglers and commands Israel to erase Amalek’s memory after receiving rest in the land.

sections.heading: A Brother’s Duty to Preserve a Name
Punishment for Intervening in a Fight

Deuteronomy 26.overview: Moses instructs Israel to bring firstfruits to the place the LORD chooses, recite the account of deliverance from Egypt, and rejoice in the land’s abundance. He prescribes the third-year tithe and its declaration, then describes Israel’s mutual commitment with the LORD and its status as His treasured, holy people.

Deuteronomy 27.overview: Moses and Israel’s elders direct the people to inscribe the law on plastered stones at Mount Ebal, build an uncut-stone altar, and offer sacrifices there. Moses and the Levitical priests declare Israel the LORD’s people, assign tribes to Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and proclaim curses that the people affirm with “Amen.”

sections.heading: Law Stones and Altar at Mount Ebal

Deuteronomy 28.overview: Moses sets out blessings for Israel if the people obey the LORD, including prosperity, security, and a place above other nations. He then details curses for disobedience, escalating from disease and defeat to siege, famine, exile, scattering, and return to Egypt.

sections.heading: Exile, scattering, and return to Egypt

Deuteronomy 29.overview: Moses recalls the LORD’s signs in Egypt, provision in the wilderness, and victory over Sihon and Og as he presents the Moab covenant to Israel. He describes the covenant’s reach across generations, warns that turning to other gods brings the covenant curses and exile, and distinguishes the LORD’s secret things from what is revealed to Israel.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Deeds and the Covenant
The Land’s Desolation and Israel’s Exile

Deuteronomy 30.overview: Moses describes Israel’s return to the LORD and the LORD’s promise to gather the people from exile, restore them to the land, and bless them as they obey. He declares that the command is near and sets before Israel life and prosperity or death and disaster, calling heaven and earth as witnesses to the choice.

sections.heading: Life and death set before Israel

Deuteronomy 31.overview: Moses tells Israel that he will not cross the Jordan, assures them that the LORD goes before them, and charges Joshua to lead them; he gives the written law to the priests and elders and commands its public reading every seven years. At the Tent of Meeting, the LORD warns that Israel will turn to other gods and break the covenant, directs Moses to write a song as a witness, commissions Joshua, and Moses places the law beside the ark before reciting the song to Israel.

sections.heading: The Law Read Every Seven Years
The LORD Warns and Commissions Joshua
The Law Preserved and the Song Recited

Deuteronomy 32.overview: Moses’ song recounts the LORD’s faithful care for Israel, Israel’s abandonment of the LORD, and the judgment and eventual vindication that follow. After Moses and Joshua recite the song, the LORD directs Moses to Mount Nebo, where he will see Canaan but die without entering it.

sections.heading: The LORD’s faithfulness and care for Israel
Moses recites the song and receives his final command

Deuteronomy 33.overview: Moses blesses Israel before his death, recalling the LORD’s appearance from Sinai and declaring him king over Jeshurun as he pronounces blessings for Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, and Joseph. He blesses Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher, then celebrates Israel’s security and salvation under the incomparable God of Jeshurun.

Deuteronomy 34.overview: The LORD shows Moses the promised land from Mount Nebo and tells him he will not enter it; Moses dies in Moab and is buried in an unknown grave. Israel mourns for Moses, Joshua takes up leadership, and the chapter describes Moses as an unmatched prophet in Israel.

Joshua 1.overview: After Moses’s death, the LORD commissions Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan, promises him the land and divine presence, and commands him to obey the law with courage. Joshua orders the people to prepare for the crossing, directs the eastern tribes to help their fellow Israelites take the land, and receives their pledge of obedience and support.

Joshua 2.overview: Joshua sends two spies from Shittim to Jericho, where Rahab hides them from the king’s men and declares her belief that the LORD has given Israel the land. She secures a promise to spare her family, helps the spies escape, and marks her house with a scarlet cord; the spies return to Joshua and report that the people of the land fear Israel.

sections.heading: Rahab Seeks Protection for Her Family
The Escape and the Scarlet Cord

Joshua 3.overview: Israel leaves Shittim and camps at the Jordan, where officers direct the people to follow the ark at a distance; Joshua tells them to consecrate themselves and sends the priests ahead. The LORD promises to establish Joshua and drive out the Canaanite nations, and the Jordan’s waters stop when the priests carrying the ark enter it, allowing all Israel to cross on dry ground opposite Jericho.

Joshua 4.overview: The Israelites take twelve stones from the Jordan for a memorial at their camp in Gilgal, while Joshua also sets twelve stones where the priests stood in the river. After the priests carrying the ark leave the Jordan, its waters return, and Joshua explains that the stones will remind future generations of Israel’s crossing and the LORD’s mighty power.

sections.heading: Twelve Stones Taken from the Jordan
The Crossing Ends and the Waters Return

Joshua 5.overview: The Amorite and Canaanite kings fear Israel after hearing of the Jordan crossing, while Joshua circumcises the wilderness-born generation at Gilgal, where Israel keeps Passover and begins eating Canaan’s produce as the manna ceases. Near Jericho, Joshua encounters the Commander of the LORD’s army, who declares the ground holy.

sections.heading: Passover and the End of Manna
The Commander of the LORD’s Army

Joshua 6.overview: The LORD gives Jericho to Joshua and directs Israel to march around the city with the ark and priests sounding rams’ horns, then shout on the seventh day. The walls collapse, Israel captures and destroys the city while sparing Rahab and her family and placing the metals in the LORD’s treasury, and Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho as the LORD establishes his fame.

Joshua 7.overview: After Achan takes items devoted to destruction, Israel is defeated at Ai, and Joshua appeals to the LORD, who reveals that Israel’s disobedience has caused the defeat. The LORD directs Israel to identify the offender, Achan confesses and the stolen goods are found, and he and his household are put to death in the Valley of Achor, after which the LORD’s anger turns away.

sections.heading: Achan’s theft and Israel’s defeat at Ai
Joshua’s appeal and the LORD’s instruction
Achan’s punishment in the Valley of Achor

Joshua 8.overview: The LORD directs Joshua to use an ambush to capture Ai, and Israel defeats its forces, takes the city, and carries off its livestock and plunder. At Mount Ebal, Joshua builds an altar, inscribes the law on stones, and reads its blessings and curses before all Israel.

sections.heading: The Law Is Read at Mount Ebal

Joshua 9.overview: The kings west of the Jordan unite against Israel, while the Gibeonites disguise themselves as envoys from a distant land and secure a treaty from Joshua and Israel’s leaders, who do not seek the LORD’s counsel. When Israel discovers that Gibeon and its neighboring towns are nearby, the leaders honor their oath and make the Gibeonites woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation and the LORD’s altar.

Joshua 10.overview: Adoni-zedek and four Amorite kings attack Gibeon, and Joshua marches from Gilgal to its defense; the LORD routs the armies, sends hailstones, and, in response to Joshua’s appeal, the sun and moon stand still until Israel completes the victory. Joshua captures and kills the five kings, then conquers Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir, taking the surrounding region before returning to Gilgal.

sections.heading: The Amorite Alliance and Israel’s Victory

Joshua 11.overview: Jabin of Hazor gathers northern kings and peoples at the waters of Merom, where Joshua’s army defeats them and destroys their horses and chariots as the LORD commands. Joshua captures Hazor and other cities, takes the land from Mount Halak to Baal-gad, defeats the Anakim except in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod, and assigns the land to Israel’s tribes, after which the land rests from war.

Joshua 12.overview: The chapter recounts the lands east of the Jordan conquered by Moses and assigned to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, listing Sihon and Og as the defeated kings. It then lists the western lands conquered by Joshua and Israel and names the thirty-one kings defeated there.

sections.heading: Kings and Lands East of the Jordan
The Thirty-One Kings of the West

Joshua 13.overview: The LORD tells the aged Joshua that much land remains unconquered and directs him to allot it to the nine tribes and half-tribe of Manasseh. The chapter records the eastern inheritances Moses assigned to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, and states that the LORD is Levi’s inheritance.

Joshua 14.overview: Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads oversee the division of Canaan, with the nine and a half tribes receiving land west of the Jordan and the Levites receiving cities and pasturelands rather than a tribal allotment. Caleb recalls Moses’ promise at Kadesh-barnea, asks Joshua for the hill country, and receives Hebron as his inheritance.

Joshua 15.overview: Joshua assigns Judah its boundaries and records Caleb’s inheritance at Hebron, his defeat of Anak’s descendants, and Othniel’s capture of Debir, after which Caleb gives Acsah the upper and lower springs. The chapter lists Judah’s cities by region and notes that Judah’s descendants do not drive the Jebusites from Jerusalem, where they continue to live among them.

Joshua 16.overview: The allotment for Joseph’s descendants is described, and Ephraim and Manasseh receive their inheritance, with Ephraim’s borders and cities detailed. Ephraim’s territory includes cities within Manasseh’s inheritance, while the Canaanites in Gezer remain as forced laborers.

Joshua 17.overview: Manasseh’s allotment includes land east of the Jordan, shares for Zelophehad’s daughters, and territories bordered by Ephraim, Asher, and Issachar; the tribe does not fully displace the Canaanites from several assigned cities. When the house of Joseph asks for more land because of its population, Joshua directs it to clear the hill country and says it can drive out the Canaanites despite their iron chariots.

sections.heading: Joshua’s Response to the House of Joseph

Joshua 18.overview: Israel assembles at Shiloh, where the Tent of Meeting is set up, and Joshua directs the seven tribes without allotments to survey the land before he distributes it by lot. The chapter records Benjamin’s assigned boundaries and lists its cities and villages.

Joshua 19.overview: The lots assign territories to Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, with Simeon’s towns lying within Judah’s inheritance and Dan later capturing Leshem and renaming it. After the tribal allotments are completed at Shiloh, the Israelites give Joshua Timnath-serah in Ephraim, and Eleazar, Joshua, and the family heads finish distributing the land by lot.

sections.heading: Joshua’s Inheritance and the Completed Allotments

Joshua 20.overview: The LORD instructs Joshua to establish cities of refuge for people who kill unintentionally, where they receive protection and remain until trial and the death of the high priest. Israel designates six cities across the land for Israelites and foreigners, so an accidental manslayer can escape the avenger of blood until standing trial before the assembly.

sections.heading: Instructions for the Cities of Refuge
