Ezra 8.overview: Ezra records the families returning from Babylon and arranges for Levites and temple servants to join the group at the Ahava Canal. After fasting and receiving protection for the journey, Ezra entrusts sacred offerings to priests and Levites, and the group reaches Jerusalem, delivers the treasures and the king’s edicts, and offers sacrifices.

Ezra 9.overview: The leaders report to Ezra that Israelites, including priests and Levites, have intermarried with the surrounding peoples, and Ezra responds with grief as others gather around him. At the evening offering, Ezra prays, recalling Israel’s guilt and the grace that has preserved a remnant and enabled the temple’s restoration, then confesses the community’s renewed breach of God’s commands and acknowledges God’s righteousness.

sections.heading: Prayer for Israel’s Guilt and Remnant

Ezra 10.overview: As Ezra mourns Israel’s marriages to foreign women, Shecaniah proposes a covenant to send the wives and their children away, and Ezra secures the people’s oath. The assembled exiles agree to an investigation by town, which identifies the men involved and concludes with a list of their names.

sections.heading: The Men Who Married Foreign Women

Nehemiah 1.overview: Nehemiah hears from Hanani that the returned Jews are in distress and that Jerusalem’s wall and gates are ruined, and he responds with mourning, fasting, and prayer. He confesses Israel’s sins, recalls God’s covenant promises to gather the exiles, and asks for success and mercy before the king, whom he serves as cupbearer.

Nehemiah 2.overview: Nehemiah tells King Artaxerxes of Jerusalem’s ruined state and receives permission, letters, and timber to travel to Judah and rebuild the city. After inspecting Jerusalem’s walls by night, he calls the people to rebuild, and answers Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem that God will grant success and they have no claim in Jerusalem.

Nehemiah 3.overview: Nehemiah 3 records Eliashib the high priest and Jerusalem’s residents, leaders, priests, Levites, and tradespeople rebuilding successive sections of the city wall and its gates. The account traces the work from the Sheep Gate around Jerusalem, naming the builders and their assigned sections, including the Tekoite nobles who do not join the labor.

sections.heading: The Sheep Gate and Fish Gate
The Jeshanah Gate and Broad Wall
The Valley, Dung, and Fountain Gates

Nehemiah 4.overview: Sanballat and Tobiah ridicule the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s wall, while Nehemiah prays and the Jews rebuild it to half its height. As Sanballat, Tobiah, and their allies threaten an attack amid the workers’ fatigue, Nehemiah organizes armed guards and coordinated day-and-night work.

Nehemiah 5.overview: Jews complain to Nehemiah that famine, taxes, and debts have forced them to mortgage their property and enslave their children, and he rebukes the nobles and officials for exacting interest and requires them to restore what they took. Nehemiah describes refusing the governor’s provisions and land while supporting the wall’s construction, and asks God to remember his service to the people.

Nehemiah 6.overview: Sanballat, Geshem, and their allies try to draw Nehemiah away from the wall project, spread accusations of rebellion, and intimidate him through Shemaiah and other prophets, but Nehemiah refuses their schemes. The wall is completed in fifty-two days, while surrounding nations recognize God’s role in the work and Judah’s nobles maintain ties with Tobiah, who continues to threaten Nehemiah.

sections.heading: The invitation to meet at Ono
The wall completed and Tobiah’s ties

Nehemiah 7.overview: Nehemiah appoints Hanani and Hananiah to oversee Jerusalem and orders the gates guarded while the sparsely populated city is prepared for settlement. He records the returned exiles by family and role, notes those whose ancestry is unverified, and lists the assembly’s totals, contributions, and settlement in their towns.

sections.heading: Families and towns of the returnees

Nehemiah 8.overview: At the Water Gate in Jerusalem, Ezra reads and explains the Law to the gathered people, while Nehemiah and the Levites tell them to replace their mourning with rejoicing. The family heads, priests, and Levites study the Law, and the returned exiles celebrate the Feast of Booths as Ezra continues reading for seven days.

sections.heading: Ezra Reads and Explains the Law

Nehemiah 9.overview: The Israelites gather in fasting, hear the Law, confess their sins, and join the Levites in a prayer recounting God’s faithfulness from creation through Israel’s history. The prayer acknowledges Israel’s guilt and present subjection, asks God to regard their distress, and concludes with a written, sealed agreement.

sections.heading: Prayer Recounts God’s Faithfulness and Israel’s Rebellion

Nehemiah 10.overview: Nehemiah, the priests, the Levites, and the leaders seal a covenant, and the rest of the people join in a sworn commitment to follow the Law of God. They pledge to avoid intermarriage with the people of the land, keep the Sabbath and seventh year, and provide for the service of the house of God through offerings, firstfruits, and tithes.

sections.heading: Provisions for the House of God

Nehemiah 11.overview: Leaders settle in Jerusalem, and the people cast lots for one in ten to live there while blessing those who volunteer. The chapter lists Jerusalem’s residents and officials, describes the towns and villages occupied by the rest of Judah and Benjamin, and notes that some Levite divisions live in Benjamin.

Nehemiah 12.overview: The chapter records the priests and Levites who serve from the days of Zerubbabel and Jeshua through the time of Nehemiah, along with their family heads, offices, and duties. At the dedication of Jerusalem’s wall, two choirs process along it and gather at the house of God for singing and sacrifices, while the people organize contributions for the temple servants.

Nehemiah 13.overview: After the Law excludes Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly, Nehemiah returns to Jerusalem and removes Tobiah from the temple storeroom, restores support for the Levites, and enforces Sabbath observance. He confronts intermarriage with foreign women, purifies the priests and Levites, assigns their duties, and arranges contributions, closing with appeals to God to remember his actions.

Esther 1.overview: King Xerxes holds lavish feasts in Susa, while Queen Vashti gives a banquet for the women. After Vashti refuses his summons, Xerxes follows Memucan’s counsel to remove her as queen and sends a decree throughout the kingdom.

Esther 2.overview: After Xerxes orders a search for a new queen, Esther is brought to the palace under Hegai’s care while Mordecai watches over her and she keeps her Jewish identity secret. Xerxes chooses Esther as queen, and Mordecai later uncovers a plot against the king that Esther reports, leading to the conspirators’ execution and the event’s recording in the royal chronicles.

sections.heading: The Search for a New Queen

Esther 3.overview: King Xerxes elevates Haman, but Mordecai refuses to bow to him, prompting Haman to plot the destruction of all the Jews. Haman secures the king’s approval, and an edict ordering the Jews’ destruction is sent throughout the empire, leaving Susa in confusion.

Esther 4.overview: Mordecai and the Jews mourn the decree to destroy their people, and Mordecai sends Esther a copy of the decree with a plea to approach the king. After explaining the danger of appearing before the king uninvited, Esther agrees to go after the Jews of Susa fast for her, and Mordecai carries out her instructions.

sections.heading: Esther prepares to approach the king

Esther 5.overview: Esther approaches the king, receives his favor, and invites him and Haman to a banquet, where she postpones her petition until a second banquet. Haman leaves pleased but becomes enraged when Mordecai does not honor him, then follows Zeresh and his friends’ advice to build a gallows for Mordecai.

Esther 6.overview: King Xerxes cannot sleep and discovers in the royal records that Mordecai exposed a plot against him but received no honor. Haman, who has come to seek Mordecai’s execution, is ordered to honor him instead; afterward Haman grieves, Zeresh and his advisers predict his downfall, and the king’s eunuchs take him to Esther’s banquet.

Esther 7.overview: At a banquet with King Xerxes and Haman, Esther pleads for her life and the lives of her people, then identifies Haman as their enemy. Xerxes orders Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai, after Harbonah reports its existence.

Esther 8.overview: Xerxes gives Haman’s estate and signet ring to Esther and Mordecai, and Esther pleads for a way to avert Haman’s decree against the Jews. Mordecai issues a royal edict allowing the Jews to defend themselves on the appointed day, and news of it brings rejoicing in Susa and throughout the provinces.

sections.heading: Esther and Mordecai receive Haman’s estate

Esther 9.overview: On Adar 13, the Jews defeat their enemies across Xerxes’ provinces, with Mordecai’s authority and the king’s officials supporting them; at Esther’s request, the Jews in Susa continue their defense on Adar 14 and hang Haman’s ten sons. Mordecai and Esther establish Purim on Adar 14 and 15 to commemorate the Jews’ deliverance, with letters confirming the annual observance.

sections.heading: Esther’s petition and the days of rest

Esther 10.overview: King Xerxes imposes tribute throughout his realm, and the account points to the royal chronicles as the record of Mordecai’s achievements and rise. Mordecai stands second to Xerxes, honored among the Jews as he seeks his people’s good and speaks peace to them.

Job 1.overview: In the land of Uz, Job is described as upright and wealthy, with seven sons and three daughters, and he regularly offers sacrifices for his children. In the heavenly court, Satan challenges Job’s devotion and receives permission to take his possessions; after messengers report the loss of his property and children, Job worships the LORD without charging him with wrongdoing.

sections.heading: Job loses his possessions and children

Job 2.overview: Satan argues that Job will curse God if his health is taken, and the LORD permits him to afflict Job while sparing his life. Job endures severe suffering without sinning, and his friends Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar come to mourn with him and sit in silence for seven days and nights.

sections.heading: Satan’s challenge and the LORD’s permission

Job 3.overview: Job curses the day and night of his birth, wishing darkness and barrenness upon them. He asks why he survived birth and why life continues for the miserable, describing death as rest and lamenting that his feared trouble has come.

Job 4.overview: Eliphaz recalls how Job strengthened others and questions why he is dismayed now, arguing that the innocent do not perish while those who sow trouble reap destruction. He recounts a frightening night vision in which a spirit declares that mortals are less pure than God and fragile, short-lived, and lacking wisdom.

sections.heading: Job’s Past Counsel and Present Distress

Job 5.overview: Eliphaz describes the ruin of the fool and argues that human trouble is part of life, while urging Job to appeal to God, who overturns the schemes of the crafty and rescues the needy. He presents God’s correction as a path to healing and promises Job protection, prosperity, and a full life, then affirms that this counsel has been tested and is true.

sections.heading: The Fool’s Ruin and Human Trouble

Job 6.overview: Job says his grief outweighs the sand of the seas, describes the Almighty’s arrows, and longs for God to end his life because he has no strength to hope. He compares his friends to unreliable streams, denies asking them for rescue or payment, and asks them to show his error while he defends his integrity.

sections.heading: Grief and the wish for death

Job 7.overview: Job describes human life as exhausting and brief, recounting his sleepless misery and bodily suffering. He turns to God with a complaint about relentless scrutiny and asks why his sin is not forgiven before he dies.

sections.heading: The misery and brevity of life

Job 8.overview: Bildad the Shuhite rebukes Job’s words and claims that God gave Job’s children over to their sin, while promising that God will restore Job if he seeks mercy and is upright. He appeals to the wisdom of past generations and compares the hope of those who forget God to fragile plants and a spider’s web, then says God rejects neither the blameless nor strengthens evildoers.

sections.heading: Tradition and the Fate of the Godless

Job 9.overview: Job says no mortal can be righteous before God or answer Him, whose power over creation is beyond challenge. He questions why God destroys the blameless and longs for a mediator who can remove God's terror and let him speak without fear.

sections.heading: A Mediator Between God and Job

Job 10.overview: Job voices his bitter complaint to God, asking why God prosecutes him despite knowing his innocence and questioning whether God takes pleasure in oppressing him. He recalls that God formed and preserved him, yet sees God’s scrutiny and hostility as relentless, and pleads for relief before he descends to the land of darkness.

Job 11.overview: Zophar the Naamathite rebukes Job’s claims of sound doctrine and purity, arguing that God’s wisdom is beyond human reach and that God exacts less than Job’s iniquity deserves. He calls Job to put away wrongdoing and promises renewed security and brightness, while warning that the wicked lose hope and escape.

Job 12.overview: Job answers his friends, rejecting their claim to superior wisdom and describing how the righteous are mocked while robbers remain secure. He points to creation as witness to God’s sovereignty over life, wisdom, rulers, and nations.

sections.heading: God’s Sovereignty Over Rulers and Nations

Job 13.overview: Job rejects his friends’ claims as lies and worthless counsel, and says he will present his case to God despite the danger. He expresses hope and confidence in vindication, then asks God to withdraw his hand, reveal his sins, and explain why he treats him as an enemy before describing human life as wasting away.

Job 14.overview: Job describes human life as brief and troubled, questions why God judges mortals, and asks for respite within the limits God has set. He contrasts a tree’s renewal with human death, imagines being hidden in Sheol until God remembers him, then concludes that God erodes human hope and the dead know nothing of their descendants.

sections.heading: Human Frailty and a Plea for Respite
A Tree’s Renewal and Human Death
Eroded Hope and the Dead Unaware

Job 15.overview: Eliphaz rebukes Job, accusing him of undermining reverence for God and claiming that no human being is pure before God. He recounts the inherited wisdom that the wicked face terror, loss, and destruction because they oppose the Almighty.

Job 16.overview: Job calls his friends miserable comforters and says he would offer them encouragement if their places were reversed. He describes God’s assault on him, maintains that his hands are free of violence and his prayer is pure, and appeals to his heavenly witness and advocate as he faces death.

sections.heading: Job Appeals to His Heavenly Witness

Job 17.overview: Job describes his broken spirit, approaching death, and surrounding mockers, then asks God for a pledge and says God has denied understanding to his friends. He recounts his public disgrace, affirms that the righteous persist, rejects his companions as unwise, and asks whether any hope remains as he faces Sheol.

sections.heading: Broken Spirit and Plea for a Pledge

Job 18.overview: Bildad the Shuhite challenges Job’s speeches and anger, asking whether the earth and rocks should change on his account. He describes the wicked person’s light going out, traps and terrors closing in, and his dwelling, family line, and memory disappearing.

sections.heading: The Wicked Person’s Light and Traps
The Wicked Person’s Ruin and Erasure

Job 19.overview: Job rebukes his friends and describes God’s assault on him, his loss of honor, and the abandonment of his family and companions. He asks for pity and a permanent record of his words, declares that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God, and warns his friends that judgment brings punishment.

sections.heading: Job Describes His Ruin and Isolation
Job Appeals for Pity and Remembrance
Job’s Redeemer and Warning of Judgment

Job 20.overview: Zophar answers Job by arguing that the wicked prosper only briefly and disappear without a trace. He describes their wealth turning to poison and loss, their oppression of the poor, and God’s judgment as their appointed inheritance.

Job 21.overview: Job asks his friends to listen as he describes the prosperity and security of many wicked people, despite their rejection of God. He challenges claims that the wicked are regularly punished, notes that death comes to people in very different circumstances, and rejects his friends’ arguments as false comfort.

Job 22.overview: Eliphaz accuses Job of exploiting the vulnerable and claims that his alleged injustice explains his distress. He recalls the fate of the wicked, then urges Job to return to God and describes the restoration and deliverance that would follow.

sections.heading: A Call to Return to God

Job 23.overview: Job longs to find God and present his case, believing God would hear him and deliver him as an upright man. Though Job affirms his faithful conduct, he is terrified by God’s unchangeable purposes and remains outspoken amid the darkness.

sections.heading: Job’s Wish to Plead His Case

Job 24.overview: Job asks why the Almighty does not set times for judgment, describing boundary theft and the suffering of the poor, widows, and fatherless. He portrays murderers and adulterers hiding in darkness, then describes the wicked as briefly secure before their downfall and challenges anyone to disprove his account.

Job 25.overview: Bildad the Shuhite replies that dominion and awe belong to God, who orders heaven, commands an innumerable host, and sends light to all. He argues that no human can be just or pure before God, since even the moon and stars are not pure in God’s sight and humanity is frail.

Job 26.overview: Job sarcastically questions how his companions’ counsel has helped the powerless and asks whose spirit speaks through them. He describes God’s rule over the dead, the cosmos, and the sea, then calls these works only the fringes of God’s power.

Job 27.overview: Job swears that he will maintain his integrity and refuse to speak deceit, despite saying that God has deprived him of justice. He questions the hope of the godless and describes the destruction and loss that come as the wicked man’s portion from the Almighty.

Job 28.overview: The poem describes miners extracting precious metals and stones from hidden places, then contrasts their skill with humanity’s inability to find or value wisdom. God alone knows wisdom’s way, and he declares that fearing the Lord is wisdom and turning from evil is understanding.

Job 29.overview: Job longs for the days when God watched over him, his family surrounded him, and prosperity marked his life. He recalls his honor at the city gate, his defense of the vulnerable, and the respect and leadership he expects to regain.

sections.heading: Honor and Justice at the City Gate

Job 30.overview: Job contrasts his former standing with the contempt of younger outcasts, who mock and threaten him as his dignity and prosperity disappear. He describes unrelenting pain, accuses God of opposing him and leaving his cries unanswered, anticipates death, recalls his compassion for the troubled, and ends in mourning.

Job 31.overview: Job lists the wrongs he denies, including sexual misconduct, deceit, injustice toward servants and the poor, trust in wealth, idolatry, and hostility toward enemies. He describes his hospitality and care for his land, then asks the Almighty to answer his written defense and calls for his fields to bear witness.

sections.heading: Care for the poor and fatherless

Job 32.overview: Job’s three friends stop answering, and Elihu becomes angry with Job for justifying himself and with the friends for condemning him without refuting him. Elihu explains that he waited because he is younger, argues that understanding comes from the Almighty rather than age, and declares that he is compelled to answer Job impartially.

Job 33.overview: Elihu invites Job to answer him, recalls Job’s claim of innocence and complaint that God treats him as an enemy, and argues that God is greater than humanity and speaks through dreams and suffering. He describes how a mediator can secure a person’s rescue and restoration, then asks Job to respond or listen to his teaching.

sections.heading: God Speaks Through Dreams and Suffering

Job 34.overview: Elihu addresses the wise, condemning Job’s claims that he is righteous yet denied justice and that serving God brings no profit. He argues that God acts justly, sees every person’s deeds, judges the wicked, and governs without partiality, then challenges Job to respond and calls for him to be tested for his words against God.

Job 35.overview: Elihu challenges Job’s claim to be more righteous than God and argues that human sin or righteousness does not affect God but does affect other people. He says the oppressed fail to seek God their Maker, that God does not heed empty pleas, and that Job’s words lack knowledge.

Job 36.overview: Elihu describes God as just toward the afflicted and righteous, using suffering to correct people and distinguishing the outcomes of obedience and refusal. He addresses Job with a warning against turning to iniquity, then proclaims God’s greatness and describes his power in the rain, clouds, thunder, and lightning.

sections.heading: Elihu’s Claim to Speak for God

Job 37.overview: Elihu describes thunder, lightning, snow, rain, wind, ice, and clouds as forces directed by God for his purposes. He calls Job to consider these wonders, contrasts human limits with God's power and justice, and concludes that people fear God, who is impartial toward the wise.

Job 38.overview: The LORD answers Job from the whirlwind, questioning his knowledge of the foundations of the earth, the boundaries of the sea, and the ordering of dawn. He continues by describing realms of light and darkness, weather, the heavens, and the provision of food for lions and ravens.

sections.heading: The Earth and the Boundaries of the Sea
Dawn, the Deep, and the Realms of Light
Weather, the Heavens, and Their Order

Job 39.overview: The LORD questions Job about the births and habits of mountain goats, wild donkeys, wild oxen, and ostriches. He describes the horse’s strength in battle and the hawk’s and eagle’s flight and hunting, showing the range of animal life beyond Job’s control.

Job 40.overview: The LORD challenges Job to answer, and Job admits his insignificance and falls silent. The LORD questions whether Job can execute justice like God and describes Behemoth as a powerful creature made by its Maker.

sections.heading: The strength and security of Behemoth

Job 41.overview: God challenges Job with questions about capturing Leviathan and declares that everything under heaven belongs to him. He describes Leviathan’s fearsome body, resistance to weapons, and unmatched dominion over the proud.

Job 42.overview: Job acknowledges God's sovereignty, withdraws his uninformed claims, and repents. The LORD rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends, accepts Job's prayer after their offerings, restores Job's prosperity and family, and the account ends with Job's long life and death.

sections.heading: The Friends' Offering and Job's Prayer

Psalms 1.overview: The psalm describes the blessed person who avoids the wicked, delights in the LORD’s law, and thrives like a well-watered tree. It contrasts the wicked, who are like windblown chaff and perish, with the righteous, whose path the LORD guards.

sections.heading: The righteous person and the law

Psalms 2.overview: The nations and their rulers rebel against the LORD and His Anointed, and the LORD responds by installing His King on Zion. The King declares his sonship and dominion over the nations, while the rulers are warned to serve the LORD and take refuge in the Son.

Psalms 3.overview: David laments the growing number of his foes and reports that many say the LORD will not deliver him, while declaring that the LORD is his shield and sustainer. He asks the LORD to defeat his enemies and affirms that salvation belongs to the LORD, whose blessing is on his people.

Psalms 4.overview: The psalmist calls on God to hear him, challenges those who malign his honor, and affirms that the LORD hears the godly. He urges restraint and trust in the LORD, then contrasts others’ search for good with his joy and confidence in God’s protection.

sections.heading: Prayer and challenge to the slanderers
Restraint and trust in the LORD
Joy and confidence in God’s protection

Psalms 5.overview: The psalmist asks the LORD, his King and God, to hear his morning plea and lead him in righteousness amid his enemies. He contrasts the LORD’s rejection of the wicked with his welcome of the faithful, asks for judgment on his enemies, and declares that the LORD shelters and blesses the righteous.

Psalms 6.overview: David pleads with the LORD for mercy, healing, and deliverance, describing his distress and arguing that the dead cannot praise God. He recounts his grief, declares that the LORD has heard his prayer, and predicts the shame and retreat of his enemies.

Psalms 7.overview: David seeks refuge from his pursuers and declares his innocence in the matter of Cush the Benjamite. He calls on the LORD, the righteous judge, to judge the peoples and end wickedness, describes the wicked man’s ruin by his own violence, and closes with praise.

sections.heading: Plea for Deliverance and Declaration of Innocence
Praise to the LORD Most High

Psalms 8.overview: The psalmist praises the LORD’s majestic name, whose glory is established above the heavens and whose praise from children silences adversaries. Looking at the heavens, the psalmist marvels that God cares for humanity and grants people honor and rule over the creatures of the earth and sea, then repeats the opening praise.

Psalms 9.overview: The psalmist thanks and praises the LORD for defeating his enemies, judging the nations, and ruling with justice from an enduring throne. He describes the LORD as a refuge for the oppressed, asks for deliverance from his enemies, and calls for the nations to be judged and humbled.

Psalms 10.overview: The psalmist asks why the LORD seems distant as the wicked boast, deny God, and prey on the needy and helpless. The psalmist calls on God to judge the wicked and defend the fatherless and oppressed, affirming the LORD’s kingship and care for the humble.

sections.heading: The wicked boast and deny God
The wicked prey on the helpless
A plea for God to act

Psalms 11.overview: David rejects advice to flee, affirming refuge in the LORD despite the wicked’s attack on the upright and the threatened foundations. He declares that the LORD observes and tests humanity, judges the violent, and loves justice, while the upright see his face.

Psalms 12.overview: The psalmist laments the disappearance of the faithful and condemns deceitful, flattering speech, asking the LORD to silence the boastful. The LORD promises safety for the oppressed, whose words are affirmed as flawless, while the psalmist trusts in divine protection amid the wickedness of the generation.

Psalms 13.overview: David asks the LORD how long he will remain forgotten, distressed, and dominated by his enemy, then pleads for attention and help. He trusts in the LORD’s loving devotion and salvation and vows to sing because the LORD has been good to him.

Psalms 14.overview: David describes human corruption and the LORD’s search from heaven for anyone who understands or seeks God. He contrasts the workers of iniquity with God’s protection of the righteous and the oppressed, and anticipates Israel’s restoration from Zion.

Psalms 15.overview: David asks who may dwell in the LORD’s tent and on his holy mountain. The answer describes a person marked by integrity, truthful speech, just conduct, reverence for the LORD, faithful oaths, and refusal of interest or bribes, who will never be shaken.

sections.heading: Who May Dwell with the LORD

Psalms 16.overview: David seeks refuge in the LORD, rejects other gods, and describes the LORD as his secure portion and inheritance. He rejoices in the LORD’s counsel and presence, expressing confidence that God will not abandon him to Sheol but makes known the path of life.

sections.heading: Refuge in the LORD, Rejection of Other Gods
The LORD as Portion and Counselor
Confidence in the Path of Life

Psalms 17.overview: David appeals to the LORD for vindication, citing his integrity and asking for protection from enemies who surround and threaten him. He calls for the LORD to confront the wicked and deliver him, while affirming that he will be satisfied in God's presence.

sections.heading: Deliverance and satisfaction in God's presence

Psalms 18.overview: David praises the LORD as his strength and recounts how God heard his distress, came in power, and rescued him from death and his enemies. He attributes his victories and rule over nations to God’s strength and salvation, vows to praise the LORD among the nations, and declares God’s lasting devotion to David and his descendants.

sections.heading: Praise and a Cry for Help
The LORD Comes and Rescues David

Psalms 19.overview: The heavens and the sun declare God’s glory, while the LORD’s law, testimony, precepts, commandments, fear, and judgments are praised for their perfection and value. David asks to be cleansed from hidden faults and kept from willful sins, and prays that his words and thoughts be pleasing to the LORD, his Rock and Redeemer.

sections.heading: The Perfection of the LORD’s Law

Psalms 20.overview: The congregation asks the LORD to protect the king in trouble, sustain him from Zion, remember his offerings, and grant his plans and petitions. It declares confidence in the LORD’s saving power over reliance on chariots and horses, then asks him to save the king and answer the people.

sections.heading: Confidence in the LORD’s Saving Power

Psalms 21.overview: The king rejoices in the LORD’s strength and salvation, recalling the blessings, life, glory, and joy granted to him as he trusts in the Most High. The psalm describes the LORD’s judgment of the king’s enemies and closes with a declaration of praise for the LORD’s power.

Psalms 22.overview: David laments his abandonment and suffering, recalls Israel’s trust in God, and pleads for deliverance from hostile enemies. After declaring that God has answered him, he promises praise in the assembly and describes the nations and future generations worshiping the Lord.

Psalms 23.overview: David portrays the LORD as his shepherd, who provides rest, restores him, and guides him in righteous paths. The LORD accompanies and comforts him through danger, welcomes him in the presence of his enemies, and grants him goodness, mercy, and a lasting place in the LORD’s house.

Psalms 24.overview: The psalm declares that the earth and all who live in it belong to the LORD, who founded and established the world. It describes the clean and truthful worshipper who seeks God, then calls the gates to welcome the King of Glory, identified as the LORD, mighty in battle and LORD of Hosts.

sections.heading: The LORD owns and establishes the earth
Those who may enter God’s holy place
The gates welcome the King of Glory

Psalms 25.overview: The psalmist trusts the LORD, asks to be taught His ways and forgiven, and describes the LORD’s guidance and covenant faithfulness. In distress among many enemies, the psalmist asks for protection and deliverance and closes by asking God to redeem Israel.

Psalms 26.overview: David appeals to the LORD for vindication, declaring his integrity, trust, and separation from the wicked. He describes worship at the LORD’s altar and love for the LORD’s dwelling, then asks not to be taken with sinners and closes with confidence and praise.

sections.heading: Integrity and separation from the wicked
A plea for mercy and confidence

Psalms 27.overview: The psalmist declares the LORD his light and stronghold amid enemies and war, and expresses his desire to dwell in the LORD’s house and worship there. He asks the LORD for mercy, guidance, and protection from his foes and false witnesses, then affirms confidence in the LORD’s goodness and calls for patient waiting.

sections.heading: Trust in the LORD and desire for his house
A plea for help and guidance

Psalms 28.overview: David calls on the LORD to hear his plea, distinguish him from the wicked, and repay those who disregard the LORD’s works. He gives thanks for the LORD’s help and declares the LORD the strength and salvation of his people, then asks him to save, shepherd, and sustain his inheritance.

Psalms 29.overview: The psalm calls the heavenly beings to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD and worship him in holiness. The LORD’s powerful voice shakes the waters, Lebanon, Sirion, and the wilderness, while the temple cries “Glory”; enthroned over the flood, he gives his people strength and peace.

sections.heading: The LORD Reigns and Blesses His People

Psalms 30.overview: The psalmist praises the LORD for lifting him from danger and healing him, and calls the faithful to praise God’s enduring favor. He recalls confidence in prosperity, distress when God hides his face, and his plea for mercy, then celebrates mourning turned to joy and vows lasting thanks.

Psalms 31.overview: David appeals to the LORD for refuge and deliverance, affirming his trust in God amid distress, slander, and threats from enemies. He praises the LORD’s goodness and protection, recalls being heard in a city under siege, and calls the faithful to love and hope in the LORD.

sections.heading: Distress and Trust in the LORD

Psalms 32.overview: The psalm declares that those whose sins the LORD forgives are blessed. The speaker recounts the distress of keeping silent and the relief of confessing, then describes the LORD as refuge and instructor and contrasts the sorrows of the wicked with the joy of the righteous.

Psalms 33.overview: The psalm calls the upright to praise the LORD, whose trustworthy word creates the heavens and whose counsel governs the nations and blesses the people who belong to him. It contrasts human strength with the LORD’s watchful care for those who fear and trust him, and closes with the community waiting for his help and loving devotion.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Care and His People’s Trust

Psalms 34.overview: David praises the LORD for hearing and delivering him, and calls the oppressed to join in honoring the LORD and taking refuge in him. He teaches the fear of the LORD and contrasts the LORD’s care for the righteous with the fate of the wicked.

sections.heading: Praise and refuge in the LORD
Instruction in the fear of the LORD
The LORD’s care for the righteous

Psalms 35.overview: David asks the LORD to fight his pursuers and turn their traps back on them, trusting in the LORD’s salvation. He recounts his enemies’ false charges and hostility, then asks for vindication and promises public praise.

sections.heading: A plea for rescue from pursuers
A plea for vindication and praise

Psalms 36.overview: David describes the wicked person’s lack of fear of God, pride, deceit, and persistent plotting of evil. He praises the LORD’s steadfast love, faithfulness, righteousness, and life-giving care, then asks for protection and declares the downfall of evildoers.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Steadfast Love and Care
A Plea for Protection and the Wicked’s Fall

Psalms 37.overview: David contrasts the brief prosperity of evildoers with the lasting inheritance of those who trust the LORD and do good. He describes the LORD sustaining the righteous, bringing the wicked to an end, and delivering those who take refuge in him.

sections.heading: Trusting the LORD and inheriting the land
The wicked fall and the righteous endure

Psalms 38.overview: David pleads for the LORD to withhold anger as he describes bodily suffering, guilt, and isolation while enemies plot against him. He waits for God to answer, confesses his sin, and asks the LORD his Savior not to forsake him but to come quickly to his aid.

sections.heading: A plea amid guilt and suffering

Psalms 39.overview: The psalmist resolves to guard his speech, but inner sorrow and a burning heart lead him to ask the LORD about life’s brevity and to place his hope in God. He seeks deliverance from sin and affliction, describes human life as fleeting under divine discipline, and pleads for the LORD to hear him and restore his joy before he dies.

Psalms 40.overview: The psalmist recalls waiting for the LORD, who rescues him, gives him a new song, and does wondrous deeds; he declares that God desires obedience and proclaims God’s righteousness and faithfulness. He asks the LORD for mercy and deliverance amid overwhelming troubles, and calls for his enemies’ shame and for those who seek God to rejoice.

sections.heading: Rescue and trust in the LORD

Psalms 41.overview: The psalm declares that the LORD delivers, protects, and sustains the one who cares for the poor, while David seeks healing after confessing his sin. He describes the malice of his enemies and the betrayal of a trusted friend, asks the LORD to raise him up, affirms the LORD’s favor, and closes with praise to the God of Israel.

Psalms 42.overview: The psalmist longs for the living God and recalls leading a joyful procession to the house of God, while tears and taunts deepen the sense of absence. From Jordan, Hermon, and Mount Mizar, the psalmist describes overwhelming trouble, appeals to God as Rock, and repeatedly calls the downcast soul to hope in God and anticipate praise.

sections.heading: Longing for God and remembered worship
Downcast soul and hope in God
Appeal amid oppression and renewed hope

Psalms 43.overview: The psalmist asks God to vindicate him against an ungodly nation and questions why God seems to have rejected him amid oppression. He asks God to lead him to the holy mountain, vows to worship at the altar, and urges his downcast soul to hope in God.

Psalms 44.overview: The sons of Korah recall how God gave Jacob victory and the land, then contrast that history with Israel’s present defeat, scattering, and disgrace. The people maintain that they have not abandoned God’s covenant and plead for him to rise, help them, and redeem them.

Psalms 45.overview: The psalmist celebrates the king’s beauty, victories, just and enduring reign, and divine anointing. The bride is welcomed with honor and led to the king, whose descendants and name are praised among the nations for generations.

Psalms 46.overview: The psalm presents God as refuge and strength amid cosmic upheaval, while the city of God remains secure because God dwells within it. It depicts the LORD of Hosts as sovereign over raging nations and wars, declaring that God will be exalted throughout the earth.

sections.heading: The City of God and His Presence
The LORD Ends War and Is Exalted

Psalms 47.overview: The psalm calls all peoples to acclaim the LORD Most High, who subdues nations and chooses Jacob’s inheritance. It celebrates God’s ascent and kingship over the earth, as nations and their nobles gather under his reign and exalt him.

sections.heading: Acclaim for the King over all

Psalms 48.overview: The psalm praises the LORD’s city, Mount Zion, where God stands as a fortress and the great King reigns. It recalls the terror of assembled kings, celebrates God’s enduring protection and righteous judgments, and calls for Zion’s strength to be told to future generations.

sections.heading: The Kings’ Flight and Zion’s Security

Psalms 49.overview: The sons of Korah summon all peoples to hear a wisdom poem that asks why the speaker should fear the wealthy wicked, since no one can pay God a ransom to escape death. The poem contrasts the fate of the rich, who die and leave their wealth behind, with God’s promise to redeem the speaker from Sheol, and concludes that wealth without understanding cannot endure.

sections.heading: Call to Hear the Wisdom Poem
The Fate of the Foolish and Redemption
The Rich Leave Their Wealth Behind

Psalms 50.overview: Asaph portrays God summoning the earth from Zion to judge his covenant people, with the heavens proclaiming his righteousness. God declares that he needs no offerings, calls Israel to thanksgiving and fulfilled vows, and rebukes the wicked for hypocrisy and deceit while warning of judgment and promising salvation to those who rightly order their way.

sections.heading: God Summons His People to Judgment

Psalms 51.overview: David confesses his sin and guilt and pleads with God for cleansing, forgiveness, a renewed heart, and restored joy. He promises praise and instruction for sinners, declares that God desires a contrite heart rather than sacrifice, and asks for Zion’s prosperity and acceptable offerings in Jerusalem.

Psalms 52.overview: In the setting of Doeg’s report to Saul, David condemns the deceitful man who trusts in wealth and destruction, declaring that God will uproot him. The righteous witness the downfall, while David trusts in God’s enduring loving devotion and promises praise in the presence of the faithful.

sections.heading: God’s Judgment and the Righteous Response

Psalms 53.overview: The psalm declares that the fool denies God and that God finds no one among humanity who seeks him or does good. It condemns those who devour God’s people, describes their coming dread and defeat, and longs for Israel’s salvation from Zion.

Psalms 54.overview: David appeals to God for rescue from the ruthless men who seek his life, recalling the Ziphites’ report to Saul. He declares God his helper, asks for judgment on his enemies, and praises God for deliverance.

Psalms 55.overview: The speaker pleads with God amid fear, violence in the city, and pressure from enemies, longing to flee to a place of rest. He describes betrayal by a close companion, calls on God for deliverance and judgment, and declares trust in the LORD.

sections.heading: City violence and a companion’s betrayal

Psalms 56.overview: David pleads for mercy as enemies pursue and plot against him, recalling his trust in God and asking God to judge them. He finds confidence that God records his suffering and will be on his side, and he promises thank offerings for deliverance from death.

Psalms 57.overview: David appeals to God for refuge from violent enemies, trusting God to fulfill his purpose, rebuke his attackers, and send loving devotion and truth. He declares that his pursuers fall into their own pit, then calls for praise among the nations and repeats the prayer for God's glory to fill the earth.

sections.heading: God's glory and the enemies' downfall

Psalms 58.overview: David challenges rulers’ justice, condemns their violence, and describes the wicked as venomous and deaf to correction. He asks God to destroy them and declares that the righteous rejoice in their defeat, affirming that God rewards the righteous and judges the earth.

sections.heading: Rulers’ Injustice and the Wicked’s Deceit
A Plea for the Wicked’s Destruction
The Righteous Rejoice in God’s Judgment

Psalms 59.overview: David, watched by Saul’s men who seek to kill him, asks the LORD to deliver him and judge his enemies, who attack without cause. He describes their prowling and violent speech, asks God to scatter and consume them, and declares that he will sing of God’s strength and loving devotion.

sections.heading: Enemies’ threats and appeal for judgment
God as refuge and cause for praise

Psalms 60.overview: The psalm laments Israel’s defeat and asks God to restore and deliver his people, recalling their hardship and the banner raised for those who fear him. It recounts God’s declaration over Israel’s territories and neighboring nations, then asks for aid against enemies and affirms victory through God.

sections.heading: A Plea for Aid and Victory

Psalms 61.overview: The psalmist calls to God from the ends of the earth when his heart is faint, recalling God as his refuge and asking for shelter in God’s presence. He recalls that God has heard his vows and asks for the king’s life to be lengthened and guarded by God’s devotion and faithfulness, promising continual praise.

sections.heading: The king’s life and the psalmist’s praise

Psalms 62.overview: The psalmist declares that salvation and security come from God alone while describing enemies who plot against him and speak deceitfully. He calls the people to trust God rather than human status or wealth, and affirms that power, loving devotion, and just recompense belong to God.

Psalms 63.overview: David longs for God in the wilderness, recalling God’s power and glory and praising his loving devotion as he blesses God and finds satisfaction in him. He remembers God’s help through the night, trusts God to uphold him, and contrasts the destruction of his enemies with the king’s rejoicing and the silencing of liars.

sections.heading: Longing for God and praising him
Enemies’ fate and the king’s joy

Psalms 64.overview: David asks God to protect him from enemies who plot in secret and attack the innocent with words. God turns their schemes against them, prompting people to recognize his work and the righteous to rejoice and take refuge in him.

sections.heading: David’s plea and the enemies’ schemes
The righteous rejoice in the LORD

Psalms 65.overview: The psalm praises God in Zion, who hears prayer, forgives transgressions, and welcomes the chosen into the temple. It celebrates God’s power over creation and nations and describes the abundance he provides for the earth.

sections.heading: Praise, Forgiveness, and Welcome in Zion
God’s Power Over Creation and Nations

Psalms 66.overview: The psalm calls all the earth to praise God for his awesome deeds, power, and rule, recalling the passage through the sea and God’s care for the nations. The speaker recounts God’s testing and deliverance, vows offerings at God’s house, and testifies that God hears prayer and shows steadfast love.

Psalms 67.overview: The psalm asks God to bless his people so that his ways and salvation become known among the nations. It calls all peoples to praise him for his just rule, celebrates the earth’s harvest, and connects God’s blessing with reverence throughout the earth.

sections.heading: Blessing and God’s Ways Made Known
The Nations Praise God’s Just Rule
Harvest and Blessing for the Earth

Psalms 68.overview: The psalm celebrates God’s victory over his enemies, care for the vulnerable, leadership of Israel through the wilderness, and choice of Mount Zion as his dwelling. It proclaims God’s power to deliver and judge, depicts Israel’s procession into the sanctuary, and calls the kingdoms of the earth to praise him.

sections.heading: God’s Victory and Care for the Vulnerable
God Leads Israel and Chooses Zion
Procession to the Sanctuary and Praise

Psalms 69.overview: The psalmist describes sinking distress, unjust hatred, and reproach suffered for zeal for God’s house, then pleads for rescue and compassion. He calls for judgment on his persecutors, vows praise, and declares that God hears the needy, saves Zion, and gives its cities to his servants’ descendants.

Psalms 70.overview: The psalmist urgently asks God to deliver him and calls for his pursuers and mockers to be shamed and turned back. He asks that those who seek God rejoice and magnify him, while affirming his own need and God as his help and deliverer.

sections.heading: A plea for deliverance from enemies
Joy in God and urgent appeal

Psalms 71.overview: The psalmist seeks refuge and deliverance from the wicked, recalling lifelong trust in God and asking not to be forsaken in old age. The psalmist vows to proclaim God's righteousness to future generations, anticipates renewed life and honor, and praises God as enemies are disgraced.

sections.heading: Appeal Amid Enemies and Old Age
Renewal and Praise for God's Righteousness

Psalms 72.overview: The psalm petitions God to grant the king justice and righteousness, protect the needy, and establish enduring peace and prosperity. It depicts the king's rule extending across nations and receiving tribute, then invokes an enduring blessed name before praising the LORD and noting the conclusion of David's prayers.

sections.heading: Universal Rule and Care for the Needy

Psalms 73.overview: Asaph affirms that God is good to Israel, but recounts how the prosperity and arrogance of the wicked nearly make him doubt the value of keeping his heart pure while he suffers. In God’s sanctuary he sees their ruin and declares God his guide, strength, portion, and refuge, while the faithless perish.

Psalms 74.overview: The psalmist laments the enemy’s destruction of the sanctuary and the absence of signs or prophets, asking God how long the devastation will continue. He recalls God’s acts of deliverance and rule over creation, then appeals for God to remember the covenant and defend the afflicted against those who mock him.

Psalms 75.overview: The people give thanks to God and declare his wondrous works, while God says he judges fairly, supports the earth, and warns the proud and wicked against boasting. The psalmist praises the God of Jacob, who judges the wicked and exalts the righteous.

sections.heading: Praise and the Fall of the Wicked

Psalms 76.overview: The psalm declares that God is known in Judah and dwells in Zion, where he shatters weapons and defeats enemy warriors. It describes his judgment from heaven, his salvation of the lowly, and the tribute and fear owed to him by rulers and nations.

sections.heading: God’s dwelling and victory in Zion

Psalms 77.overview: Asaph cries to God in distress and questions whether the Lord has withdrawn his favor, compassion, and promises. He recalls God’s wonders and describes the divine power that redeems Jacob and Joseph and leads the people through the sea under Moses and Aaron.

sections.heading: Distress and Questions About God’s Favor
God Leads His People Through the Sea

Psalms 78.overview: Asaph calls Israel to pass the LORD’s works and commands to future generations, then recounts the people’s repeated rebellion and unbelief despite God’s provision and compassion in the wilderness. He recalls the plagues in Egypt, Israel’s settlement in the land and rejection at Shiloh, and God’s choice of Judah, Mount Zion, and David to shepherd Israel.

sections.heading: Rebellion and Provision in the Wilderness
The Exodus and Settlement in the Land

Psalms 79.overview: Asaph describes the nations’ destruction of Jerusalem, the defilement of the temple, and the deaths and humiliation of God’s people. The psalmist asks God to forgive and deliver them, judge the nations, preserve the captives, and receive the people’s enduring praise.

Psalms 80.overview: Asaph calls on Israel’s Shepherd and God of Hosts to restore the people, describing their tears, conflict with neighbors, and enemies’ mockery. He recalls Israel as a vine brought from Egypt and asks God to look upon its ruin, uphold the one raised at his right hand, and restore the people.

Psalms 81.overview: The psalm summons Israel to celebrate the appointed feast with music and recalls the LORD’s rescue of Joseph from Egypt and Israel at Meribah. The LORD warns Israel against foreign gods, recounts its refusal to listen, and describes the deliverance and abundance that would follow obedience.

Psalms 82.overview: Asaph portrays God presiding over the divine assembly and confronting the gods for unjust judgments and partiality toward the wicked. God calls them to defend the weak, warns that they will die like mortals despite being called sons of the Most High, and receives a plea to judge the earth and its nations.

sections.heading: A charge to defend the vulnerable
A plea for God to judge

Psalms 83.overview: Asaph’s psalm calls on God to answer as a coalition of nations plots to erase Israel and forms an alliance against him. It asks God to defeat the coalition as he defeated Midian, Sisera, and Jabin, and to bring its members to shame so they recognize that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth.

sections.heading: A Plea for the Coalition’s Defeat
Shame and Recognition of the LORD

Psalms 84.overview: The psalmist longs for the LORD’s dwelling, where even birds nest near the altars, and calls blessed those who worship there and journey to Zion. The psalmist asks God to look favorably on the anointed and declares that life in God’s courts is better than elsewhere, for the LORD protects and blesses those who trust in him.

Psalms 85.overview: The sons of Korah recall the LORD’s favor, forgiveness, and withdrawal of anger, then ask God to restore the people and revive them. The speaker listens for God’s promise of peace as the psalm describes salvation near to those who fear him, the joining of faithfulness and righteousness, and the land’s abundance.

Psalms 86.overview: David asks the LORD to hear, preserve, and comfort him in distress, appealing to the LORD’s kindness, forgiveness, and faithfulness. He praises the LORD as the one incomparable God whom the nations will worship, asks for an undivided heart, and seeks deliverance from arrogant enemies.

sections.heading: A plea for mercy and help
The LORD’s greatness and David’s praise
A plea for deliverance from enemies

Psalms 87.overview: The psalm declares that the LORD founds Zion on the holy mountains and loves its gates, while glorious things are spoken of the city of God. It names Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Cush among those who know the LORD, and says that the LORD records Zion-born peoples as singers and pipers proclaim their joy in God.

Psalms 88.overview: Heman the Ezrahite cries to the LORD amid troubles, approaching death, isolation, and the weight of divine wrath. He asks whether the dead can declare God’s faithfulness, renews his plea for help, and ends with darkness as his closest companion.

sections.heading: Questions about praise from the dead

Psalms 89.overview: The psalmist proclaims the LORD’s enduring faithfulness, praises his rule over creation, and recounts his covenant with David and promise of an enduring dynasty. He then laments the apparent rejection and defeat of the anointed king, appeals for the LORD to remember his covenant and the people’s reproach, and closes with a blessing.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Faithfulness and David’s Covenant

Psalms 90.overview: Moses contrasts God’s everlasting dwelling and rule with human mortality, describing how divine anger exposes sin and shortens life. He asks God for compassion, lasting joy, wisdom, and favor, and for God to establish the work of his servants’ hands.

Psalms 91.overview: The psalmist describes the Most High as refuge and shelter, promising protection from disease, violence, and other dangers for those who trust in the LORD. The LORD promises to answer, deliver, and honor the one who loves him, granting long life and salvation.

Psalms 92.overview: The psalmist praises the LORD’s loving devotion, faithfulness, and mighty works in a song for the Sabbath day. The psalm contrasts the destruction of the wicked with the lasting flourishing of the righteous, who proclaim that the LORD is upright and their Rock.

sections.heading: The wicked perish; the psalmist is exalted

Psalms 93.overview: The psalm declares the LORD’s majestic reign, strength, and eternal throne as the world stands firm. It contrasts the rising waters with the LORD’s supremacy and affirms his reliable testimonies and the holiness of his house.

Psalms 94.overview: The psalmist calls the LORD, Judge of the earth, to repay the wicked, who oppress the vulnerable and claim that God does not see. He argues that God knows human thoughts, disciplines and preserves his people, supports the righteous, and will destroy corrupt rulers and evildoers.

Psalms 95.overview: The psalm calls the people to sing, give thanks, and worship the LORD, whose greatness and creative power encompass the earth and sea. It identifies Israel as the LORD’s flock and warns against hardening their hearts as at Meribah and Massah, recalling the wilderness generation’s rejection and the oath that bars them from God’s rest.

sections.heading: Worship and Warning from the Wilderness

Psalms 96.overview: The psalm calls all the earth and the nations to sing to the LORD, proclaim his salvation and glory, and worship him as creator above the nations’ idols. It declares that the LORD reigns and will judge the world with righteousness and faithfulness, prompting all creation to rejoice at his coming.

sections.heading: A New Song to the Creator

Psalms 97.overview: The psalm proclaims the LORD’s reign, depicting the earth trembling before his power as the heavens and peoples see his righteousness and glory. It contrasts the shame of idol worshipers with Zion’s rejoicing, declares the LORD supreme over all gods, and celebrates his care for the righteous.

Psalms 98.overview: The psalm celebrates the LORD’s victory, salvation, and righteousness, made known among the nations and remembered for Israel. It calls all the earth and creation to praise the LORD as King, who comes to judge the world with righteousness and equity.

sections.heading: Creation Rejoices at the LORD’s Coming

Psalms 99.overview: The psalm proclaims the LORD’s reign from above the cherubim and in Zion, calling the nations and peoples to acknowledge his holiness and justice. It recalls Moses, Aaron, and Samuel calling on the LORD, who answers from the cloud, forgives, and avenges wrongdoing, and concludes with worship at his holy mountain.

Psalms 100.overview: The psalm calls all the earth to joyful service and song, declaring the LORD to be God, creator, and shepherd of his people. It summons worshipers to enter his gates with thanksgiving and praise, grounding this praise in the LORD’s goodness, enduring love, and faithfulness to every generation.

Psalms 101.overview: David praises the LORD’s loving devotion and justice and commits to walk with integrity. He rejects deceit, pride, and wickedness while favoring the faithful and removing evildoers from the land and the city of the LORD.

Psalms 102.overview: The afflicted speaker pleads with the LORD for help, describing physical decline, isolation, enemy taunts, and divine anger. The speaker trusts that the LORD will restore Zion, hear the destitute and prisoners, and draw nations to worship, then appeals to God’s permanence as the earth and heavens pass away.

sections.heading: A Plea to the Eternal God

Psalms 103.overview: The psalmist calls his soul to bless the LORD and recalls the LORD’s forgiveness, healing, deliverance, compassion, and care for the oppressed. He contrasts human frailty with the LORD’s enduring loving devotion to those who fear him, recalls the LORD’s covenant and rule, and summons angels, hosts, and all creation to praise him.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Benefits to the Psalmist
The LORD’s Compassion and Enduring Devotion
The LORD’s Universal Reign and Praise

Psalms 104.overview: The psalmist praises the LORD as creator, describing the heavens, the earth, and the boundaries set for the waters. The psalm describes God’s provision for creatures and the cycles of life, then closes with praise, a prayer for God’s enduring glory, and a plea for sinners and the wicked to vanish.

sections.heading: The LORD Establishes the Heavens and Earth
Water, Food, and Habitats for Creatures
The Rhythms and Renewal of Life
Praise and Prayer to the LORD

Psalms 105.overview: The psalm calls Israel to praise the LORD, remember his deeds, and rejoice in his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It recounts Joseph’s rise in Egypt, Moses and Aaron leading Israel out through the plagues, God’s provision in the wilderness, and the gift of the nations’ lands so Israel can keep his laws.

Psalms 106.overview: The psalm praises the LORD’s enduring goodness and recounts Israel’s repeated rebellion, from the Red Sea and wilderness through its later idolatry, while recalling God’s judgment, rescue, and covenant mercy. It closes with a plea for the LORD to gather Israel from the nations and with praise to the God of Israel.

sections.heading: Rebellion in Egypt and the wilderness
Prayer for gathering and final praise

Psalms 107.overview: The psalm calls the redeemed, gathered from many lands, to thank the LORD and recounts how he delivers wanderers, prisoners, and the afflicted who cry out to him. It describes sailors rescued from a storm and the LORD’s reversals of land and human fortunes, concluding that the wise consider his loving devotion.

Psalms 108.overview: The psalmist praises God’s steadfastness, loving devotion, and faithfulness, and asks God to deliver his beloved people. God claims the lands and peoples from Shechem and Succoth to Moab, Edom, and Philistia, while the psalmist seeks aid against the enemy and expresses confidence that God will bring victory.

sections.heading: Appeal for Aid and Confidence in Victory

Psalms 109.overview: David asks God to answer the deceitful accusers who repay his love with hatred, and he pronounces judgment on the wicked man and his descendants. He appeals for deliverance from his poverty and distress, trusts that God will bless him while shaming his accusers, and vows public praise because God stands beside the needy.

sections.heading: Plea for help and confidence in God

Psalms 110.overview: The psalm presents the LORD’s declaration that David’s lord rules from Zion with willing people and receives an eternal priesthood in the order of Melchizedek. The Lord at his right hand judges the nations, crushes kings and leaders, and lifts his head after drinking from the brook.

Psalms 111.overview: The psalmist praises the LORD’s great and enduring works, recalling his wonders, compassion, provision, covenant, and gift of the nations to Israel. The psalm declares that the LORD’s works and precepts are trustworthy, celebrates redemption and his holy name, and identifies fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom.

Psalms 112.overview: Psalm 112 describes the blessings of the person who fears the LORD and delights in his commandments: descendants are blessed, prosperity and enduring righteousness mark his household, and light comes to the upright. The generous and just person remains secure, trusts the LORD amid bad news, gives to the poor, and is honored, while the wicked grieve and perish.

Psalms 113.overview: The psalm calls the LORD’s servants to praise his name forever and throughout the earth, declaring his glory above all nations and the heavens. Though enthroned on high, the LORD looks upon heaven and earth, raises the poor and needy to places of honor, and gives the barren woman a joyful family.

Psalms 114.overview: The psalm recalls Israel’s departure from Egypt, when Judah becomes God’s sanctuary and Israel his dominion. It portrays the sea, the Jordan, and the mountains responding to God’s presence, and declares that he turns rock and flint into water.

Psalms 115.overview: The psalm asks that glory belong to the LORD, contrasts Israel’s living God with powerless idols, and calls Israel, Aaron’s house, and all who fear the LORD to trust in him. It declares the LORD’s blessing over his people, distinguishes his heavenly rule from the earth given to humanity, and affirms that the living will praise him forever.

Psalms 116.overview: The psalmist recalls calling to the LORD in distress and being rescued from death, sorrow, and stumbling. He responds with trust, thanksgiving, and vows to honor the LORD publicly in Jerusalem.

sections.heading: Thanksgiving and vows before the people

Psalms 117.overview: The psalm calls all nations and peoples to praise and extol the LORD. It grounds this praise in his great loving devotion and enduring faithfulness, ending with “Hallelujah.”

Psalms 118.overview: The psalmist summons Israel, Aaron’s house, and those who fear the LORD to praise his enduring love, then recounts the LORD’s rescue from distress and enemies. He approaches the gates of righteousness, celebrates the rejected stone made cornerstone, and joins the community in blessing and thanksgiving.

Psalms 119.overview: The psalmist praises the LORD’s law and repeatedly seeks instruction, understanding, life, and steadfastness through the LORD’s word. Amid affliction, enemies, and longing for rescue, the psalmist trusts the enduring righteousness of the LORD’s commandments and ends by asking to be sought as a straying servant.

sections.heading: Seeking and keeping the LORD’s instruction
Trust in the word amid affliction
The enduring word and its wisdom
Love for the law and plea for rescue

Psalms 120.overview: The psalmist cries to the LORD in distress and asks for deliverance from lying lips and a deceitful tongue, whose punishment is pictured as a warrior’s sharp arrows and burning broom-tree coals. He laments living among the peoples of Meshech and Kedar, who hate peace and seek war despite his desire for peace.

Psalms 121.overview: The song of ascents asks where help comes from and identifies the LORD, Maker of heaven and earth, as the singer’s help. It declares that the LORD guards Israel and preserves the singer through every danger, now and forever.

Psalms 122.overview: The psalmist rejoices at the invitation to worship in Jerusalem, describing the city as the gathering place of Israel’s tribes and the seat of Davidic judgment. He calls for Jerusalem’s peace and prosperity for the sake of his companions and the house of the LORD.

Psalms 123.overview: The psalmist lifts his eyes to the God enthroned in heaven and compares the community’s watchful dependence on the LORD to servants looking to their masters’ hands. The community pleads for mercy after enduring contempt and scorn from the arrogant and proud.

Psalms 124.overview: The psalm calls Israel to declare that the LORD’s presence prevents its attackers from swallowing or sweeping it away. It blesses the LORD for Israel’s escape from their grasp and identifies the LORD, Maker of heaven and earth, as its help.

Psalms 125.overview: The psalm compares those who trust in the LORD to enduring Mount Zion and says the LORD surrounds his people as mountains surround Jerusalem. It asks the LORD to do good to the upright, declares that the wicked will not rule over the righteous, and says those who turn to crooked ways are banished with evildoers, ending with peace for Israel.

Psalms 126.overview: The psalm recalls the LORD’s restoration of Zion’s captives, which fills the people with laughter and joy and is acknowledged among the nations. It asks the LORD to restore the captives again and compares sorrowful sowing with a joyful harvest.

sections.heading: A plea for restoration and harvest

Psalms 127.overview: The psalm declares that building, guarding, and laboring are in vain without the LORD, who gives sleep to those he loves. It describes children as the LORD’s heritage and reward, comparing them to arrows and portraying a father with a full quiver as secure before enemies at the gate.

sections.heading: The LORD’s care in work and rest

Psalms 128.overview: The psalm declares that those who fear the LORD and walk in his ways receive blessing and prosperity from their labor, with a fruitful household of wife and sons. It invokes blessing from Zion, long life to see Jerusalem prosper and grandchildren, and peace upon Israel.

sections.heading: Blessing for the One Who Fears the LORD
Blessing from Zion and Peace for Israel

Psalms 129.overview: Israel recalls repeated persecution from its youth, comparing its oppressors’ actions to plowing, but declares that the LORD has freed it from the wicked. The psalm calls for those who hate Zion to be turned back in shame, like rooftop grass that withers before harvest and receives no blessing.

sections.heading: A Curse on Those Who Hate Zion

Psalms 130.overview: The psalmist cries to the LORD from the depths, asks for mercy, and declares that forgiveness with God makes reverence possible. He waits for the LORD and urges Israel to hope in him, who has abundant loving devotion and will redeem Israel from all iniquity.

sections.heading: A plea for mercy and forgiveness

Psalms 131.overview: The psalmist rejects pride and ambition beyond his measure, describing his soul as quieted like a weaned child with its mother. He calls Israel to hope in the LORD now and forever.

Psalms 132.overview: The song recalls David’s hardships and oath to find a dwelling for the LORD, then summons the LORD and the ark to enter and bless the priests and worshipers. It recounts the LORD’s oath to David and his choice of Zion, promising provision, salvation, a Davidic ruler, and shame for the ruler’s enemies.

sections.heading: David’s Oath to Find a Dwelling
The Ark and Prayer for Blessing
The LORD’s Promises to David and Zion

Psalms 133.overview: David’s song celebrates the goodness and delight of brothers living together in harmony. It compares this harmony to oil flowing over Aaron and dew from Hermon on Zion, where the LORD bestows the blessing of life forevermore.

sections.heading: Oil, Dew, and the LORD’s Blessing

Psalms 134.overview: The psalm calls the LORD’s servants who serve by night in the temple to bless him with raised hands. It concludes with a blessing from the LORD, Maker of heaven and earth, from Zion.

Psalms 135.overview: The psalm summons the LORD’s servants to praise him, declaring his greatness, his choice of Jacob and Israel, and his rule over creation and history from Egypt to Canaan. It contrasts the LORD’s enduring name and care for his people with powerless idols, then calls Israel, Aaron’s house, Levi’s house, and all who fear the LORD to bless him in Zion and Jerusalem.

Psalms 136.overview: The psalm repeatedly gives thanks to the LORD, God of gods and Lord of lords, declaring that his loving devotion endures forever. It recounts his creation, deliverance of Israel from Egypt and through the wilderness, defeat of kings and gift of their land, remembrance of the lowly, rescue from enemies, and provision for all creatures.

sections.heading: Defeat of kings and gift of land

Psalms 137.overview: The exiles in Babylon weep for Zion, refuse their captors’ demand for a song, and pledge never to forget Jerusalem. The psalmist calls for the LORD to remember Edom’s role in Jerusalem’s fall and describes repayment against Babylon, including its infants.

sections.heading: Calls for Judgment on Edom and Babylon

Psalms 138.overview: David gives thanks to the LORD for answering him, strengthening him, and exalting his name and word. He declares that kings will praise the LORD, who attends to the lowly, preserves David from his foes, and will fulfill his purpose.

sections.heading: The LORD’s glory and care for the lowly

Psalms 139.overview: The psalmist declares that the LORD knows every thought and action and is present everywhere, beyond the reach of darkness or distance. He praises God for forming him and knowing his days, denounces God’s enemies, and asks God to search him and lead him in the way everlasting.

sections.heading: God forms and knows the psalmist
The psalmist’s appeal for judgment and guidance

Psalms 140.overview: David asks the LORD for protection from violent men who devise harm, use deceitful speech, and lay traps. He appeals to the LORD as his shield, asks that the wicked’s plans fail and their violence bring calamity, and affirms that the LORD upholds the needy and welcomes the upright.

sections.heading: Appeal for Protection from Violent Men
Trust in the LORD and Judgment on the Wicked

Psalms 141.overview: David calls on the LORD for a swift answer, asking that his prayer be received and his speech and heart guarded from evil. He welcomes the righteous person’s rebuke, describes the wicked rulers’ downfall and the scattering of bones, and seeks refuge from his enemies’ traps while asking that they fall into their own nets.

sections.heading: Rebuke and the wicked rulers’ downfall

Psalms 142.overview: David cries aloud to the LORD, pours out his complaint, and describes hidden danger, isolation, and a lack of refuge. He declares the LORD his refuge and portion, asks for rescue and release from confinement, and anticipates praise and the gathering of the righteous.

Psalms 143.overview: David appeals to the LORD for a hearing and mercy, describing enemy oppression, despair, and his longing for God. He asks for swift deliverance, guidance by God's Spirit, revival, and the defeat of his enemies.

Psalms 144.overview: David praises the LORD as his defender and reflects on human frailty. He asks God to rescue him from deceitful foreigners, promises a song of praise, and describes the prosperity and security of the people whose God is the LORD.

Psalms 145.overview: David’s psalm praises the LORD as King, recounting his unsearchable greatness and the declaration of his mighty works, goodness, and righteousness from one generation to the next. It describes the LORD’s everlasting kingdom, compassion, provision, and care for those who fear and love him, while declaring the destruction of the wicked and closing with praise from all creation.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Greatness and Mighty Works
The LORD’s Compassion and Everlasting Kingdom
The LORD’s Care for All Creation

Psalms 146.overview: The psalmist calls for lifelong praise to the LORD and warns against trusting mortal rulers, whose plans perish at death. It blesses those who rely on the God of Jacob, describing the LORD’s justice, care for the vulnerable, and everlasting reign over Zion.

Psalms 147.overview: The psalm praises the LORD for rebuilding Jerusalem, gathering Israel’s exiles, healing the brokenhearted, and ruling the stars with limitless power. It calls Jerusalem to praise God for sustaining the humble, providing for creation, governing the weather, and giving his word and judgments to Israel.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Word and Care for Israel

Psalms 148.overview: The psalm calls the heavens and their hosts, then the creatures and peoples of the earth, to praise the LORD, who creates and establishes them by command and decree. It declares the LORD’s exalted name and splendor and says he raises a horn for Israel, his people near to him.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Exalted Name and Israel’s Horn

Psalms 149.overview: The psalm calls Israel and the people of Zion to praise the LORD, their Maker and King, with song, dance, and instruments because he delights in his people and saves the afflicted. It joins the saints’ praise with a sword-bearing commission to execute the written judgment on the nations and their rulers, an honor given to all the LORD’s saints.

sections.heading: Praise for the LORD and His People

Psalms 150.overview: The psalm calls for praise of God in his sanctuary and mighty heavens, citing his mighty acts and excellent greatness. It names a range of instruments and dance, then extends the call to everything that has breath.

Proverbs 1.overview: Solomon presents proverbs designed to teach wisdom, discipline, insight, and just living, declaring that fear of the LORD begins knowledge. A father’s instruction warns against joining violent, greedy sinners, while personified Wisdom calls publicly and describes the consequences of rejecting counsel and the safety of listening.

Proverbs 2.overview: The father urges his son to seek wisdom, which the LORD gives and uses to teach justice and guard the upright. Wisdom protects him from evil people and the forbidden woman, while the upright remain in the land and the wicked are cut off.

sections.heading: The Paths of the Upright and Wicked

Proverbs 3.overview: The chapter urges trust in the LORD, adherence to his instruction, honor for him through wealth, and acceptance of his discipline, presenting wisdom as more valuable than riches and as the means by which the LORD created the world. It commends sound judgment, security under the LORD’s care, generosity and fairness toward neighbors, and contrasts the LORD’s treatment of the wicked and the righteous, the humble and the proud, and the wise and fools.

sections.heading: The Value and Foundation of Wisdom
Conduct Toward Neighbors and Divine Reversals

Proverbs 4.overview: A father recounts the instruction he received from his own father and urges his son to acquire, love, and hold fast to wisdom. He contrasts the bright path of the righteous with the dark way of the wicked, then calls his son to guard his heart, speech, gaze, and steps.

sections.heading: The Paths of Wisdom and Wickedness

Proverbs 5.overview: The speaker warns his son that the forbidden woman’s seductive words lead to death, loss, and regret. He commends faithfulness to one’s wife and declares that the LORD sees every path, while sin entraps the wicked and leads to death.

Proverbs 6.overview: The chapter warns against securing another person’s debt, urges the slacker to learn foresight from the ant, and describes the conduct and sudden ruin of a deceitful person. It lists seven things the LORD hates, then presents parental teaching as protection against adultery and describes the lasting disgrace and vengeance that follow it.

sections.heading: The deceitful person and what the LORD hates

Proverbs 7.overview: The teacher urges his son to keep wisdom and understanding close as protection from the adulteress. He recounts how a young man is enticed by her and warns his sons that her house leads to death.

sections.heading: The Young Man and the Adulteress

Proverbs 8.overview: Wisdom calls publicly, describes her truthful and righteous instruction, and declares her value, role in just rule, and gifts to those who love her. She recounts her existence before and participation in creation, then promises life and the LORD’s favor to those who heed her, while warning that rejecting her leads to harm and death.

Proverbs 9.overview: Wisdom builds her house, prepares a feast, and invites the simple to leave folly and follow understanding. Sayings contrast the response of mockers and the teachable, identify fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom, and set Folly’s deceptive invitation and deadly outcome against Wisdom’s call.

sections.heading: Correction and the Way of Wisdom

Proverbs 10.overview: Solomon’s proverbs contrast wisdom and foolishness, righteousness and wickedness, and describe their effects on family, work, speech, security, and reputation. They also portray the LORD as sustaining the righteous and bringing the wicked to ruin.

sections.heading: The Outcomes of Wisdom and Wickedness

Proverbs 11.overview: The proverbs contrast honest dealings, humility, and integrity with pride and wickedness, declaring that wealth cannot deliver from wrath and that the righteous are delivered while the wicked face ruin. They also describe how speech, counsel, generosity, and treatment of others affect a city and bring contrasting outcomes to the righteous and the wicked.

sections.heading: Integrity and the fate of the wicked
