Proverbs 12.overview: The chapter contrasts the teachable, righteous person with the one who rejects correction and devises evil, describing their differing prospects, relationships, and conduct. It sets wise and truthful speech, prudent responses, and diligent work against deceit, folly, and laziness, and concludes that the path of righteousness leads to life while another leads to death.

Proverbs 13.overview: Proverbs contrasts the outcomes of wisdom and folly in speech, work, integrity, wealth, and response to instruction. It portrays discipline, wise company, justice, and righteousness as sources of favor and provision, while folly and wickedness lead to strife, trouble, and loss.

Proverbs 14.overview: The chapter contrasts wisdom and folly in household life, speech, work, judgment, and conduct toward others. It links reverence for the LORD with security and life, and describes how righteousness, wise service, and care for the poor shape households and nations.

Proverbs 15.overview: Proverbs 15 contrasts wise and foolish speech, teachability and rejection of correction, and the outcomes of righteous and wicked ways under the LORD’s watch. It commends upright prayer, measured anger, good counsel, and humility, while comparing the value of reverence and love with wealth and strife.

sections.heading: Speech, Wisdom, and the LORD’s Watch

Proverbs 16.overview: The chapter contrasts human plans with the LORD’s direction and judgment, declaring that the LORD weighs motives, establishes outcomes, and governs even the casting of lots. It links righteous conduct and wise speech with sound kingship, while warning against pride, deceit, violence, and paths that lead to ruin.

sections.heading: Human Plans and the LORD’s Purpose
Conduct, Character, and the LORD’s Rule

Proverbs 17.overview: The chapter contrasts peace with strife, wise servants with foolish sons, and the LORD’s testing of hearts with human responses to evil, poverty, and calamity. It examines friendship, justice, family grief, and the effects of speech, concluding that even a fool seems wise when silent.

Proverbs 18.overview: Proverbs 18 contrasts isolation, foolish speech, partiality, and laziness with wisdom, justice, humility, and refuge in the name of the LORD. It describes the effects of words on conflict and judgment, and contrasts the poor and rich, a wife as a good gift, and unreliable companions with a faithful friend.

Proverbs 19.overview: The sayings contrast integrity and wisdom with folly, haste, dishonesty, and laziness, and describe how wealth shapes friendships and family relationships. They also address discipline, patience, care for the poor, the LORD’s purpose, and the consequences of rejecting instruction and justice.

Proverbs 20.overview: The chapter contrasts folly and wisdom in drinking, disputes, diligence, integrity, honest trade, and the exercise of royal judgment. It also describes human limits before the LORD, the consequences of family and financial choices, and the roles of justice, loyalty, age, and discipline.

Proverbs 21.overview: The proverbs affirm the LORD’s rule over the king and the heart, favor justice over sacrifice, and contrast the paths and outcomes of the righteous and the wicked. They address conflict, diligence, generosity, speech, and wisdom, concluding that no counsel prevails against the LORD and that victory comes from him.

sections.heading: The LORD Weighs Hearts and Ways

Proverbs 22.overview: The proverbs contrast riches with a good name, describe the LORD as Maker of rich and poor, and commend prudence, humility, child training, generosity, and justice while warning against debt, folly, and deceit. The speaker introduces sayings of wisdom and knowledge, then warns against oppressing the poor, associating with the hot-tempered, guaranteeing debts, moving boundary stones, and neglecting skilled work.

Proverbs 23.overview: Proverbs warns against deceptive feasts, fleeting wealth, stinginess, fools, and encroaching on the fields of the fatherless. A father instructs his son in discipline, wisdom, fear of the LORD, and restraint from sexual immorality and drunkenness.

sections.heading: Wisdom and Protection of the Vulnerable

Proverbs 24.overview: The sayings warn against envying the wicked, describe how wisdom builds and strengthens a household, and call for rescue of the endangered while affirming wisdom’s lasting hope. They contrast the fate of the righteous and wicked, address justice, honesty, and loyalty to the LORD and the king, and conclude with the neglected field as a lesson about sloth and poverty.

Proverbs 25.overview: The chapter identifies these sayings as Solomon’s proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men, and contrasts God’s hidden purposes with kings’ search for understanding and the removal of wickedness from royal courts. It presents sayings on humility before rulers, careful handling of disputes and confidences, fitting speech, reliable service, moderation, neighborly and enemy relations, and self-control.

Proverbs 26.overview: The chapter uses comparisons to describe the disorder caused by honoring fools, the risks of entrusting them with tasks, and the limits of responding to their folly. It also portrays the slacker’s excuses, warns against meddling and gossip that fuel conflict, and describes the deceit and eventual exposure of hatred.

Proverbs 27.overview: The sayings warn against boasting about tomorrow and praising oneself, and contrast faithful correction and counsel with deceitful affection and unstable attachment. They commend prudence, mutual sharpening, and diligent care of flocks, whose produce sustains a household despite the impermanence of wealth and rank.

sections.heading: Care of Flocks and Household Provision

Proverbs 28.overview: The chapter contrasts the fear and instability of the wicked with the boldness and security of the righteous, and links just leadership and respect for the law with social order. Its sayings address integrity, confession, wealth, honest speech, trust in the LORD, care for the poor, and the changing fortunes of rulers and their people.

Proverbs 29.overview: The chapter contrasts the consequences of righteousness and wickedness in personal conduct and public life, including the effects of just or exploitative rulers on the people. It also addresses discipline, speech, anger, humility, trust in the LORD, and the claim that justice comes from the LORD rather than merely from a ruler’s favor.

Proverbs 30.overview: Agur son of Jakeh acknowledges his limits, questions who commands creation, affirms the purity of God’s word, and asks for truth and sufficient provision. He then presents sayings about harmful generations, insatiable desires, puzzling and unbearable things, small creatures, stately figures, and the consequences of stirring anger.

Proverbs 31.overview: King Lemuel’s mother warns him against sexual excess and strong drink, and urges him to defend the poor and those without a voice. The chapter praises a capable wife whose industry, care for her household, generosity, wisdom, and fear of the LORD earn her trust, praise, and recognition.

Ecclesiastes 1.overview: The Teacher, identified as a son of David and king in Jerusalem, declares that everything is futile and asks what people gain from their labor. He describes nature’s recurring cycles and the fading of human memory, then recounts his search for wisdom, which brings sorrow and proves to be a pursuit of the wind.

Ecclesiastes 2.overview: The Teacher tests laughter, wine, great projects, wealth, and every desired pleasure, but finds them futile and gains nothing lasting from his labor. He weighs wisdom against folly and toil against death and inheritance, then concludes that enjoyment comes from God, who gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please him while assigning the sinner the task of gathering for another.

Ecclesiastes 3.overview: The Teacher lists appointed times for opposing human activities and reflects on God’s ordering of events, the limits of human understanding, and the gifts of work and enjoyment. He observes injustice in earthly courts, affirms that God will judge, and considers the shared fate of humans and animals in death.

Ecclesiastes 4.overview: The Teacher observes oppression without comfort, the futility of envy-driven labor and hoarded wealth, and the advantage of contentment over toil. He contrasts isolation with the benefits of companionship, then describes a poor, wise youth who succeeds an old, foolish king and later loses public favor.

Ecclesiastes 5.overview: The Teacher urges careful listening before God, restrained speech, and fulfillment of vows, then describes oppression and the dissatisfaction and insecurity that accompany wealth. He contrasts the rich person’s unrest and the futility of hoarding with the good of enjoying one’s labor and possessions as gifts from God.

Ecclesiastes 6.overview: The Teacher describes the misery of a wealthy man who cannot enjoy his possessions, contrasting his long but unsatisfied life with the rest of a stillborn child. He observes that labor and desire remain unfulfilled, that people cannot contend with what is stronger than they are, and that no one knows what is good or what will come after life under the sun.

Ecclesiastes 7.overview: The Teacher contrasts wisdom with folly, saying that mourning, rebuke, patience, and wisdom offer more than feasting, foolish laughter, and pride, while God governs prosperity and adversity. He considers moderation, human sin, and the limits of his search for wisdom, concluding that God made humanity upright but people pursued many schemes.

sections.heading: The Limits of the Search for Wisdom

Ecclesiastes 8.overview: The Teacher describes wisdom as discerning and counsels obedience to the king, while noting that human beings cannot control death or know what lies ahead. He observes oppression and unfair outcomes, affirms that it goes well with those who fear God, commends enjoyment of life, and concludes that people cannot comprehend God’s work.

sections.heading: The king’s authority and human limits
Injustice and the outcomes of righteousness
Enjoyment of life and God’s work

Ecclesiastes 9.overview: The Teacher says the righteous and wicked share one earthly fate, while the living can still enjoy life and the dead have no further part in what happens under the sun. He urges joyful living and diligent work, then observes that time and chance overtake everyone and recounts how a poor wise man saves a city but is forgotten.

Ecclesiastes 10.overview: The chapter contrasts wisdom with folly, showing how even a little folly damages honor and how a fool exposes himself through his conduct and speech. It describes the effects of rulers’ appointments and temper, the risks of work done without skill, and the consequences of foolish speech, poor leadership, idleness, and careless words about the king.

sections.heading: Wisdom, Folly, and a Ruler’s Anger

Ecclesiastes 11.overview: The Teacher commends casting bread and sharing portions broadly, then contrasts the uncertainty of outcomes and God’s work with the need to sow diligently. He reflects on the goodness and brevity of life, calling for joy in youth while noting the days of darkness and God’s judgment.

Ecclesiastes 12.overview: The Teacher urges remembrance of the Creator before old age and death, depicting declining faculties and the return of dust and spirit to God. He calls everything futile, describes his work arranging truthful proverbs, and concludes that fearing God and keeping his commandments are central because God judges every deed.

Song of Solomon 1.overview: The woman expresses desire for the beloved, praises his love and fragrance, and describes her sun-darkened appearance and labor in the vineyards. The beloved answers with praise and a promise of ornaments, and the two exchange images of fragrance, beauty, and a shared dwelling.

Song of Solomon 2.overview: The woman and her beloved compare each other to flowers, fruit, and shelter, while she addresses the daughters of Jerusalem with a warning not to awaken love before its time. She hears her beloved arrive and invite her into the spring landscape, asks him to catch the foxes that threaten the vineyards, affirms their mutual belonging, and calls him toward the mountains of Bether.

sections.heading: The Lovers’ Praise and the Warning

Song of Solomon 3.overview: The speaker searches the city for the one she loves, finds him, brings him to her mother’s chamber, and adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time. A procession bearing Solomon in a richly adorned carriage approaches from the wilderness, and the daughters of Zion are invited to see him crowned on his wedding day.

Song of Solomon 4.overview: The beloved praises his bride’s beauty, invites her from Lebanon, and compares her love and fragrance to wine, spices, and a sealed garden. The bride calls on the north and south winds to spread the garden’s fragrance and invites her beloved to enjoy its fruits.

sections.heading: The Bride as a Fragrant Garden

Song of Solomon 5.overview: The beloved enters the garden and invites his companions to eat and drink. The woman recounts missing his arrival and searching for him, then asks the daughters of Jerusalem to find him; when they ask what distinguishes him, she describes his beauty.

sections.heading: The Woman Searches for Her Beloved

Song of Solomon 6.overview: The women ask where the beloved has gone, and the woman says he is in his garden, affirming their mutual belonging. The beloved praises her beauty and uniqueness among queens and maidens, while the poem turns to a walnut grove, royal chariots, and repeated calls for the Shulammite to return.

sections.heading: The Walnut Grove and the Shulammite

Song of Solomon 7.overview: The beloved praises the woman’s beauty, comparing her features and stature to precious objects, landscapes, and fruit. She declares that she belongs to him and invites him to the countryside and vineyards, where she offers him her love and treasured delicacies.

sections.heading: The Beloved’s Praise of Her Beauty

Song of Solomon 8.overview: The woman longs for public intimacy with her beloved and invokes the warning not to awaken love before its time. The poem recalls their beginnings and celebrates love’s strength, then turns to the brothers’ concern for their sister, the woman’s maturity and vineyard, and the lovers’ final invitation.

sections.heading: Longing and the warning about love

Isaiah 1.overview: Isaiah introduces his vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem and presents the LORD’s indictment of a rebellious people whose land is desolate and whose worship is rejected because of injustice. The LORD calls them to turn from evil, promises cleansing and restoration for the willing, and declares judgment on rebels while Zion is redeemed and restored as the faithful city.

sections.heading: Rejected Worship and Call for Justice

Isaiah 2.overview: Isaiah presents a vision of nations streaming to the LORD’s house in Jerusalem, where the LORD teaches and judges them and war ends. He contrasts this future with Jacob’s idolatry and pride, describes the LORD’s day of judgment against human arrogance and idols, and warns against trusting mortal people.

sections.heading: The Nations Come to the LORD’s Mountain

Isaiah 3.overview: The LORD removes Jerusalem and Judah’s food, water, and established leaders, leaving the people oppressed and unable to find a willing ruler. He judges the people and their corrupt leaders, distinguishes the fate of the righteous and wicked, and announces the humiliation of Zion’s women and the city’s mourning.

sections.heading: Judgment on Judah and Its Leaders
Zion’s Women and the City’s Ruin

Isaiah 4.overview: Seven women ask one man to let them bear his name and remove their disgrace. The LORD’s Branch brings beauty to Israel’s survivors, while the Lord purifies Jerusalem and provides a protective canopy over Mount Zion.

sections.heading: Seven Women Seek a Man’s Name

Isaiah 5.overview: Isaiah presents the LORD’s vineyard as Israel and Judah, whose failure to produce justice and righteousness leads to its desolation. He pronounces woes on the people’s greed, drunkenness, defiance, moral confusion, pride, and corruption, then describes the LORD’s judgment through a swiftly advancing foreign army.

Isaiah 6.overview: Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned in the temple, hears the seraphim proclaim his holiness, and receives cleansing for his unclean lips. The Lord sends Isaiah to pronounce judgment on the people, and declares that desolation will continue until only a stump remains as the holy seed.

sections.heading: The Lord’s holiness and Isaiah’s cleansing

Isaiah 7.overview: Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel threaten Jerusalem, and Isaiah tells Ahaz that their plan will fail and that Ephraim will be shattered. When Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, Isaiah announces Immanuel and describes the coming devastation of Judah by Assyria, including depopulated fields and thorn-covered land.

Isaiah 8.overview: The LORD directs Isaiah to name his son Maher-shalal-hash-baz as a sign that Assyria will carry off the wealth of Damascus and Samaria, and warns that the Assyrian flood will reach Judah. The LORD tells Isaiah to regard him as holy rather than share the people’s fears, while Isaiah preserves the testimony and rejects consultation of mediums as the chapter describes the distress awaiting those without the LORD’s light.

sections.heading: Assyria’s Flood and the Nations’ Defeat
The LORD as Sanctuary and Stumbling Stone

Isaiah 9.overview: Isaiah announces light and joy for Galilee, the end of oppression, and the reign of a child on David’s throne with justice and peace. He then declares judgment against Israel for its pride, refusal to return to the LORD, corrupt leadership, and violence, while the LORD’s anger remains unappeased.

Isaiah 10.overview: Isaiah pronounces judgment on unjust rulers and describes Assyria as the instrument of divine anger, while condemning the empire’s ambition and declaring that the Lord will punish its arrogance. A remnant of Israel will return and rely on the LORD, who promises to break Assyria’s yoke as its forces advance toward Jerusalem and are finally cut down.

Isaiah 11.overview: A shoot from Jesse’s stump rules with the Spirit of the LORD, judges the poor with righteousness, and brings peace across creation. The Root of Jesse becomes a banner for the nations as the LORD gathers Israel’s and Judah’s exiles, reunites Ephraim and Judah, and opens a way for the remnant to return.

sections.heading: The Gathering and Return of the Remnant

Isaiah 12.overview: The speaker praises the LORD because his anger has turned away and God has become his salvation, strength, and song. The people are called to proclaim the LORD’s works among the nations, sing of his glorious deeds, and celebrate the Holy One of Israel in Zion.

Isaiah 13.overview: Isaiah presents an oracle against Babylon, as the LORD of Hosts summons a distant army to carry out his wrath. The Day of the LORD brings terror, cosmic upheaval, and judgment, as the Medes attack and Babylon is overthrown and left desolate.

Isaiah 14.overview: The LORD restores Jacob and Israel, and a taunt song describes the fall of Babylon’s king, whose ambition ends in humiliation and burial denied. The LORD declares Babylon’s destruction, Assyria’s defeat, and a coming threat to Philistia, while affirming that Zion is a refuge for his afflicted people.

Isaiah 15.overview: The oracle announces the nighttime destruction of Ar and Kir and depicts mourning across Moab’s towns, including Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon, and Elealeh. Moab’s fugitives flee as drought and loss spread, while the outcry reaches its borders and a further judgment is threatened against Dimon and the land’s survivors.

Isaiah 16.overview: Moab is urged to send tribute to Zion, and its refugees seek shelter as the oracle describes a faithful ruler established on David’s throne. Moab’s pride, devastated vineyards, and futile worship are lamented, and the LORD declares that its splendor will fall within three years.

Isaiah 17.overview: Isaiah announces the ruin of Damascus and Aroer, the loss of power in Aram and Ephraim, and the fading of Jacob’s splendor, though a remnant remains. He describes Israel turning from handmade idols to its Maker, warns that forgotten trust brings a failed harvest, and depicts the LORD driving away the raging nations.

Isaiah 18.overview: The oracle describes Cush’s swift messengers and calls the peoples of the earth to watch for a signal as the LORD observes quietly and cuts down the nation before harvest. At that time, gifts from the people of Cush are brought to the LORD of Hosts at Mount Zion.

sections.heading: The Signal and the LORD’s Judgment

Isaiah 19.overview: Isaiah announces the LORD’s judgment on Egypt through civil conflict, the drying of the Nile, economic distress, and the failure of its rulers and counselors. He then describes Egypt’s fear and turn to the LORD, followed by worship and peace among Egypt, Assyria, and Israel.

sections.heading: The Nile’s Decline and Egypt’s Confusion
Egypt’s Turn and the Nations’ Unity

Isaiah 20.overview: After the commander sent by Sargon king of Assyria captures Ashdod, Isaiah removes his sackcloth and sandals and walks naked and barefoot as a sign against Egypt and Cush. The LORD declares that Assyria will deport Egypt’s and Cush’s people, leaving those who trusted in them dismayed, while the coastland’s inhabitants question how they can escape.

sections.heading: Assyria’s Captives and the Coastland’s Fear

Isaiah 21.overview: Isaiah describes the fall of Babylon, as Elam and Media are summoned against it and a lookout reports that the city has fallen. He then records the watchman’s answer to Seir and the call to shelter Dedanite caravans, while declaring that Kedar’s strength will soon diminish.

Isaiah 22.overview: Isaiah describes the tumult and coming judgment of Jerusalem, where its people prepare defenses and provisions but fail to turn to the Lord, while choosing feasting instead of mourning. The Lord removes Shebna from his palace office, appoints Eliakim with authority over the house of David, and declares that the firm peg bearing his family’s honor will eventually give way.

sections.heading: Jerusalem’s preparations and refusal to mourn

Isaiah 23.overview: Isaiah announces Tyre’s destruction, bringing grief to its merchants and neighboring peoples, including Sidon, Egypt, and Tarshish. The LORD brings down Tyre and later restores its trade after seventy years, with its profits set apart for those who live before him.

Isaiah 24.overview: The LORD lays waste the earth and scatters its inhabitants, bringing judgment for their violation of the everlasting covenant as wine, music, and the city of chaos disappear. Voices from the ends of the earth proclaim the LORD’s glory, while a speaker laments amid treachery and the shaking earth, and the LORD punishes heavenly and earthly powers before reigning on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem.

Isaiah 25.overview: Isaiah praises the LORD for faithful wonders, the destruction of a fortified city, and refuge from ruthless nations. The LORD prepares a banquet on the mountain, removes death and disgrace, and saves his people, while Moab is humbled and its fortress falls.

sections.heading: Praise for the LORD’s works and refuge
Moab’s humiliation and fortress brought down

Isaiah 26.overview: Judah’s song celebrates a secure city, the LORD’s peace for those who trust him, and the humbling of the lofty city, while the people wait for his judgments and confess that he alone has acted for them. The people describe their distress and failed efforts to bring salvation, then declare that the dead will rise and that the LORD will leave his dwelling to punish the earth’s inhabitants.

sections.heading: Judah’s Song of the Secure City
The Righteous and the LORD’s Judgments

Isaiah 27.overview: The LORD judges Leviathan, guards his vineyard, and offers peace, while Jacob takes root and bears fruit as its guilt is removed and its idolatrous altars are destroyed. The fortified city lies abandoned, but the LORD gathers the Israelites from the Euphrates to Egypt, and exiles return to worship on Jerusalem’s holy mountain.

Isaiah 28.overview: Isaiah announces the fall of Ephraim’s drunken leaders and contrasts their ruined crown with the LORD’s glory and justice for the remnant. He condemns Jerusalem’s rulers for trusting a covenant with death, declares a tested cornerstone in Zion and judgment on their refuge of lies, then compares the LORD’s instruction to a farmer’s varied work.

sections.heading: Ephraim’s fallen crown and the remnant’s hope
Drunken leaders reject the LORD’s instruction
Jerusalem’s false refuge and coming judgment
The farmer’s work as a picture of wisdom

Isaiah 29.overview: The LORD declares that Ariel will be besieged, brought low, and then delivered as its attacking nations vanish like a dream. Isaiah exposes Judah’s spiritual blindness and hidden schemes, then describes the LORD’s renewal of the land, vindication of the humble, and restoration of Jacob.

Isaiah 30.overview: The LORD condemns Judah’s reliance on Egypt and its rejection of prophetic instruction, warning that misplaced trust brings shame and sudden collapse. He promises compassion, guidance, and renewal for Zion, while the LORD’s arrival brings judgment on the nations and the destruction of Assyria.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Compassion and Zion’s Renewal

Isaiah 31.overview: Isaiah warns those who seek Egypt’s help that the LORD will bring down both Egypt and its allies, while the Egyptians are merely human. The LORD promises to protect Jerusalem, calls Israel to reject its idols and return to him, and declares that Assyria will fall by no human sword.

Isaiah 32.overview: Isaiah describes a righteous king and just princes, then contrasts the protection and understanding they bring with the conduct of fools, scoundrels, and noble people. He warns complacent women of failed harvests and the city’s desolation, then portrays the Spirit’s outpouring, renewed justice and peace, judgment on the city, and abundant life beside the waters.

Isaiah 33.overview: The chapter pronounces woe on the destroyer, calls on the LORD for help, and depicts Zion filled with justice, wisdom, and salvation amid the nations’ devastation. The LORD rises in judgment, provides refuge for the righteous, and secures Jerusalem under the King’s rule, with its people forgiven and free from sickness.

sections.heading: Judgment and Refuge for the Righteous

Isaiah 34.overview: Isaiah summons the nations to hear the LORD’s judgment, describing the destruction of their armies and the collapse of the heavens before the LORD’s sword falls on Edom. The LORD’s vengeance for Zion leaves Edom desolate and inhabited by wild creatures, and the concluding decree affirms that its allotted fate will endure.

sections.heading: Judgment on the Nations and Heavens

Isaiah 35.overview: Isaiah describes the wilderness and desert blooming with the glory of the LORD, while God comes to save those with anxious hearts and restore the blind, deaf, lame, and mute. A holy highway leads the redeemed safely to Zion, where they return with everlasting joy as sorrow and sighing flee.

Isaiah 36.overview: Sennacherib captures Judah’s fortified cities and sends the Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem, where Hezekiah’s officials meet him. The Rabshakeh challenges Judah’s trust in Egypt and the LORD, urges the people to surrender, and the officials return to Hezekiah with his words.

Isaiah 37.overview: Hezekiah responds to the Assyrian threat by sending officials to Isaiah, then spreads Sennacherib’s letter before the LORD and prays for Jerusalem’s deliverance. Isaiah declares that the LORD will turn Sennacherib back and defend Jerusalem; the angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, where his sons kill him.

Isaiah 38.overview: Isaiah tells Hezekiah that he will die, then reports that the LORD hears Hezekiah’s prayer, grants him fifteen more years, promises to defend Jerusalem from Assyria, and confirms the promise with the sun’s shadow moving backward. Hezekiah’s song describes his anguish at the prospect of death and his gratitude for restored life, while the chapter closes with Isaiah’s fig treatment and Hezekiah’s question about a sign.

sections.heading: Hezekiah’s Song of Anguish and Thanks
The Fig Treatment and Hezekiah’s Question

Isaiah 39.overview: Merodach-baladan of Babylon sends envoys and a gift to Hezekiah, who shows them all his treasures and armory. Isaiah announces that Babylon will carry away the palace treasures and take some of Hezekiah’s descendants, and Hezekiah accepts the word because he expects peace during his lifetime.

Isaiah 40.overview: The LORD promises comfort and pardon for Jerusalem, announces a way prepared for his coming, and declares that his enduring word and shepherd care surpass human frailty. Isaiah proclaims the LORD’s unmatched power as Creator and ruler of the nations, then assures Jacob and Israel that he renews the strength of those who wait for him.

sections.heading: Comfort and the Coming of the LORD

Isaiah 41.overview: The LORD summons the nations to hear his case, declares that he raises a conqueror from the east, and contrasts their fear and idol-making with his choice of Israel and promises to help, strengthen, and restore the people. He challenges the nations’ gods to prove their power by foretelling events, declares their images and works empty, and says he has announced a messenger and raised a ruler to march over kings.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Announcement and Empty Idols

Isaiah 42.overview: The LORD presents his servant as the one who brings justice to the nations, appoints him as a covenant and light, and declares new things. A call to praise the LORD accompanies his promises to guide the blind and defeat idols, while Israel’s blindness, plunder, and disobedience are linked to the LORD’s anger.

sections.heading: The Servant’s Mission and the LORD’s Promise
A New Song and Divine Deliverance

Isaiah 43.overview: The LORD promises to protect and gather Israel, identifies the people as his witnesses to his uniqueness as God, and announces Babylon’s defeat and a new way through the wilderness. He contrasts Israel’s neglect and sins with his forgiveness, then declares judgment on Jacob and Israel for their rebellion.

sections.heading: Babylon’s defeat and a new exodus

Isaiah 44.overview: The LORD addresses Jacob and Israel as his chosen servants, promises blessing for their descendants, and declares that he alone is God. He exposes the folly of idol-making, promises to redeem and forgive Israel, and announces Jerusalem’s rebuilding through Cyrus.

sections.heading: Israel Chosen and the LORD Alone

Isaiah 45.overview: The LORD commissions Cyrus to subdue nations and free Israel’s exiles, declaring that he alone creates and governs all things. The LORD rebukes those who challenge their Maker, promises Israel lasting salvation, and calls the nations to turn from idols, as every people acknowledges his sovereignty and Israel is vindicated.

sections.heading: The Maker and his purpose for Cyrus
The LORD’s call to all nations

Isaiah 46.overview: Bel and Nebo’s idols burden their carriers and go into captivity, while God says he has carried Israel from birth and contrasts his power with lifeless images. God declares his purpose and coming action from the east, then promises that his righteousness and salvation will come to Zion and Israel.

sections.heading: Bel and Nebo Go into Captivity
God’s Purpose and Salvation for Zion

Isaiah 47.overview: The LORD, Israel’s Redeemer, announces Babylon’s fall, stripping the Daughter of the Chaldeans of her throne and exposing her shame. He recalls her merciless rule over Israel and declares that her pride, sorceries, and astrologers cannot avert sudden disaster or save her.

Isaiah 48.overview: The LORD addresses Jacob and Israel as covenant people who invoke him without truth, recalls his foretold acts, and announces new things despite their stubbornness. He restrains judgment for his name, declares his sovereignty and the success of his chosen ally against Babylon, then calls Jacob to leave Babylon, recalls provision in the wilderness, and declares no peace for the wicked.

sections.heading: The LORD’s glory and Babylon’s defeat
Departure from Babylon and no peace

Isaiah 49.overview: The LORD calls and equips the Servant, who is identified as Israel, and commissions him to restore Jacob and bring salvation to the nations. The LORD promises to free and regather his people, comfort Zion with images of enduring remembrance and renewed population, and defeat her oppressors so all humanity will know him as Savior and Redeemer.

sections.heading: The Servant and the People’s Restoration
The LORD Remembers and Rebuilds Zion

Isaiah 50.overview: The LORD denies that Israel was rejected through a divorce or sale to creditors, attributing the separation to the people’s sins and declaring his power to redeem. The Servant describes his instruction, suffering, and confidence in the LORD’s vindication, and the chapter contrasts those who trust God in darkness with those who rely on their own fire.

Isaiah 51.overview: The LORD calls those who seek righteousness to remember Abraham and Sarah, promising Zion’s restoration, justice for the nations, and enduring salvation despite the passing of heaven and earth. The LORD promises the redeemed’s return to Zion, comforts Jerusalem’s afflicted people, and removes the cup of fury from her, placing it instead in the hands of her tormentors.

Isaiah 52.overview: The LORD calls Zion to rise and be restored, declaring that Jerusalem will be redeemed without payment and that his people will know his name after oppression by Egypt, Assyria, and their current rulers. Heralds proclaim that God reigns and returns to Zion, the people depart under his protection, and the LORD’s Servant is exalted after being disfigured, bringing astonishment and understanding to nations and kings.

sections.heading: Good news and departure from exile

Isaiah 53.overview: The speakers describe the servant’s humble appearance, rejection, suffering, and death as bearing the people’s sins and bringing them peace. The LORD’s purpose for the servant includes vindication, offspring, prolonged days, and a portion among the great.

Isaiah 54.overview: The LORD promises the desolate woman many descendants and calls her back, declaring that he is her Maker and Redeemer. He pledges everlasting compassion and a covenant of peace, then promises to rebuild the afflicted city in splendor, establish its people in righteousness, and protect his servants from attack and accusation.

Isaiah 55.overview: The LORD invites the thirsty to receive freely and promises an everlasting covenant tied to David, with nations drawn to Israel. He calls the wicked to return, declares that his ways and word surpass human understanding and accomplish his purpose, and promises joyful, lasting renewal.

sections.heading: Return to the LORD and trust his word

Isaiah 56.overview: The LORD calls for justice and Sabbath observance as His salvation approaches. He promises eunuchs and foreigners who hold to His covenant lasting honor and a place in His house of prayer, then condemns Israel’s blind, self-serving watchmen and shepherds.

Isaiah 57.overview: The chapter says the righteous die and enter peace while the living ignore their removal, then condemns the people’s idolatry, child sacrifice, and alliances. The LORD promises to restore the humble and contrite, while declaring that the wicked have no peace.

Isaiah 58.overview: The LORD commands the prophet to expose Jacob’s sins, contrasting the people’s apparent devotion with oppression and conflict during their fasts. He defines chosen fasting as liberation and care for the needy, promises guidance and restoration, and links Sabbath honor with delight and Jacob’s inheritance.

Isaiah 59.overview: The people’s violence, deceit, and rebellion separate them from God, while they confess that justice and salvation remain far off. The LORD sees that no one intercedes, brings salvation and judgment, comes as Redeemer to Zion, and promises an enduring covenant of Spirit and word.

sections.heading: Confession and the Absence of Justice

Isaiah 60.overview: The LORD’s glory rises over Zion, drawing returning children, nations, kings, and their wealth to the city and its sanctuary. The LORD promises Zion restoration, peace, enduring light, a righteous people, and growth into a mighty nation.

sections.heading: Nations and wealth come to Zion

Isaiah 61.overview: An anointed speaker announces good news, liberty, comfort, and restoration for Zion’s mourners, who will rebuild ruined cities and receive honor and provision among the nations. The LORD promises justice, an everlasting covenant, and blessing for the people’s descendants, while the speaker rejoices in salvation and righteousness that will flourish before all nations.

sections.heading: Good News and Comfort for Zion
Salvation and Righteousness Before the Nations

Isaiah 62.overview: The speaker vows to keep proclaiming for Zion until her righteousness and salvation shine, and describes Jerusalem’s new name, honor, and marriage-like joy with the LORD. Watchmen call continually for Jerusalem’s restoration, the LORD swears that its harvest will no longer be taken by enemies, and a proclamation announces the coming Savior and Zion’s new names.

sections.heading: The Way Prepared for Zion’s Savior

Isaiah 63.overview: The chapter depicts the divine warrior returning from Edom and Bozrah after treading the nations in wrath, bringing vindication and redemption by his own strength. Israel recounts the LORD’s past compassion and deliverance through Moses, then laments the people’s rebellion, the loss of the sanctuary, and their estrangement from God while pleading for him to return.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Past Compassion and Deliverance
A Plea for the LORD to Return

Isaiah 64.overview: The speaker calls for the LORD to descend in power, recalling his awesome works and declaring that no other God acts for those who wait for him. The community confesses its sin and desolation, appeals to the LORD as Father and maker, and asks him not to remain silent or afflict them beyond measure.

sections.heading: A Plea for God to Descend
Appeal to the LORD as Father

Isaiah 65.overview: The LORD contrasts judgment on those who persist in idolatry and reject his calls with preservation and blessing for his servants, including descendants of Jacob and Judah. He promises a new creation centered on Jerusalem, where his people enjoy long life, the fruit of their labor, answered prayer, and peace among living creatures.

sections.heading: Preservation of servants and judgment of the unfaithful
New creation and peace in Jerusalem

Isaiah 66.overview: The LORD rejects worship that is joined to disobedience, esteems the humble who heed his word, and promises judgment on his enemies. He promises Jerusalem’s restoration and comfort, gathers the nations to witness his glory and bring Israel’s dispersed people home, and declares enduring worship alongside the rebels’ punishment.

sections.heading: True Worship and the LORD’s Judgment

Jeremiah 1.overview: The chapter identifies Jeremiah of Anathoth and dates his prophetic ministry from Josiah’s reign through Jerusalem’s exile under Zedekiah, as the LORD appoints him prophet to the nations and equips him to speak. Through visions of an almond branch and a boiling pot, the LORD announces judgment from the north against Judah for its idolatry and promises to deliver Jeremiah despite opposition.

sections.heading: Visions of Judgment from the North

Jeremiah 2.overview: The LORD recalls Israel’s early devotion, then accuses its people and leaders of abandoning him for idols despite his deliverance and provision. He describes the resulting devastation, condemns Judah’s idolatry and injustice, and warns that reliance on Egypt and Assyria will fail.

Jeremiah 3.overview: The LORD condemns Israel’s and Judah’s idolatry, declaring Judah’s pretense worse than Israel’s open unfaithfulness. He calls Israel to return, promises restoration in Zion and the reunion of Israel and Judah, and concludes with Israel’s confession of sin and appeal for mercy.

sections.heading: Call to Return and Promise of Restoration

Jeremiah 4.overview: The LORD calls Israel and Judah to return, reform their hearts, and live in truth, while warning that an invading force from the north will bring judgment on Jerusalem. Jeremiah laments the coming devastation as the land is laid waste, its people flee, and Daughter Zion cries out before her attackers.

sections.heading: Jeremiah’s Lament and the Desolate Land

Jeremiah 5.overview: The LORD finds no one in Jerusalem who acts justly or seeks truth, and Jeremiah describes the people’s hardened rebellion, idolatry, and unfaithfulness. The LORD announces invasion and exile while sparing a remnant, then condemns the people’s disregard for him, social injustice, and acceptance of false prophets and self-appointed priests.

Jeremiah 6.overview: Jeremiah warns Benjamin and Jerusalem of an invading army from the north and describes the city’s oppression, violence, and coming destruction. The people reject the LORD’s word, the ancient paths, and the warnings of watchmen, while corrupt leaders offer false assurances; the chapter ends with the enemy’s approach and Judah’s failed refining.

sections.heading: The Northern Army and Rejected Silver

Jeremiah 7.overview: Jeremiah proclaims at the temple gate that Judah’s safety depends not on the temple but on just conduct, care for the vulnerable, and exclusive worship of the LORD; he warns that continued violence and idolatry will bring judgment like Shiloh’s. The LORD rejects the people’s sacrifices and recounts their refusal to obey the prophets, then condemns the idols in the temple and the child sacrifices at Topheth, foretelling slaughter and the end of celebration in Judah and Jerusalem.

sections.heading: Judgment for Worship of the Queen of Heaven

Jeremiah 8.overview: The LORD announces the exposure of Judah’s graves and condemns Jerusalem’s persistent refusal to repent, false claims of wisdom, and deceitful assurances of peace. He declares judgment through failed harvests, enemy invasion, and affliction, while Jeremiah voices grief over the people’s devastation and lack of healing.

sections.heading: Jeremiah’s Grief and the People’s Wound

Jeremiah 9.overview: Jeremiah laments Judah’s deceit and faithlessness as the LORD announces punishment, Jerusalem’s desolation, and the people’s scattering. The chapter calls for mourning, rejects boasting in wisdom, strength, or wealth, and warns that circumcision of the flesh cannot protect those uncircumcised in heart.

sections.heading: True Boasting and Circumcision of the Heart

Jeremiah 10.overview: The LORD warns Israel against the customs and idols of the nations, contrasting powerless images with the living God, King and Creator. He announces the displacement of the land’s inhabitants and devastation from the north, while the speaker laments Judah’s ruin and asks the LORD for just correction and judgment on the nations.

Jeremiah 11.overview: The LORD reminds Jeremiah to proclaim the covenant to Judah and Jerusalem, recounts their persistent disobedience and idolatry, and announces disaster from which neither the people nor their gods can deliver them. The LORD forbids Jeremiah to intercede, describes Judah’s destruction, and answers the plot against Jeremiah by declaring judgment on the men of Anathoth who seek his life.

Jeremiah 12.overview: Jeremiah questions why the wicked prosper, affirms that the LORD knows his heart, and asks how long the land will suffer for its people’s evil; the LORD warns Jeremiah about greater trials and betrayal by his family. The LORD describes the devastation of his inheritance by enemies and declares that he will uproot hostile nations, later show them compassion if they learn his people’s ways, and destroy any nation that refuses to obey.

sections.heading: Warning of Greater Trials and Betrayal
The Desolation of the LORD’s Inheritance
Uprooting and Restoration of the Nations

Jeremiah 13.overview: Jeremiah acts out the sign of a ruined linen loincloth, which the LORD uses to declare that Judah and Jerusalem have become useless through pride, disobedience, and worship of other gods; he also warns that their leaders and people will be filled with drunkenness and destroyed. The chapter calls for attention to the LORD’s warning, announces the king and queen mother’s humiliation and Judah’s exile, and attributes Jerusalem’s coming disgrace to its entrenched sin and false worship.

Jeremiah 14.overview: Jeremiah describes the drought devastating Judah and the people’s pleas for the LORD to act despite their sins. The LORD rejects prayer and offerings, condemns the prophets who promise peace, and Jeremiah voices the people’s confession and appeal to the LORD’s covenant.

Jeremiah 15.overview: The LORD rejects even hypothetical intercession by Moses and Samuel, assigns Judah death, sword, famine, and captivity, and links Jerusalem’s devastation to Manasseh’s deeds. Jeremiah laments his conflict and suffering, recalls his devotion to the LORD’s words, and receives a promise of restoration and protection amid further judgment on Judah.

sections.heading: Jeremiah’s Plea and the LORD’s Promise

Jeremiah 16.overview: The LORD forbids Jeremiah to marry, mourn, or feast in Judah as signs that disease, violence, exile, and the loss of communal joy are coming. He explains that judgment follows the people’s idolatry and disobedience, promises their return from exile, and declares that the nations will recognize his power and name.

Jeremiah 17.overview: Judah’s idolatry is engraved on its heart and altars, bringing exile, while Jeremiah contrasts trust in the LORD with trust in human strength and declares that the LORD searches the heart. Jeremiah asks the LORD for healing and protection, then delivers a warning at Jerusalem’s gates that Sabbath observance will bring the city’s continued life, while disobedience will bring its destruction by fire.

sections.heading: The Sabbath Warning at Jerusalem’s Gates

Jeremiah 18.overview: The LORD sends Jeremiah to a potter’s house, then uses the potter’s reshaping of flawed clay to explain how he may change his purposes for Israel and other nations in response to their conduct; Judah and Jerusalem are warned to turn from evil, but they reject the warning. The LORD condemns Israel’s idolatry and announces disaster, while Jeremiah’s opponents plot against him and he asks the LORD to judge them.

Jeremiah 19.overview: The LORD sends Jeremiah with Judah’s elders and priests to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, where he announces Jerusalem’s coming devastation because its people have abandoned the LORD, worshiped other gods, and shed innocent blood. Jeremiah shatters a clay jar as a sign that Judah and Jerusalem will be irreparably broken, then proclaims in the temple courtyard that disaster will come on the city and surrounding villages because the people refuse to heed the LORD’s words.

sections.heading: The Shattered Jar as a Sign

Jeremiah 20.overview: Pashhur has Jeremiah beaten and confined, but Jeremiah renames him Magor-missabib and announces captivity for Pashhur, his household, and Judah. Jeremiah laments the ridicule and danger surrounding his prophetic work, affirms the LORD’s support and rescue, then curses the day of his birth and grieves over his life of trouble and shame.

sections.heading: Jeremiah’s lament and confidence in the LORD
Jeremiah curses the day of his birth

Jeremiah 21.overview: Zedekiah sends Pashhur and Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to seek the LORD’s help against Nebuchadnezzar, but Jeremiah announces that Jerusalem will fall and its survivors will be handed over to Babylon. He sets before the people a choice between death in the besieged city and life through surrender, then calls the house of David to administer justice and warns that judgment will consume its stronghold.

sections.heading: The Way of Life and Death
Warning to the House of David

Jeremiah 22.overview: Jeremiah delivers the LORD’s warning to Judah’s king and officials: justice for the vulnerable will preserve the royal house, but disobedience will bring Jerusalem’s desolation. He announces the exile of Shallum, the dishonorable death of Jehoiakim, and the removal of Coniah and the end of his descendants’ rule in Judah.

Jeremiah 23.overview: The LORD condemns Israel’s negligent shepherds, promises to gather the scattered people and raise a righteous Branch from David, and foretells their return to the land. He denounces prophets who speak lies and false assurances, declares that his word exposes and judges them, and announces punishment for those who misuse the phrase “the burden of the LORD.”

sections.heading: Negligent shepherds and the righteous Branch
The LORD’s word against deceptive prophecy
Misuse of “the burden of the LORD”

Jeremiah 24.overview: After Jeconiah and other Judeans are taken to Babylon, Jeremiah sees two baskets of figs beside the temple. The LORD identifies the good figs with the exiles whom he will restore and the bad figs with Zedekiah, his officials, and the remaining Judeans, whom he will judge.

sections.heading: The Good Figs and the Exiles

Jeremiah 25.overview: Jeremiah recounts Judah’s rejection of repeated prophetic warnings and announces its devastation under Nebuchadnezzar, seventy years of service to Babylon, and Babylon’s later punishment. He gives the nations the cup of the LORD’s wrath and proclaims judgment across the earth, including the slaughter of its leaders and people.

sections.heading: Judah’s judgment and Babylon’s seventy years
The cup of wrath for the nations
The LORD’s judgment across the earth

Jeremiah 26.overview: At the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, the LORD sends Jeremiah to warn Judah that the temple and Jerusalem will become like Shiloh unless the people listen; priests and prophets demand his death, but officials and people acquit him after his defense. Judah’s elders cite Micah’s similar prophecy and Hezekiah’s response, while Jehoiakim has Uriah brought back from Egypt and executed, and Ahikam protects Jeremiah.

Jeremiah 27.overview: The LORD commands Jeremiah to wear a yoke and tell the envoys of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon that Nebuchadnezzar will rule the nations, while those who resist him face judgment and those who submit remain in their lands. Jeremiah gives the same warning to Zedekiah, the priests, and the people, rejecting false promises of deliverance and declaring that the remaining temple and royal objects will be taken to Babylon until the LORD restores them.

Jeremiah 28.overview: Hananiah prophesies in the temple that the LORD will break Babylon’s yoke within two years and restore the temple articles and exiles, while Jeremiah says that peace is confirmed only when prophecy comes true. After Hananiah breaks Jeremiah’s wooden yoke and repeats his prediction, the LORD declares that an iron yoke will bind the nations to Nebuchadnezzar, condemns Hananiah for false prophecy, and announces his death that year.

sections.heading: The Iron Yoke and Hananiah’s Death

Jeremiah 29.overview: Jeremiah sends a letter to the Judean exiles in Babylon, instructing them to settle there and promising their eventual restoration after seventy years while warning them against false prophets. The LORD announces judgment on those remaining in Jerusalem and on the false prophets Ahab, Zedekiah, and Shemaiah, whose claims oppose Jeremiah’s message.

sections.heading: Judgment on Jerusalem and False Prophets

Jeremiah 30.overview: The LORD tells Jeremiah to record his promise to restore Israel and Judah, deliver Jacob from distress, free the people from foreign rule, and raise up David as their king. He describes Zion’s grievous wounds and punishment, then promises healing, rebuilding, renewed honor, and a ruler from the people while declaring judgment on the wicked.

Jeremiah 31.overview: The LORD promises to restore Israel and Judah, gathering the exiles, turning mourning to joy, and renewing the land. He announces a new covenant written on the people’s hearts, assures Israel’s lasting place as a nation, and promises Jerusalem’s rebuilding and holiness.

Jeremiah 32.overview: While Jerusalem is under siege and Jeremiah is imprisoned for prophesying its capture, he buys his cousin Hanamel’s field at Anathoth and has the deeds preserved as a sign that land will again be purchased. In response to Jeremiah’s prayer, the LORD confirms Jerusalem’s judgment for Judah’s idolatry and promises to gather the people, establish an everlasting covenant with them, and restore the land.

Jeremiah 33.overview: While Jeremiah is confined, the LORD promises to answer him and to restore Jerusalem and Judah with healing, forgiveness, renewed life, and abundant peace. The LORD promises a righteous Branch from David, enduring roles for David’s line and the Levite priests, and compassion for the descendants of Jacob.

sections.heading: The Righteous Branch and Enduring Promises

Jeremiah 34.overview: During the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem, Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that the city will fall and he will be taken to Babylon, where he will die in peace. After Jerusalem’s people free their Hebrew slaves and then enslave them again, the LORD condemns their broken covenant and declares that Babylon will return to destroy the city and devastate Judah.

sections.heading: The people free and re-enslave Hebrew slaves
The covenant penalty and Babylon’s return

Jeremiah 35.overview: During Jehoiakim’s reign, Jeremiah brings the Rechabites to a chamber in the temple and offers them wine, but they refuse, citing their forefather Jonadab’s commands. The LORD contrasts their obedience with Judah’s refusal to heed his words, announces disaster for Judah and Jerusalem, and promises that Jonadab’s line will continue to serve before him.

sections.heading: Jeremiah Brings the Rechabites to the Temple
The Rechabites Explain Their Ancestral Commands

Jeremiah 36.overview: In Jehoiakim’s reign, Jeremiah dictates the LORD’s warnings to Baruch, who reads the scroll to the people and then to Judah’s officials. Jehoiakim burns the scroll and orders Jeremiah and Baruch seized, but the LORD has them hidden, directs Jeremiah to produce another scroll, and declares judgment on the king and his house.

Jeremiah 37.overview: Zedekiah and Judah’s leaders reject Jeremiah’s words, though Zedekiah asks him to pray, and the Chaldeans withdraw from Jerusalem when Pharaoh’s army approaches. The LORD says the Chaldeans will return and capture the city; Jeremiah is arrested, then tells Zedekiah he will be handed over to Babylon before being moved to the guard’s courtyard.

sections.heading: Zedekiah’s Reign and the Siege’s Pause

Jeremiah 38.overview: Officials accuse Jeremiah of weakening Jerusalem and have him thrown into a cistern, but Ebed-melech persuades Zedekiah to order his rescue. In a private meeting, Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that surrender to Babylon will spare him and the city from destruction, while the king conceals their conversation and Jeremiah remains in the courtyard of the guard.

Jeremiah 39.overview: Nebuchadnezzar’s army besieges and breaches Jerusalem, and Zedekiah flees, is captured near Jericho, and is blinded after his sons and Judah’s nobles are killed at Riblah. The Chaldeans burn and break down the city, deport many inhabitants while leaving some poor people in Judah, release Jeremiah into Gedaliah’s care, and receive the LORD’s promise to rescue Ebed-melech.

Jeremiah 40.overview: Nebuzaradan frees Jeremiah at Ramah, explains that Judah’s disaster fulfills the LORD’s judgment, and offers him the choice to go to Babylon or remain; Jeremiah stays with Gedaliah at Mizpah. Gedaliah welcomes the field commanders and returning Judeans, urges them to live peacefully under Babylonian rule, and rejects Johanan’s warning that Ishmael plans to kill him.

sections.heading: Gedaliah and the Remnant at Mizpah

Jeremiah 41.overview: Ishmael son of Nethaniah murders Gedaliah at Mizpah, kills Jews and Chaldeans there, slaughters visiting worshipers, and takes the remaining people captive toward the Ammonites. Johanan son of Kareah and the army commanders recover the captives near Gibeon, while Ishmael escapes and Johanan’s group stays near Bethlehem before planning to flee to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans.

Jeremiah 42.overview: Johanan, the commanders, and the remnant of Judah ask Jeremiah to seek the LORD’s direction and pledge to obey it. After ten days, Jeremiah tells them to remain in Judah for protection and restoration, warns that Egypt will bring sword, famine, and plague, and accuses them of insincerity when they refuse to obey.

sections.heading: The Remnant Seeks the LORD’s Direction
Promise for Those Who Remain in Judah

Jeremiah 43.overview: Azariah, Johanan, and the other leaders reject Jeremiah’s warning and take the remnant of Judah, including Jeremiah and Baruch, to Egypt, settling at Tahpanhes. There the LORD tells Jeremiah to bury stones at Pharaoh’s palace as a sign that Nebuchadnezzar will conquer Egypt, strike its people, and destroy its temples and sacred pillars.

Jeremiah 44.overview: Jeremiah recounts Judah’s destruction as the result of persistent idolatry and warns the Jews living in Egypt that they too will die by sword or famine, with only a few escaping. The people reject his warning and defend their worship of the Queen of Heaven, while Jeremiah declares that their conduct brought disaster on Judah and foretells their destruction and the downfall of Pharaoh Hophra.

sections.heading: The people defend the Queen of Heaven worship
Jeremiah confirms judgment and its sign

Jeremiah 45.overview: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Jeremiah delivers the Lord’s message to Baruch, who laments his sorrow, exhaustion, and lack of rest. The Lord announces the destruction of what he has built and planted, warns Baruch not to seek great things for himself, and promises to preserve his life amid disaster.

Jeremiah 46.overview: Jeremiah recounts Egypt’s defeat by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, portraying the Egyptian army’s flight and the LORD’s judgment by the Euphrates. He announces Babylon’s coming attack on Egypt and its eventual recovery, then promises Jacob’s return from captivity while affirming that the LORD will discipline Israel.

Jeremiah 47.overview: The chapter introduces the LORD’s word to Jeremiah concerning the Philistines, delivered before Pharaoh strikes Gaza, and describes an invading force from the north as a flood that brings terror and destruction. The LORD declares the destruction of the Philistines and their allies, while Gaza and Ashkelon mourn and the LORD’s sword continues against Ashkelon and its coast.

sections.heading: Philistine mourning and the LORD’s sword

Jeremiah 48.overview: Jeremiah announces Moab’s devastation, naming its cities and describing its people’s flight, the exile of Chemosh, and the collapse of Moab’s strength. He portrays the judgment as the result of Moab’s pride and mockery of Israel, laments the nation’s loss, and concludes with a promise of restoration in later days.

Jeremiah 49.overview: The LORD announces judgment on Ammon for taking Israel’s territory, on Edom and Damascus, and on Kedar and Hazor through Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign. He also declares judgment on Elam, including the scattering of its people, and promises restoration for Ammon and Elam afterward.

sections.heading: Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign against Kedar and Hazor

Jeremiah 50.overview: Jeremiah announces Babylon’s capture by a northern alliance and its judgment for plundering Israel and defying the LORD. Israel and Judah seek the LORD, return toward Zion in an everlasting covenant, and receive forgiveness and restoration as the LORD their Redeemer brings Babylon to ruin.

sections.heading: The northern army and Babylon’s fall

Jeremiah 51.overview: The LORD announces Babylon’s destruction by the Medes, vindication for Israel and Judah, and Babylon’s lasting desolation, while calling the LORD’s people to flee. Jeremiah gives Seraiah a scroll of the judgment to read in Babylon and sink in the Euphrates as a sign that the city will never rise again.

sections.heading: Babylon’s judgment and the LORD’s sovereignty
The scroll sunk in the Euphrates

Jeremiah 52.overview: The chapter recounts Zedekiah’s rebellion, Babylon’s siege and capture of Jerusalem, the destruction of the temple and city, and the deportation of Judah’s people. It concludes with the release and favored treatment of Jehoiachin in Babylon.

Lamentations 1.overview: Jerusalem is portrayed as a deserted widow and captive, grieving exile, betrayal, hunger, and the loss of her former splendor; the lament attributes her suffering to the LORD’s judgment for her transgressions. The city acknowledges the LORD’s righteousness, describes its affliction and lack of comfort, and appeals for the LORD to see its suffering and judge its enemies.

Lamentations 2.overview: The Lord brings down Zion, Judah, and Jerusalem, destroying their cities, sanctuary, walls, and political order while famine and violence claim the people. The speaker grieves over the suffering, recalls the failures of Jerusalem’s prophets and the triumph of her enemies, and calls for the people to cry out to the Lord as he pleads for God to consider their devastation.

sections.heading: Jerusalem’s Ruin and Her Enemies’ Scorn
A Cry for the Lord to Consider

Lamentations 3.overview: The speaker recounts affliction under the LORD’s anger, then finds hope in the LORD’s unfailing mercies and describes the good of waiting through grief. The speaker calls the people to examine their ways, laments Jerusalem’s suffering and persecution, and appeals to the LORD for vindication and judgment on his enemies.

sections.heading: Hope, waiting, and the LORD’s justice

Lamentations 4.overview: The lament contrasts Zion’s former splendor with famine, death, and social collapse, including the suffering of children and the starvation of the people. It attributes Jerusalem’s destruction to the sins of its prophets and priests, recounts failed hopes for rescue and the capture of the LORD’s anointed, and declares that Zion’s punishment ends while Edom faces judgment.

sections.heading: Failed Rescue and the Anointed’s Capture

Lamentations 5.overview: The people of Judah lament lost homes and inheritance, family hardship, hunger, forced labor, violence, and the desolation of Zion, while acknowledging their ancestors’ sins and their own. They affirm that the LORD reigns forever and ask why he has forsaken them, pleading for restoration despite the possibility of his continued anger.

Ezekiel 1.overview: Ezekiel dates his vision by the River Kebar during the exile of King Jehoiachin and describes a storm cloud containing four living creatures. He then sees their accompanying wheels, an expanse and sapphire-like throne above them, and a humanlike figure surrounded by fire and brilliant light, whose appearance resembles the glory of the LORD.

sections.heading: The Throne and the Glory of the LORD

Ezekiel 2.overview: The Spirit sets Ezekiel on his feet, and the Lord commissions him to speak to rebellious Israel whether the people listen or refuse, without fearing their opposition. The Lord tells Ezekiel not to rebel and gives him a scroll covered with words of lamentation, mourning, and woe.

Ezekiel 3.overview: The LORD has Ezekiel eat the scroll and commissions him to speak to Israel, whose resistance he is equipped to withstand. The Spirit brings Ezekiel to the exiles at Tel-abib, where the LORD appoints him as a watchman and later confines him to his house, making his speech dependent on the LORD’s words.

Ezekiel 4.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to portray Jerusalem under siege and to lie on his sides for assigned periods, bearing the iniquity of Israel and Judah. He prescribes meager, measured food and water for Ezekiel as a sign of Jerusalem’s coming famine, allowing cow dung instead of human excrement for baking the bread.

sections.heading: Ezekiel Bears Israel and Judah’s Iniquity

Ezekiel 5.overview: The LORD commands Ezekiel to shave and divide his hair as a sign of Jerusalem’s coming destruction, with a few strands preserved and then burned. He condemns Jerusalem’s rebellion and defilement of the sanctuary, declaring judgments of famine, plague, sword, and scattering that will leave the city a ruin among the nations.

sections.heading: The Sign of the Divided Hair
The Terms and Effects of Judgment

Ezekiel 6.overview: The LORD commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Israel’s mountains, announcing the destruction of its high places, altars, idols, and cities. He preserves a remnant scattered among the nations, while sword, famine, and plague bring judgment and leave the land desolate.

sections.heading: A Remnant Scattered Among the Nations
Judgment by Sword, Famine, and Plague

Ezekiel 7.overview: Ezekiel announces that the end has come upon Israel, as the LORD brings judgment for the people’s ways and abominations. He describes violence, invasion, famine, plague, the loss of wealth and sanctuary, and the collapse of leadership, concluding that the people will know the LORD has judged them.

sections.heading: Survivors and the Loss of Wealth and Sanctuary

Ezekiel 8.overview: Ezekiel is carried in a vision from the elders in exile to Jerusalem, where he sees the idol of jealousy at the temple and is shown Israel’s escalating acts of worship: elders honoring idols in secret, women weeping for Tammuz, and men worshiping the sun. God declares that Judah’s abominations and violence provoke his wrath, and that he will show no pity or hear the people’s cries.

Ezekiel 9.overview: Ezekiel sees six armed executioners and a linen-clothed man summoned to the temple, where the LORD orders the man to mark those grieving Jerusalem’s abominations and the others to kill the unmarked, beginning at the sanctuary. Ezekiel pleads for Israel’s remnant, but the LORD cites the land’s bloodshed and the people’s claim that he does not see, declares that their deeds will fall on them, and receives the linen-clothed man’s report that he has obeyed.

sections.heading: The executioners arrive at the temple
The marked are spared; the killing begins
Ezekiel pleads and the man reports back

Ezekiel 10.overview: Ezekiel sees the LORD’s glory above the cherubim and watches a man clothed in linen receive burning coals from among them. The vision describes the cherubim and their wheels as the glory moves from the temple threshold and the cherubim rise to the east gate.

sections.heading: The Glory Moves to the East Gate

Ezekiel 11.overview: At Jerusalem’s eastern gate, the LORD condemns Jaazaniah, Pelatiah, and the other leaders for their counsel and violence, declares judgment on them, and Pelatiah dies as Ezekiel prophesies. The LORD promises to gather the exiles, give them a new heart and spirit, and judge the rebellious, while his glory leaves Jerusalem and Ezekiel returns to the exiles in Chaldea to report the vision.

Ezekiel 12.overview: The LORD commands Ezekiel to act out an exile, then explains that the sign concerns Jerusalem’s prince and people: they will be taken captive, the prince will be caught and brought to Babylon, and a remnant will survive to testify among the nations. The LORD also portrays the fear and devastation awaiting Jerusalem and rejects sayings that visions fail or concern only the distant future, declaring that his words will be fulfilled without delay.

sections.heading: The prince and people taken captive

Ezekiel 13.overview: The LORD commands Ezekiel to condemn Israel’s prophets for false visions and assurances of peace, and declares that they will be excluded from the people as Jerusalem’s whitewashed wall is torn down. He also condemns women who use charms and veils to deceive the people, promising to free those they ensnare and end their false visions and divination.

sections.heading: The Fall of the Whitewashed Wall
Judgment on the Women Who Prophesy

Ezekiel 14.overview: Elders of Israel come to Ezekiel, and the LORD says that those who inquire while harboring idols will receive judgment, calling Israel to turn from its idols and declaring that inquirers and prophets share punishment. The LORD says that even the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job cannot save others from famine, beasts, sword, or plague, but survivors from Jerusalem will be brought out as evidence of the city’s judgment.

sections.heading: Idolatry and inquiry before the prophet

Ezekiel 15.overview: The LORD asks Ezekiel whether vine wood is more useful than other forest wood, and the answer is that it serves only as fuel and is useless once charred. The Lord GOD compares Jerusalem’s people to the vine, says he will set his face against them and give them to destruction, and declares that their unfaithfulness will leave the land desolate.

Ezekiel 16.overview: The LORD recounts how he found Jerusalem abandoned, raised and adorned her, and made a covenant with her, but she trusted in her beauty, worshiped idols, and sacrificed her children. He announces judgment through her former lovers, compares her guilt with that of Samaria and Sodom, and promises to restore them and establish an everlasting covenant with Jerusalem.

sections.heading: Jerusalem’s origins and the LORD’s care
Judgment and comparison with her sisters

Ezekiel 17.overview: The LORD gives Ezekiel a parable of two eagles and a vine, then explains that Babylon’s king takes Jerusalem’s king and establishes him under covenant, but the king turns to Egypt and breaks his oath. The LORD declares that the rebel will be captured and judged in Babylon, then promises to plant a cedar shoot on Israel’s heights, where it will flourish and display the LORD’s power to humble and exalt.

sections.heading: The Parable of the Eagles and Vine
The Parable Explained and Judgment Declared
The Cedar Shoot on Israel’s Heights

Ezekiel 18.overview: The LORD rejects Israel’s sour-grapes proverb and declares that each person is accountable for their own conduct, illustrating the principle through a righteous man, his wicked son, and a grandson who acts righteously. He says the wicked who turn to justice will live and the righteous who turn to wrongdoing will die, then calls the house of Israel to turn from its transgressions because he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death.

sections.heading: A Call to Turn and Live

Ezekiel 19.overview: Ezekiel is told to lament Israel’s princes through the image of a lioness whose first cub is taken to Egypt and whose second is captured by the nations and brought to Babylon. The lament then portrays Israel as a fruitful vine uprooted and dried by the east wind, with fire consuming its fruit and leaving no branch fit for a ruler’s scepter.

sections.heading: The First Lion Cub Taken to Egypt
The Second Lion Cub Taken to Babylon

Ezekiel 20.overview: When Israel’s elders inquire of the LORD, Ezekiel recounts Israel’s repeated rebellion from Egypt through the wilderness and into the land, while the LORD withholds judgment for the sake of his name and promises to gather, judge, and restore his people. The LORD then announces fire against the forest of the Negev, and Ezekiel objects that the people dismiss his prophecy as a parable.

sections.heading: The elders’ inquiry and Israel in Egypt
Rebellion and judgment in the wilderness
Idolatry in the land and future restoration

Ezekiel 21.overview: The LORD announces that His sword will strike Jerusalem and Israel, cutting off both righteous and wicked, and Ezekiel’s grief signifies the terror of the coming slaughter. The king of Babylon chooses Jerusalem by an omen, the prince of Israel loses his crown until the rightful ruler comes, and the Ammonites face judgment by the sword.

Ezekiel 22.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to indict Jerusalem for bloodshed, idolatry, oppression, sexual offenses, and profanation, and announces that its people will be scattered among the nations. The LORD then portrays Israel as dross to be melted in Jerusalem and condemns the princes, priests, officials, prophets, and people for corruption, noting that no one stands in the gap before judgment falls.

sections.heading: Israel as Dross in the Furnace

Ezekiel 23.overview: Ezekiel portrays Samaria and Jerusalem as the sisters Oholah and Oholibah, recounting Samaria’s pursuit of Assyria and Jerusalem’s pursuit of Assyria and Babylon before those powers turn against them. The LORD charges both cities with idolatry, child sacrifice, and profaning the sanctuary, and declares that judgment will expose and punish their sins.

sections.heading: Oholibah and the cup of judgment
Charges and judgment against both sisters

Ezekiel 24.overview: Ezekiel dates the start of Babylon’s siege of Jerusalem and gives a boiling-pot parable portraying the city’s bloodshed, uncleanness, and coming judgment. After Ezekiel’s wife dies and he is forbidden to mourn, he explains that Jerusalem’s sanctuary and its people will fall, and that a fugitive’s arrival will end his silence and confirm his role as a sign.

sections.heading: The Boiling Pot and Jerusalem’s Judgment
The Fugitive and Ezekiel’s Open Mouth

Ezekiel 25.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to announce judgment against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia for their contempt, claims, or hostility toward Israel and Judah. He describes each nation’s punishment and declares that they will know he is the LORD.

Ezekiel 26.overview: Because Tyre rejoices over Jerusalem’s ruin and expects to profit, the LORD declares that many nations, beginning with Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, will destroy the city and its mainland settlements. The coastlands mourn Tyre’s fall, and the LORD declares that the city will become desolate, descend to the Pit, and never be found again.

Ezekiel 27.overview: Ezekiel is commanded to lament Tyre, whose beauty and strength are depicted through a richly outfitted ship and an extensive trade network linking many lands. An east wind shatters the ship in the sea, sinking Tyre’s wealth and people as sailors and coastal nations mourn its downfall.

Ezekiel 28.overview: Ezekiel declares judgment on Tyre’s ruler for claiming divine status, predicting his death at the hands of foreigners, and laments the king’s fall from splendor through pride, violence, and dishonest trade. He then prophesies judgment against Sidon and Israel’s restoration to its land, where the people will dwell securely.

sections.heading: Lament for the King of Tyre

Ezekiel 29.overview: The LORD condemns Pharaoh and Egypt for claiming the Nile as their own and for failing Israel as a broken reed, declaring Egypt’s desolation and scattering for forty years before its restoration as a lowly kingdom. In a later oracle, the LORD gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment for his army’s labor against Tyre and promises a horn for Israel and speech for Ezekiel.

Ezekiel 30.overview: The LORD announces the approaching Day of the LORD, when Egypt, its allies, and Cush face destruction, and names Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon as the agent who devastates Egypt and its cities. In a dated oracle, the LORD declares that Pharaoh’s arms will be broken, Babylon’s king will be strengthened against him, and the Egyptians will be scattered among the nations.

Ezekiel 31.overview: In the eleventh year, the LORD tells Ezekiel to address Pharaoh and compares Assyria to a towering cedar nourished by abundant waters, sheltering nations and surpassing the trees of Eden. The LORD recounts Assyria’s cutting down and descent to Sheol as a warning of Pharaoh’s and Egypt’s coming downfall.

sections.heading: Descent to Sheol and Pharaoh’s fate

Ezekiel 32.overview: Ezekiel delivers a lament for Pharaoh, depicting Egypt’s defeat by Babylon, its desolation, and the terror its downfall brings among the nations. In a second lament, Egypt descends to the Pit among slain nations including Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, and the leaders of the north, while Pharaoh finds comfort among the dead.

sections.heading: Pharaoh’s downfall and its cosmic signs

Ezekiel 33.overview: The LORD appoints Ezekiel as a watchman for Israel, then declares that each person is judged according to whether they turn from righteousness or wickedness. After a fugitive reports Jerusalem’s fall, the LORD condemns the survivors’ claim to the land and says Ezekiel’s hearers listen to him without acting on his words.

sections.heading: Judgment According to Each Person’s Ways
Jerusalem’s Fall and the Land’s Judgment

Ezekiel 34.overview: The LORD condemns Israel’s shepherds for exploiting and neglecting the flock, scattering the people, and announces that he will remove them and search for and restore his scattered sheep. He promises to judge between the sheep, appoint his servant David as their shepherd, and establish security, abundance, and a covenant of peace for Israel.

sections.heading: The LORD gathers and tends his flock
Judgment among the flock and David’s rule

Ezekiel 35.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to prophesy against Mount Seir, declaring that its cities will be ruined and its land made desolate because Edom attacked Israel during its disaster. The LORD also condemns Edom’s claim to Israel’s lands and its contemptuous words and rejoicing over Israel’s desolation, promising judgment on Mount Seir and all Edom.

Ezekiel 36.overview: The LORD promises the mountains of Israel fertility, resettlement, and freedom from the nations’ reproach, while declaring judgment against those who seized the land. He explains Israel’s exile as the result of its defilement and promises to gather, cleanse, and renew the people for the sake of his holy name, restoring the land and filling its cities with people.

sections.heading: Exile and the vindication of God’s name

Ezekiel 37.overview: Ezekiel sees dry bones come to life through the LORD’s word and breath, and the LORD identifies them as the whole house of Israel, whom he promises to restore to their land. Ezekiel joins the sticks of Judah and Joseph, and the LORD promises to reunite Israel under one king, cleanse the people, and dwell among them forever.

sections.heading: The Dry Bones Come to Life
One King and an Everlasting Covenant

Ezekiel 38.overview: The LORD directs Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, who gathers a multinational army and advances against Israel, a land whose people dwell securely. The LORD declares that Gog’s attack brings divine wrath and judgment, including earthquake, mutual slaughter, and calamities, through which he reveals his holiness to the nations.

Ezekiel 39.overview: The LORD declares Gog’s defeat on the mountains of Israel, the destruction of his forces, and the cleansing of the land through the burning of weapons and burial of the dead. The nations recognize the LORD’s judgment, while Israel is restored from exile, gathered to its land, and assured that the LORD will no longer hide His face but will pour out His Spirit.

sections.heading: Gog’s Defeat and the LORD’s Name
Weapons Burned and the Dead Buried
