Ezekiel 40.overview: In a vision, Ezekiel is brought to a high mountain in Israel, where a bronze-like man measures the temple’s wall, courts, and gates. The man identifies the chambers and tables for priestly service and sacrifices, names the Zadokite priests, and measures the temple entrance.

Ezekiel 41.overview: The man measures the outer and inner sanctuaries, the Most Holy Place, the surrounding side rooms, and the buildings and courts of the temple. He describes the wood paneling, carved cherubim and palm trees, the wooden altar, and the sanctuary doors and portico.

sections.heading: The Sanctuaries and Most Holy Place
The Side Rooms and Open Area
The Rear Building and Temple Interior

Ezekiel 42.overview: The man leads Ezekiel through the north and south chamber buildings, describing their dimensions, levels, galleries, and entrances. He identifies the chambers as places for priests to handle and eat holy offerings and change garments, then measures the 500-cubit square boundary that separates the holy from the common.

sections.heading: Measured Boundary of the Temple Area

Ezekiel 43.overview: Ezekiel sees the glory of the God of Israel enter the temple through the east gate and fill it, and hears God declare the temple his dwelling while calling Israel to abandon the practices that profaned his holy name. God instructs Ezekiel to describe the temple to Israel, gives the altar’s measurements, and sets out its purification and consecration rites for the priests of Zadok.

sections.heading: The Glory Returns to the Temple

Ezekiel 44.overview: The LORD declares that the east gate remains shut because He entered through it, then rebukes Israel for defiling the sanctuary and assigns distinct duties to the Levites and the priests descended from Zadok. He sets out the priests’ clothing, conduct, teaching, judicial and purity duties, and provisions, declaring that the LORD is their inheritance.

sections.heading: Duties and Regulations for the Priests

Ezekiel 45.overview: Ezekiel describes the holy district set apart for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, and city, with the prince’s land bordering it and the remaining tribal land protected from oppression. The chapter sets standards for fair measures and contributions, assigns the prince responsibility for offerings, and prescribes sanctuary purification and offerings for the Passover and seventh-month feast.

sections.heading: The Holy District and the Prince’s Land

Ezekiel 46.overview: The LORD sets rules for the east gate, the prince’s and people’s worship, appointed offerings, and the prince’s handling of inheritances. Ezekiel is shown the priests’ chambers and the courts with kitchens where temple servants cook the people’s sacrifices.

Ezekiel 47.overview: Ezekiel sees water flowing from the temple and growing into a river that freshens the Dead Sea, sustains abundant fish, and nourishes trees whose fruit and leaves provide food and healing, while marshes remain salty. The Lord GOD sets the boundaries for Israel’s land inheritance, assigns Joseph two portions, and includes resident foreigners and their children in the tribal allotments.

Ezekiel 48.overview: Ezekiel describes the east-to-west land allotments for Israel’s tribes, with a central holy district for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, city, and prince. He names the city’s gates for the tribes and concludes that the city will be called “THE LORD IS THERE.”

Daniel 1.overview: Nebuchadnezzar takes Jerusalem and brings some of the temple vessels and young men of Judah, including Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, to Babylon for training in the king’s service. Daniel secures a ten-day diet of vegetables and water for the four, and God grants them health, learning, and wisdom, while Daniel gains insight into visions and dreams.

sections.heading: Jerusalem’s Defeat and the Young Men’s Training
The Young Men Enter the King’s Service

Daniel 2.overview: Nebuchadnezzar demands that Babylon’s wise men reveal and interpret his troubling dream, and orders their execution when they cannot. After God reveals the mystery to Daniel, Daniel recounts the statue and interprets it as successive kingdoms overcome by God’s everlasting kingdom, and Nebuchadnezzar promotes Daniel and his friends.

sections.heading: Daniel seeks and receives the mystery
Daniel recounts and interprets the dream
Daniel and his friends are promoted

Daniel 3.overview: Nebuchadnezzar erects a golden statue on the plain of Dura and commands officials and people of every nation to worship it or face the furnace; after astrologers accuse Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, the king threatens them, and they refuse to worship his gods. Nebuchadnezzar orders them into the furnace, but they emerge unharmed with a fourth figure seen in the fire, prompting the king to praise their God, issue a decree protecting his worship, and promote the three men in Babylon.

sections.heading: The Golden Statue and Worship Decree
The Furnace and the Men’s Deliverance

Daniel 4.overview: Nebuchadnezzar recounts his dream of a great tree cut down at a heavenly decree, and Daniel interprets it as the king’s coming humbling until he recognizes that the Most High rules human kingdoms. After the decree is fulfilled and Nebuchadnezzar loses his reason, he looks to heaven, is restored to sanity and kingship, and praises the King of heaven.

sections.heading: The Dream of the Great Tree

Daniel 5.overview: Belshazzar’s feast profanes the Jerusalem temple vessels, and a hand writes on the palace wall; when Babylon’s wise men cannot interpret the inscription, the queen recommends Daniel. Daniel recounts Nebuchadnezzar’s humbling, condemns Belshazzar’s pride, interprets the writing as the end of his reign and kingdom, and sees Belshazzar slain as Darius the Mede receives the kingdom.

Daniel 6.overview: Darius appoints Daniel over the kingdom, and jealous officials exploit a decree against prayer to have Daniel thrown into a lions’ den. God delivers Daniel, the accusers are condemned, and Darius proclaims the power and enduring kingdom of Daniel’s God.

sections.heading: Daniel’s rise and the officials’ plot
The decree and Daniel in the den
Daniel’s deliverance and the accusers’ fate

Daniel 7.overview: Daniel records a vision of four beasts rising from the sea, followed by the Ancient of Days holding court and giving everlasting dominion to one like a Son of Man. An angel explains that the beasts are kings and kingdoms, while the fourth kingdom and its arrogant horn oppress the saints until judgment removes the horn’s power and the saints receive the kingdom.

sections.heading: Daniel’s Vision of the Four Beasts
The Court and the Son of Man

Daniel 8.overview: In a vision at Susa, Daniel sees a two-horned ram overcome by a goat, whose great horn breaks and is replaced by four horns; a little horn then attacks the host, the daily sacrifice, and the sanctuary. Gabriel interprets the beasts as the kings of Media and Persia and the king of Greece, explains the little horn’s rise and destruction, and says the sanctuary will be restored after 2,300 evenings and mornings; Daniel remains shaken and unable to understand the vision.

sections.heading: The Ram, the Goat, and the Little Horn

Daniel 9.overview: In Darius’s first year, Daniel understands from Jeremiah’s prophecy that Jerusalem’s desolation will last seventy years and prays, confessing Israel’s sin and asking God to restore Jerusalem and its sanctuary. Gabriel comes to Daniel and explains the seventy weeks decreed for his people and holy city, including Jerusalem’s rebuilding, the Messiah’s being cut off, the city and sanctuary’s destruction, and the final desolation.

Daniel 10.overview: Daniel receives a vision of a radiant man beside the Tigris after three weeks of mourning and fasting, and the vision leaves him weak and speechless. A messenger explains that the prince of Persia delayed his response until Michael helped, strengthens Daniel, and describes conflict with the princes of Persia and Greece before revealing what will happen to Daniel’s people.

Daniel 11.overview: The vision traces Persian and Greek rulers, then recounts wars between the kings of the North and South, including failed alliances, invasions, and shifts of power. It describes a contemptible ruler who attacks the holy covenant, desecrates the temple, and persecutes the faithful, before concluding with a final campaign and his death without help.

sections.heading: Wars between the North and South
The contemptible king and the covenant

Daniel 12.overview: Michael rises during a time of unprecedented distress, when Daniel’s people whose names are in the book are delivered; the dead awake to everlasting life or contempt, and the wise shine. Daniel seals the words, then hears that the wonders last for a time, times, and half a time, receives the periods of 1,290 and 1,335 days, and is told he will rest and later rise to his inheritance.

sections.heading: The Sealed Words and Daniel’s Inheritance

Hosea 1.overview: The word of the LORD comes to Hosea during the reigns of Judah’s kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah and Israel’s king Jeroboam; Hosea marries Gomer and names their children Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, and Lo-ammi. The names announce judgment on Israel and the end of its kingdom, while the LORD promises compassion for Judah and foretells Israel’s restoration and the reunion of Judah and Israel under one leader.

Hosea 2.overview: The LORD commands the children to rebuke their mother, Israel, and announces judgment for her pursuit of Baal, including the withdrawal of her provisions and the exposure of her unfaithfulness. He then promises to woo her in the wilderness, renew their covenant in faithfulness, and restore peace, fertility, and Israel’s identity as His people.

sections.heading: Judgment and the loss of blessings

Hosea 3.overview: The LORD commands Hosea to love his adulterous wife again, and Hosea buys her and requires a period of exclusive separation. The chapter says Israel will likewise live for many days without political and religious institutions, then return to seek the LORD and David their king.

sections.heading: Hosea commanded to love his wife
Hosea buys and restrains his wife

Hosea 4.overview: The LORD brings a case against Israel for violence, unfaithfulness, and lack of knowledge of God, declaring judgment on the land and on the people and priests who reject his law. He condemns Israel’s idolatry and shrine worship, warns Judah away from Gilgal and Beth-aven, and declares Ephraim joined to idols and headed for shame.

sections.heading: Israel’s Corruption and the Land’s Mourning
The People and Priests Reject Knowledge

Hosea 5.overview: The LORD indicts the priests, Israel, and its rulers for idolatry, unfaithfulness, and injustice, declaring that Israel and Judah cannot find Him through ritual while their guilt remains. He announces judgment through invasion and destruction, rejects Ephraim’s appeal to Assyria, and says He will withdraw until the people acknowledge their guilt and seek Him.

Hosea 6.overview: The people are urged to return to the LORD, who will heal and revive them, and to press on to know him. The LORD condemns the fleeting loyalty of Ephraim and Judah, their covenant violations and violence, and declares judgment alongside a harvest for Judah when he restores his people.

sections.heading: Call to Return and Know the LORD

Hosea 7.overview: The LORD exposes Israel’s and Samaria’s crimes, as Ephraim’s deceit and the rulers’ corruption spread through the nation. Ephraim mixes with foreign nations and appeals to Egypt and Assyria, but Israel refuses to seek the LORD, rebels against him, and faces judgment.

Hosea 8.overview: Hosea announces an enemy against Israel for breaking the covenant, rejecting what is good, appointing rulers without the LORD, and making idols, including Samaria’s calf. Israel’s alliances, altars, and sacrifices fail to secure protection, and the chapter declares that Israel and Judah face foreign oppression and destruction.

Hosea 9.overview: Hosea condemns Israel’s idolatry and announces failed harvests, exile to Egypt and Assyria, and the loss of its feasts and offerings. He recalls Israel’s worship of Baal-peor and declares that Ephraim will suffer punishment, barrenness, the loss of its children, and rejection among the nations.

sections.heading: Exile and the loss of feasts

Hosea 10.overview: Hosea depicts Israel as a fruitful vine that multiplies altars, and declares that its deceit, false covenants, and idolatry bring judgment on Samaria and its calf. He recalls Israel’s sin at Gibeah, announces foreign oppression, contrasts wickedness with a call to seek the LORD, and predicts Israel’s defeat and the fall of its king at Bethel.

Hosea 11.overview: The LORD recalls loving Israel as a child, calling him from Egypt and caring for Ephraim, while Israel turns to idols and refuses to return, bringing the threat of Assyrian rule and destruction. The LORD’s compassion restrains his anger and promises Israel’s return, while the chapter closes by contrasting Ephraim’s deceit with Judah’s faithfulness.

sections.heading: Israel’s childhood and the LORD’s care
The LORD’s compassion and Israel’s return

Hosea 12.overview: Hosea indicts Ephraim’s reliance on foreign powers and deceit, recalls Jacob’s struggle with God, and calls the people to love, justice, and reliance on God. The chapter exposes Ephraim’s dishonest trade and boasts of wealth, recalls God’s care through the exodus and the prophets, and declares judgment for Israel’s guilt.

sections.heading: Jacob’s Struggle and the Call to Return
Jacob, the Exodus, and Ephraim’s Guilt

Hosea 13.overview: Hosea recounts Ephraim’s rise and idolatry, then contrasts the LORD’s care for Israel with the judgment that follows the people’s pride and forgetfulness. He announces Israel’s destruction, questions the power of its kings, describes Ephraim’s accumulated sin and the threat of death, and foretells Samaria’s violent fall.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Care and Coming Attack

Hosea 14.overview: Hosea calls Israel to return to the LORD, confess its iniquity, renounce reliance on Assyria and handmade idols, and seek compassion for the fatherless. The LORD promises to heal Israel’s apostasy and restore its flourishing, while the chapter closes by declaring that the LORD’s ways are right and distinguish the righteous from the rebellious.

Joel 1.overview: The LORD’s word comes to Joel, who calls the elders and people to recount an unprecedented locust invasion that destroys crops, vines, trees, and the harvest, leaving drinkers, farmers, and priests in mourning. Joel summons the priests and inhabitants to fast and gather at the house of the LORD, warns that the Day of the LORD brings destruction, and calls to the LORD as fields, pastures, and water sources fail.

sections.heading: The Land and Its People Mourn
A Solemn Assembly and the Day of the LORD
Animals Suffer as Joel Calls to the LORD

Joel 2.overview: Joel describes the approaching Day of the LORD through the advance of a vast army, then calls Judah to return to God and gather for communal fasting and prayer. The LORD responds with deliverance and restored abundance, promises the outpouring of the Spirit and signs before the Day of the LORD, and declares that those who call on Him will be saved in Zion and Jerusalem.

sections.heading: The Army and the Day of the LORD

Joel 3.overview: The LORD gathers the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat to judge them for scattering Israel and dividing its land, and promises recompense to Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia for plundering and selling Judah’s people. He summons the nations to battle and judgment, then declares the LORD’s refuge for Israel and promises Jerusalem’s holiness and Judah’s lasting renewal while Egypt and Edom become desolate.

sections.heading: Judah’s Renewal and the LORD’s Presence

Amos 1.overview: Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa, dates his vision concerning Israel to the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam and proclaims the LORD’s roar from Zion. The LORD announces judgment on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon for violence, the betrayal of exiles, and other cruelties, declaring destruction and exile for each nation.

sections.heading: Amos’s vision and the LORD’s roar

Amos 2.overview: The LORD pronounces judgment on Moab for burning the bones of Edom’s king and on Judah for rejecting his law. He indicts Israel for oppression, sexual and religious abuses, and rejection of the prophets and Nazirites he raised up, then announces that no one will escape the coming defeat.

Amos 3.overview: The LORD declares that Israel’s privileged relationship with him brings accountability, and Amos links the LORD’s speech and coming judgment to a series of signs and the prophets’ response. He summons witnesses to see Samaria’s oppression, announces an enemy’s attack, and describes the destruction of Bethel’s altars and Israel’s houses.

sections.heading: Israel’s Accountability and the Prophet’s Call
Judgment on Bethel and Israel’s Houses

Amos 4.overview: Amos condemns the women of Samaria for oppressing the poor and declares their coming exile, then denounces Israel’s sacrifices at Bethel and Gilgal. The LORD recounts calamities that have not turned Israel back to him, announces further judgment, and identifies himself as the creator and ruler of the earth.

Amos 5.overview: Amos laments Israel’s fall and warns that its cities will be greatly diminished, calling the people to seek the LORD rather than Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba and condemning their corruption of justice. He warns that the Day of the LORD brings darkness, rejects Israel’s feasts and offerings in the absence of justice and righteousness, recalls its idolatry, and declares exile beyond Damascus.

sections.heading: Seek the LORD and uphold justice
The Day of the LORD and exile

Amos 6.overview: Amos pronounces woe on the complacent leaders of Zion and Samaria, whose luxury and feasting continue while they ignore Joseph’s ruin, and announces their exile. The LORD swears to destroy Jacob’s citadels and homes, condemns Israel’s perversion of justice and pride in Lo-debar and Karnaim, and declares that a nation will oppress Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah.

Amos 7.overview: God shows Amos visions of locusts and fire, relenting from both judgments after Amos pleads for Jacob, then shows a plumb line and announces judgment against Israel and the house of Jeroboam. Amaziah accuses Amos and orders him away from Bethel, and Amos recounts his call before declaring judgment on Amaziah and Israel’s exile.

Amos 8.overview: Amos sees a basket of summer fruit, and the LORD declares that Israel’s end has come, with temple songs turning to wailing. The LORD condemns those who exploit the poor, announces upheaval and mourning, and foretells a famine of hearing his words and the fall of those who swear by Samaria, Dan, and Beersheba.

Amos 9.overview: The Lord commands judgment at the altar and declares that no fugitive can escape, then asserts his sovereignty over creation and announces that Israel will be sifted, with sinners dying and the house of Jacob not utterly destroyed. He promises to restore David’s fallen tent, Israel’s fortunes, and the people to their land, where they rebuild and enjoy abundance.

Obadiah 1.overview: Obadiah announces the LORD’s judgment on Edom for its pride, the plunder of Jacob, and its violence against Judah, declaring that Edom’s allies, wisdom, and warriors will fail. The prophecy then describes deliverance on Mount Zion, the restoration of Israel’s territory, and the LORD’s rule over the kingdom.

Jonah 1.overview: The LORD sends Jonah son of Amittai to preach against Nineveh, but Jonah flees by ship toward Tarshish, and a storm threatens the vessel. After the sailors identify Jonah as the cause and throw him overboard, the sea calms, they fear the LORD, and a great fish swallows Jonah.

sections.heading: Jonah Is Cast into the Sea
Jonah Swallowed by a Great Fish

Jonah 2.overview: Jonah prays to the LORD from inside the fish, recounting his descent into the sea, his plea toward the holy temple, and the LORD’s rescue of his life. He rejects worthless idols, vows thanksgiving and sacrifice, declares that salvation comes from the LORD, and is brought onto dry land when the LORD commands the fish to release him.

Jonah 3.overview: The LORD recommissions Jonah to go to Nineveh, where Jonah announces that the city will be overturned in forty days. The Ninevites, including their king, fast, wear sackcloth, and turn from violence, and God relents from the threatened disaster.

Jonah 4.overview: Jonah resents the LORD’s decision to spare Nineveh, explains that he fled because he knew of God’s compassion, and asks to die; the LORD questions his anger. Outside the city, Jonah grieves the loss of a plant, and the LORD contrasts Jonah’s concern for it with his own concern for Nineveh’s people and animals.

sections.heading: Jonah’s Anger and the LORD’s Question
The Plant, Worm, and East Wind

Micah 1.overview: Micah receives a word concerning Samaria and Jerusalem, as the LORD summons the earth to witness his judgment against Jacob and Israel for their sins and announces Samaria’s destruction. Micah laments as Samaria’s wound reaches Judah, naming towns in a mourning oracle that ends with the people’s exile.

Micah 2.overview: Micah condemns those who scheme to seize land and houses, and announces that the LORD will bring disaster, leaving them dispossessed and without a share in the assembly. He denounces those who reject truthful prophecy and oppress the people, then promises to gather Jacob’s remnant and lead them out under their King.

Micah 3.overview: Micah condemns Jacob’s and Israel’s rulers for exploiting the people, and denounces prophets who promise peace for payment and lose their visions. He contrasts their corruption with his Spirit-given power to proclaim Israel’s sin, then declares that Zion, Jerusalem, and the temple mount will be laid waste.

Micah 4.overview: Micah describes the LORD’s elevated mountain in the last days, where nations receive instruction from Zion, learn peace, and declare their allegiance to the LORD. The LORD gathers the lame and outcast, restores Zion’s rule, foretells the people’s exile to Babylon and redemption, and calls Zion to thresh the nations gathered against her.

sections.heading: Nations Gather at the LORD’s Mountain

Micah 5.overview: Micah portrays the siege and humiliation of Israel’s leader, then announces a ruler from Bethlehem whose ancient origins, shepherding rule, and strength bring security and deliverance from Assyria. He describes Jacob’s remnant among the nations as both life-giving and formidable, and declares that the LORD will remove Israel’s military resources, idols, and other sources of false security before taking vengeance on disobedient nations.

sections.heading: The LORD Removes Idolatry and Judges Nations

Micah 6.overview: The LORD summons the mountains as witnesses in his case against Israel, recalls the exodus and the deliverance from Balak’s counsel, and asks what he requires beyond justice, mercy, and humble walking with God. He indicts the city for dishonest trade, violence, and deceit, then announces deprivation and desolation because its people follow the practices of Omri and Ahab.

Micah 7.overview: Micah laments the scarcity of the godly, widespread corruption, and betrayal within households, then declares that he will wait for the LORD to vindicate him. He anticipates Jerusalem’s rebuilding and the nations’ submission, asks the LORD to shepherd his people, and praises God’s compassion and covenant faithfulness to Jacob and Abraham.

Nahum 1.overview: Nahum introduces his vision against Nineveh and portrays the LORD as powerful, just toward his enemies, and a refuge for those who trust him. The LORD promises Nineveh’s destruction, ends Judah’s affliction, and announces peace for Judah as the wicked no longer march through the land.

sections.heading: Good News and Peace for Judah

Nahum 2.overview: Nahum depicts an attacker advancing on Nineveh as the LORD restores Jacob and Israel, while invading forces storm the city, its palace falls, and its people are carried away. Nineveh is plundered and emptied, and the LORD declares that he will destroy the city’s power, prey, and messengers.

Nahum 3.overview: Nahum portrays Nineveh as a violent, deceitful city whose exploitation and sorcery bring the LORD’s judgment, public shame, and desolation. He compares its coming defeat with Thebes’s fall, depicts its defenses and leaders failing before invasion, and declares that its incurable wound draws applause from those harmed by Assyria.

Habakkuk 1.overview: Habakkuk laments the violence and perverted justice in Judah, and the LORD answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans to conquer nations. Habakkuk questions how the holy God can use a ruthless people who capture nations like fish and asks whether they will continue their slaughter without mercy.

Habakkuk 2.overview: Habakkuk waits for the LORD’s answer, and the LORD tells him to record the vision: the proud oppressor will face judgment, while the righteous will live by faith. A series of woes condemns the oppressor’s plunder, unjust building, violence, and humiliation of others, before the chapter contrasts powerless idols with the LORD in his holy temple.

sections.heading: The Vision and the Proud Oppressor
Woes for Plunder and Unjust Gain

Habakkuk 3.overview: Habakkuk prays for the LORD to renew his deeds and remember mercy, then portrays God’s power over creation and the nations as he comes to save his people and defeat the wicked. Habakkuk trembles as he awaits distress, yet declares that he will rejoice in the LORD and trust him as his strength despite loss.

Zephaniah 1.overview: The word of the LORD comes to Zephaniah during Josiah’s reign, announcing sweeping judgment on the earth and then on Judah and Jerusalem for idolatry and divided worship. The LORD names officials, merchants, complacent residents, and others for punishment, describing the approaching Day of the LORD as a day of devastation from which wealth cannot deliver anyone.

Zephaniah 2.overview: Zephaniah urges the shameful nation and the humble to seek the LORD before the day of his anger. He announces judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria, while the coast becomes Judah’s pasture, the LORD restores its captives, and nations worship him.

Zephaniah 3.overview: Zephaniah indicts Jerusalem for rejecting correction and describes its corrupt leaders, contrasting their injustice with the LORD’s righteousness as he announces judgment on the nations. The LORD promises purified worship among the peoples and a humble, secure remnant of Israel, then calls Zion to rejoice as he removes her punishment, saves the afflicted, and gathers his people.

Haggai 1.overview: In the second year of Darius, Haggai tells Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people that their neglect of the ruined temple contrasts with their paneled houses, and he calls them to rebuild it as the LORD explains the scarcity affecting their land. Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the remnant obey, receive the LORD’s assurance of presence, and begin work on the temple on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month.

sections.heading: The Call to Rebuild and Its Consequences

Haggai 2.overview: Haggai tells Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people to work on the temple, promising that the LORD is with them and that its latter glory and peace will exceed its former glory as the LORD shakes the nations. The LORD uses a ruling from the priests to declare the people’s work defiled, recalls their poor harvests, promises blessing from the day the temple foundation is laid, and tells Zerubbabel that he is chosen as the LORD’s signet ring when kingdoms are overturned.

sections.heading: Encouragement and the Temple’s Future Glory
Zerubbabel as the LORD’s Signet Ring

Zechariah 1.overview: Zechariah recounts the LORD’s call for Judah to return, contrasting the people’s disobedient ancestors with the fulfillment of the LORD’s words. In visions, horsemen report that the earth is at rest as the LORD promises mercy and restoration for Jerusalem, then four horns that scattered Judah are opposed by four craftsmen.

sections.heading: Call to Return to the LORD

Zechariah 2.overview: Zechariah sees a man measuring Jerusalem, and an angel announces that the city will grow beyond its walls, with the LORD as its protection and glory. The LORD calls the exiles to flee Babylon, promises judgment on those who plundered them, and declares that he will dwell among Zion, gather many nations, and again choose Jerusalem and Judah.

Zechariah 3.overview: Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest accused by Satan before the angel of the LORD, who rebukes Satan and replaces Joshua’s filthy garments with clean robes and a turban. The angel charges Joshua to keep the LORD’s instructions and announces the Branch, a stone, the removal of the land’s iniquity in one day, and peace under vine and fig tree.

sections.heading: Joshua’s Charge and the Coming Branch

Zechariah 4.overview: An angel awakens Zechariah and shows him a gold lampstand supplied by two olive trees, then explains that Zerubbabel will complete the temple not by human might but by the LORD’s Spirit. The angel says obstacles will give way, the LORD will rejoice over Zerubbabel’s work, and the two olive trees represent two anointed ones standing beside the Lord of all the earth.

Zechariah 5.overview: Zechariah sees a flying scroll that carries a curse against thieves and those who swear falsely, entering their houses and destroying them. He then sees a woman called Wickedness confined in a measuring basket and carried by two women to Shinar, where a house is to be built for it.

sections.heading: The flying scroll and its curse

Zechariah 6.overview: Zechariah sees four chariots emerge from between bronze mountains and learns that they are the four spirits of heaven sent to patrol the earth; those going north give rest to the LORD’s Spirit there. The LORD directs Zechariah to crown Joshua the high priest and proclaim the Branch, who will build the temple and rule as both king and priest, while people from far away will help build it if the people obey the LORD.

sections.heading: The Four Chariots and Their Mission
Joshua Crowned and the Branch Announced

Zechariah 7.overview: In the fourth year of Darius, messengers from Bethel ask whether they should continue the fifth-month fast, and the LORD questions whether the people’s past fasting and feasting were done for him. The LORD recalls the earlier call to justice and compassion, then describes how the people refuse to listen and are scattered, leaving the land desolate.

sections.heading: The Call to Justice and Compassion

Zechariah 8.overview: The LORD of Hosts promises to return to Zion, restore Jerusalem, gather the people, and replace hardship with safety and abundance. He calls for truth and justice, declares that Judah’s fasts will become feasts, and describes nations coming to seek the LORD in Jerusalem.

sections.heading: Zion Restored and the People Gathered
Fasts Become Feasts and Nations Come

Zechariah 9.overview: The LORD announces judgment against Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistine cities, while making a remnant of the Philistines and guarding Jerusalem. Zion’s humble king brings peace to the nations, and the LORD releases prisoners, empowers Judah and Ephraim against Greece, and saves and restores his people.

Zechariah 10.overview: The LORD calls the people to seek rain from Him rather than trust idols and false diviners, then promises to punish failed shepherds and strengthen Judah and Joseph for battle. He promises to gather and restore the scattered people from distant lands, bring down Assyria and Egypt, and strengthen them in His name.

sections.heading: Rain and False Sources of Help
The Scattered People Gathered and Restored

Zechariah 11.overview: The chapter depicts Lebanon’s forests and the shepherds’ glory in ruin, then announces that the flock marked for slaughter will be abandoned to hostile rulers. The prophet pastures the flock with staffs named Favor and Union, breaks them to signify the revocation of a covenant and the division of Judah and Israel, receives thirty pieces of silver, and pronounces judgment on a worthless shepherd.

Zechariah 12.overview: The LORD declares that the nations gathering against Jerusalem will be injured and defeated, while he protects Jerusalem and strengthens Judah. He pours out a spirit of grace and prayer on the house of David and Jerusalem, and the people mourn the pierced one with grief compared to the mourning at Hadad-rimmon and Megiddo.

sections.heading: Jerusalem and Judah against the nations

Zechariah 13.overview: The LORD promises a fountain for cleansing the house of David and Jerusalem, the removal of idols and false prophets, and the exposure of those who falsely prophesy. The LORD calls the sword against His Shepherd, says the sheep will scatter and most of the land will perish, and promises to refine the surviving third and renew their covenant relationship.

sections.heading: Cleansing and the Removal of False Prophets
The Shepherd, Judgment, and the Refined Remnant

Zechariah 14.overview: The LORD gathers the nations against Jerusalem, then fights them and brings deliverance as the Mount of Olives splits, living water flows from the city, and the LORD reigns over the earth. The nations face judgment and survivors worship the LORD in Jerusalem, while the city and its vessels become holy to Him.

sections.heading: Jerusalem Renewed Under the LORD’s Rule
Judgment on the Nations and Their Worship

Malachi 1.overview: The LORD declares his love for Israel by contrasting Jacob with Esau and describing Edom’s lasting desolation. He rebukes Israel’s priests for dishonoring him with defective offerings, rejects their sacrifices, and declares that his name will be great among the nations.

sections.heading: The LORD’s Name Among the Nations

Malachi 2.overview: The LORD threatens the priests with curses for dishonoring his name, recalls the covenant of life and peace with Levi, and condemns their corrupt teaching and partiality. Judah is accused of profaning the sanctuary through foreign marriages and of breaking faith with wives, while the people weary the LORD by calling evildoers good and questioning his justice.

sections.heading: The Priests and the Covenant of Levi

Malachi 3.overview: The LORD announces a messenger who prepares the way, followed by the Lord’s coming to the temple to refine the Levites, restore acceptable offerings, and judge wrongdoing. He calls Jacob’s descendants to return, condemns their withholding of tithes, answers their complaints about serving God, and promises to distinguish and spare those who fear and honor him.

sections.heading: Return to the LORD and Bring Tithes
The Faithful and the Wicked Distinguished

Malachi 4.overview: The LORD announces a coming day that consumes the arrogant and evildoers, while those who fear his name receive healing and trample the wicked. He calls Israel to remember the law given through Moses at Horeb and promises to send Elijah before the Day of the LORD to turn the hearts of parents and children, or bring a curse on the land.

sections.heading: Judgment and healing on the coming day
Moses, Elijah, and the Day of the LORD

Matthew 1.overview: Matthew traces Jesus Christ’s genealogy from Abraham through David and the Babylonian exile to Joseph, Mary’s husband, and presents the three periods as fourteen generations each. An angel tells Joseph in a dream that Mary’s child is conceived by the Holy Spirit, names him Jesus, and identifies his birth as fulfilling the prophecy of Immanuel.

Matthew 2.overview: Magi from the east seek the newborn King of the Jews, worship Jesus in Bethlehem, and return home by another route after a dream warns them about Herod. Joseph takes Jesus and Mary to Egypt to escape Herod’s violence, then returns after Herod’s death and settles in Nazareth, fulfilling prophetic words.

sections.heading: Flight to Egypt and Herod’s Decree

Matthew 3.overview: John the Baptist preaches repentance in the wilderness of Judea, baptizes people in the Jordan, and warns the Pharisees and Sadducees of judgment while announcing a more powerful one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, and the Spirit descends on him as a voice from heaven identifies him as God’s beloved Son.

sections.heading: John Warns the Pharisees and Sadducees

Matthew 4.overview: Jesus resists the devil’s three temptations in the wilderness, and angels minister to him after the devil leaves. After John is imprisoned, Jesus settles in Capernaum, proclaims the kingdom of heaven, calls Simon Peter, Andrew, James, and John, and teaches, preaches, and heals throughout Galilee as crowds gather from surrounding regions.

sections.heading: Jesus Is Tempted in the Wilderness

Matthew 5.overview: Jesus teaches the crowds and his disciples on a mountain, pronouncing blessings, describing them as salt and light, and affirming that he fulfills the Law and the Prophets. He contrasts traditional commands with teachings on anger, adultery, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and love for enemies, calling for righteousness that reflects the heavenly Father.

Matthew 6.overview: Jesus contrasts giving, prayer, and fasting for public recognition with practicing them in secret before the Father, teaches the Lord’s Prayer, and links divine forgiveness with forgiving others. He warns against earthly treasure, divided service to God and money, and anxiety about daily needs, pointing to God’s care and the priority of his kingdom and righteousness.

Matthew 7.overview: Jesus teaches about judgment, discernment, prayer, and the narrow way, and warns that false prophets and empty claims of allegiance are exposed by their fruit and actions. He compares those who act on his words to a house built on rock, and the crowds are astonished because he teaches with authority.

sections.heading: The narrow way and true discipleship

Matthew 8.overview: After coming down from the mountain, Jesus cleanses a leper, heals a centurion’s servant in Capernaum, and heals Peter’s mother-in-law and many others; he praises the centurion’s faith and speaks of people from east and west entering the kingdom of heaven. Jesus describes the cost of following him, calms a storm on the sea, and drives demons from two men in the region of the Gadarenes into a herd of pigs, after which the townspeople ask him to leave.

sections.heading: Demons and the herd of pigs

Matthew 9.overview: Jesus heals a paralytic and declares his sins forgiven, calls Matthew, eats with tax collectors and sinners, and explains his approach to fasting. He heals a woman and a synagogue leader’s daughter, restores sight to two blind men and speech to a mute man, then teaches, heals, and tells his disciples that the plentiful harvest needs workers.

sections.heading: Matthew’s Call and Questions About Fasting

Matthew 10.overview: Jesus appoints the twelve apostles, gives them authority to heal and cast out demons, and sends them to proclaim the kingdom of heaven to Israel. He warns them of persecution, teaches them not to fear, describes the divisions and costs of discipleship, and promises a reward for those who receive his messengers.

sections.heading: The Cost and Reward of Discipleship

Matthew 11.overview: Jesus answers John the Baptist’s question by pointing to his works, then identifies John’s role and describes the generation’s rejection of both John and the Son of Man. He pronounces judgment on unrepentant cities, praises the Father’s revelation through the Son, and offers rest to the weary.

sections.heading: Jesus on John and the Generation
The Father, the Son, and Rest

Matthew 12.overview: Jesus answers the Pharisees’ Sabbath accusations by asserting his authority as Lord of the Sabbath, heals a man, and responds to the charge that he casts out demons by Beelzebul with teachings about God’s kingdom, the Spirit, and judgment. He rejects the demand for a sign except Jonah’s, warns of the generation’s judgment, and identifies those who do his Father’s will as his family.

Matthew 13.overview: Jesus teaches the crowds in parables about the kingdom of heaven, explains the parable of the sower and the weeds to his disciples, and describes the kingdom’s growth, value, and final judgment. After teaching in parables, he returns to his hometown, where the people take offense at him and his unbelief limits his miracles there.

sections.heading: The Sower and the Purpose of Parables
The Weeds and the Kingdom’s Growth

Matthew 14.overview: Herod hears reports about Jesus and identifies him as John the Baptist risen from the dead, while the account recounts John’s execution at Herod’s order. Jesus heals the sick, feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, walks on the sea and rescues Peter, and heals the sick at Gennesaret.

Matthew 15.overview: Jesus confronts Pharisees and scribes over traditions that nullify God’s commands, then teaches that defilement comes from the heart rather than unwashed hands. In the region of Tyre and Sidon, he heals a Canaanite woman’s daughter, heals crowds near the Sea of Galilee, feeds four thousand men, and departs for Magadan.

sections.heading: Healing by the Sea of Galilee

Matthew 16.overview: The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign, and Jesus warns his disciples against their teaching after they misunderstand his reference to leaven. At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and Jesus predicts his suffering, death, and resurrection before teaching about the cost of discipleship and the Son of Man’s coming judgment.

sections.heading: The Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
Peter Confesses Jesus as the Christ
Jesus Predicts His Death and Teaches Discipleship

Matthew 17.overview: Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, and the disciples hear God’s command to listen to him; Jesus identifies John the Baptist with the Elijah who has already come. He casts a demon out of a boy and teaches about faith, predicts his death and resurrection, and provides a coin for the temple tax.

sections.heading: Healing the Boy and Teaching on Faith
Jesus Predicts His Death and Resurrection

Matthew 18.overview: When the disciples ask about greatness, Jesus uses a child to teach humility and warns against causing little ones to stumble, then describes the Father’s care for the lost. He instructs the disciples on confronting sin and gathering in his name, and answers Peter’s question about forgiveness with a parable of a servant who is forgiven a great debt but refuses mercy to a fellow servant.

sections.heading: Humility and Care for Little Ones
Confronting Sin and Gathering in Jesus’ Name

Matthew 19.overview: Jesus travels from Galilee to Judea beyond the Jordan, heals crowds, and teaches the Pharisees and disciples about marriage, divorce, and celibacy. He welcomes children, tells a wealthy young man to give to the poor and follow him, explains the difficulty of salvation and the possibility with God, and promises reward and reversal to his followers.

sections.heading: The Rich Young Man and Salvation

Matthew 20.overview: Jesus tells a parable in which a vineyard owner pays workers hired at different hours the same wage, concluding that the last will be first and the first last. On the way to Jerusalem, Jesus predicts his death and resurrection, teaches the disciples about service after a request for places of honor, and heals two blind men near Jericho.

sections.heading: Jesus Predicts His Death and Resurrection
A Request for Honor and the Way of Service
Two Blind Men Healed near Jericho

Matthew 21.overview: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the crowds acclaim him, cleanses the temple, heals the blind and lame, and teaches about faith after a barren fig tree withers. He challenges the chief priests and elders over his authority, tells parables of two sons and wicked tenants, and declares that the kingdom will be given to a people who bear its fruit.

Matthew 22.overview: Jesus tells a parable of a king’s wedding banquet, whose invited guests refuse to come and whose later guests include a man without wedding clothes. Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees test Jesus on taxes, resurrection, and the greatest commandment, and Jesus questions the Pharisees about the Christ as David’s son and Lord.

sections.heading: The Christ, David’s Son and Lord

Matthew 23.overview: Jesus contrasts the scribes’ and Pharisees’ public authority and religious display with their hypocrisy, and teaches his disciples about humility and service. He pronounces woes against the leaders, predicts judgment for their violence against God’s messengers, and laments Jerusalem’s refusal to gather under his care.

sections.heading: Warnings About the Scribes and Pharisees

Matthew 24.overview: Jesus predicts the temple’s destruction and, on the Mount of Olives, answers his disciples’ questions about his coming and the end of the age with warnings about deception, conflict, persecution, and tribulation. He describes the coming of the Son of Man and the gathering of the elect, then teaches that its timing is unknown and that faithful servants must be ready.

sections.heading: The Temple and the Disciples’ Questions
The Coming of the Son of Man
The Unknown Hour and Faithful Servants

Matthew 25.overview: Jesus tells parables of ten virgins awaiting a bridegroom and servants entrusted with talents, distinguishing those who are ready and faithful from those who are not. He describes the Son of Man’s judgment of all nations, separating the righteous, who served the least, from those who did not, and assigning them to eternal life or punishment.

sections.heading: The Ten Virgins and the Bridegroom
The Talents and the Servants’ Accounts
The Son of Man Judges the Nations

Matthew 26.overview: Jesus predicts his death as the chief priests and elders plot to arrest him, while a woman anoints him at Bethany and Judas arranges to betray him. At the Passover meal Jesus identifies his betrayer and gives the bread and cup new meaning, then prays in Gethsemane, is arrested and tried before Caiaphas, and Peter denies knowing him three times.

Matthew 27.overview: Judas returns the silver and dies, while the chief priests use it to buy a burial field; before Pilate, Jesus is condemned as the crowd chooses Barabbas and demands his crucifixion. Jesus is mocked and crucified at Golgotha, dies amid signs and the centurion’s confession, is buried by Joseph of Arimathea, and his tomb is sealed and guarded at the chief priests’ request.

sections.heading: Judas and the Field of Blood

Matthew 28.overview: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary find Jesus’ tomb open, hear from an angel that he has risen, and meet the risen Jesus; the guards report the events, but the chief priests and elders pay them to spread a false account. The eleven disciples meet Jesus in Galilee, where he declares his authority and commissions them to make disciples of all nations, baptize them, and teach them his commands, promising his presence always.

sections.heading: The Empty Tomb and the Risen Jesus
The Guards’ Report and the False Account

Mark 1.overview: John the Baptist prepares the way for Jesus, who is baptized, declared God’s beloved Son, and tempted in the wilderness. After John’s arrest, Jesus proclaims God’s kingdom in Galilee, calls disciples, teaches and heals with authority, and cleanses a leper whose report draws crowds.

Mark 2.overview: In Capernaum, Jesus heals a paralytic and asserts the Son of Man’s authority to forgive sins, then calls Levi and eats with tax collectors and sinners. He explains why his disciples do not fast and, after the Pharisees challenge their Sabbath actions, cites David and declares the Son of Man Lord of the Sabbath.

sections.heading: The Sabbath and the Son of Man

Mark 3.overview: Jesus heals a man on the Sabbath, prompting the Pharisees and Herodians to plot against him, then draws crowds from surrounding regions and appoints twelve apostles. He answers the scribes’ accusation that he drives out demons by Beelzebul and identifies those who do God’s will as his family.

Mark 4.overview: Jesus teaches beside the sea through parables of the sower, the lamp, and the growing and mustard seeds, explaining the kingdom of God and varied responses to the word. Later, he stills a storm on the sea as he crosses with his disciples, who question his authority over the wind and water.

sections.heading: The Sower and the Purpose of Parables

Mark 5.overview: In the region of the Gerasenes, Jesus drives a legion of demons from a man into a herd of pigs, and the restored man proclaims what Jesus has done throughout the Decapolis. Back across the sea, Jesus heals a woman who touches his cloak and raises Jairus’s daughter from the dead.

sections.heading: The Gerasene Man and the Legion

Mark 6.overview: Jesus faces rejection in Nazareth, sends the Twelve to preach and heal, and Herod orders John the Baptist’s execution. Jesus feeds five thousand, walks on the sea to the disciples, and heals the sick throughout Gennesaret.

sections.heading: Feeding the Crowd and Walking on the Sea

Mark 7.overview: Pharisees and scribes challenge Jesus over ritual washing, and he condemns traditions that nullify God’s commands before teaching that defilement comes from within the heart. In the region of Tyre, Jesus casts a demon from a Syrophoenician woman’s daughter, then in the Decapolis heals a deaf man who can hardly speak.

Mark 8.overview: Jesus feeds four thousand people, refuses the Pharisees’ demand for a sign, and questions the disciples about their understanding of the loaves and the leaven. At Bethsaida he heals a blind man, Peter identifies him as the Christ, and Jesus teaches about his coming suffering, death, and resurrection, then describes the cost of following him and the Son of Man’s coming in glory.

sections.heading: Suffering and the Cost of Discipleship

Mark 9.overview: Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, explains Elijah’s coming, and casts a spirit out of a boy after the disciples fail to do so. In Galilee and Capernaum, he predicts his death and resurrection, teaches the Twelve about service and welcoming others, and warns against causing believers to stumble and against sin.

Mark 10.overview: In Judea beyond the Jordan, Jesus teaches about divorce, welcomes children, and tells a wealthy man that following him requires giving up his possessions, while explaining the difficulty of wealth and the rewards of leaving things for the gospel. On the road to Jerusalem, he predicts his death and resurrection, teaches the Twelve that greatness means serving others, and restores Bartimaeus’s sight near Jericho.

sections.heading: The Rich Man and the Kingdom
Jesus Predicts His Death and Teaches Service

Mark 11.overview: Jesus enters Jerusalem to acclaim from the crowd, inspects the temple, and later curses a fruitless fig tree before driving buyers and sellers from the temple courts. After the tree withers, he teaches about faith, prayer, and forgiveness, then refuses to disclose his authority to Jerusalem’s religious leaders when they will not answer his question about John’s baptism.

sections.heading: The Fig Tree and the Temple

Mark 12.overview: Jesus tells the parable of the vineyard tenants and answers challenges from the Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees, and a scribe about taxes, resurrection, and the greatest commandment. In the temple courts, He questions how the Christ can be David’s son, warns against the scribes, and says the poor widow gives more than the wealthy because she contributes all she has.

sections.heading: The Parable of the Vineyard Tenants
The Greatest Commandment and David’s Lord
Warnings About Scribes and the Widow’s Offering

Mark 13.overview: Jesus predicts the temple’s destruction and answers Peter, James, John, and Andrew with warnings about deception, conflict, persecution, and tribulation. He describes the coming of the Son of Man and the gathering of the elect, then teaches that the time is unknown and calls for watchfulness.

sections.heading: Tribulation and the Coming of the Son of Man
The Unknown Time and the Call to Watch

Mark 14.overview: As the Passover approaches, a woman anoints Jesus at Bethany, Judas agrees to betray him, and Jesus shares the Passover meal with his disciples, predicting his betrayal, their flight, and Peter’s denial. In Gethsemane Jesus prays before Judas leads an armed crowd to arrest him; the high priest’s council condemns him, while Peter denies knowing him three times.

Mark 15.overview: The chief priests and Sanhedrin hand Jesus over to Pilate, who releases Barabbas and condemns Jesus to crucifixion. Jesus is mocked and crucified at Golgotha, dies as the temple veil is torn, and is buried by Joseph of Arimathea while women witness where he is laid.

Mark 16.overview: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome find Jesus’ tomb open, where a young man announces that Jesus has risen and tells them to inform the disciples. The risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene, two followers, and the Eleven, commissions the Eleven to proclaim the gospel, and is taken up into heaven as they preach with signs accompanying their work.

sections.heading: The Women Find the Empty Tomb
The Ascension and the Disciples’ Mission

Luke 1.overview: Luke explains that he has investigated the events handed down by eyewitnesses and writes an orderly account for Theophilus. Gabriel announces the births and roles of John and Jesus; Mary visits Elizabeth and praises God, John is born and named, and Zechariah prophesies about the coming salvation and John’s mission.

Luke 2.overview: A census ordered by Caesar Augustus brings Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born; angels announce him as Savior and shepherds visit him. In Jerusalem, Simeon and Anna recognize Jesus as God’s salvation, and later the twelve-year-old Jesus stays in the temple before returning to Nazareth and growing in wisdom and stature.

Luke 3.overview: During the rule of Tiberius Caesar, the word of God comes to John in the wilderness, and he calls people across the Jordan region to repentance, gives practical instructions, and announces a more powerful coming one. Herod imprisons John; Jesus is baptized and affirmed by a voice from heaven, and Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry back through David and Abraham to Adam and God.

Luke 4.overview: Jesus resists the devil’s three temptations in the wilderness and begins preaching in Galilee. In Nazareth, he announces the fulfillment of Isaiah’s words and is driven out, while in Capernaum he teaches with authority, heals the sick, and casts out demons before continuing to preach in other towns.

sections.heading: Jesus Ministers in Capernaum and Beyond

Luke 5.overview: Jesus teaches from Simon’s boat, provides a miraculous catch of fish, and calls Simon, James, and John to follow him. He cleanses a leper, forgives and heals a paralyzed man, calls Levi, and answers questions about eating and fasting with images of the bridegroom, new cloth, and new wine.

sections.heading: The Miraculous Catch and First Disciples
Forgiveness and Healing of a Paralytic
Fasting, the Bridegroom, and New Wine

Luke 6.overview: Jesus answers Pharisees who challenge Sabbath practices, heals a man with a withered hand, and declares the Son of Man Lord of the Sabbath. After praying on a mountain and choosing twelve apostles, Jesus heals crowds at a level place and teaches about blessing, love, mercy, judgment, the heart, and acting on his words.

sections.heading: The Twelve and the Healing Crowds
The Heart and the Firm Foundation

Luke 7.overview: In Capernaum, Jesus heals a centurion’s servant from a distance, then raises a widow’s son at Nain, prompting reports that God has visited his people. Jesus answers John’s question about his identity with accounts of his works, describes John’s role and the divided responses to both John and himself, and tells Simon that the woman who anoints his feet is forgiven.

sections.heading: The Widow’s Son Raised at Nain
The Woman Who Anoints Jesus’ Feet

Luke 8.overview: Jesus travels through Galilee with the Twelve and women who support the ministry, teaches about hearing God’s word, and identifies those who hear and carry it out as his family. He calms a storm, frees a man from demons in the region of the Gerasenes, and heals a bleeding woman and Jairus’s daughter.

sections.heading: The Woman Healed and Jairus’s Daughter Raised

Luke 9.overview: Jesus commissions the Twelve to preach and heal, Herod questions Jesus’ identity, and Jesus feeds a large crowd near Bethsaida. Peter identifies Jesus as the Christ, Jesus predicts his suffering and is transfigured with Moses and Elijah, then heals a boy, teaches the disciples, and sets out for Jerusalem while defining the demands of following him.

Luke 10.overview: Jesus sends seventy-two disciples to announce the kingdom, pronounces judgment on unresponsive towns, and teaches about the authority of their mission and the Father’s revelation. He answers a lawyer’s question with the parable of the Samaritan, then visits Martha and Mary and speaks about what is necessary.

sections.heading: The Disciples Return and Jesus Rejoices

Luke 11.overview: Jesus teaches his disciples a prayer and urges persistence in asking, then answers accusations about his power over demons and speaks about signs, light, and hearing God’s word. At a Pharisee’s dinner, he condemns the Pharisees and experts in the law for neglecting justice, burdening others, and opposing God’s messengers, after which they seek to trap him with questions.

sections.heading: Jesus’ Authority and the Sign of Jonah
Woes Against Pharisees and Experts in the Law

Luke 12.overview: Jesus warns his disciples about hypocrisy, fear, confession, and reliance on the Holy Spirit, then answers an inheritance dispute with a parable about a rich fool. He teaches trust in God and readiness for the Son of Man’s return, and tells the crowds that his coming brings division and that they must recognize the present time and settle disputes.

sections.heading: Trust in God and Heavenly Treasure

Luke 13.overview: Jesus rejects the idea that victims of Pilate’s violence or the Siloam tower collapse are worse sinners, calls for repentance, tells of a barren fig tree, and heals a disabled woman on the Sabbath. He compares God’s kingdom to a mustard seed and leaven, warns on the way to Jerusalem that entry is narrow and many will be excluded, and responds to a warning about Herod with a lament over Jerusalem.

sections.heading: Repentance and the Barren Fig Tree
The Narrow Door and the Kingdom Feast

Luke 14.overview: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee’s home, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, teaches about humility and generosity at banquets, and tells a parable about invited guests who refuse a great feast. Addressing the crowds, he describes the cost of discipleship through sayings about family, carrying the cross, counting the cost, and salt that loses its savor.

sections.heading: The Parable of the Great Banquet

Luke 15.overview: After Pharisees and scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them, he tells the parables of the lost sheep and lost coin, each ending with joy over a sinner who repents. In the parable of the two sons, the younger returns after squandering his inheritance and is welcomed by his father, while the older objects to the celebration and the father explains why it is fitting.

sections.heading: The Lost Sheep and Lost Coin

Luke 16.overview: Jesus tells the parable of a manager who reduces his master’s debtors’ bills, then teaches about faithfulness with wealth and the impossibility of serving both God and money. He rebukes the money-loving Pharisees, speaks about the Law, the kingdom, and divorce, then recounts the deaths of the rich man and Lazarus and Abraham’s warning that Moses and the Prophets are sufficient testimony.

sections.heading: Wealth, the Pharisees, and the Law

Luke 17.overview: Jesus warns his disciples against causing others to stumble, teaches repeated forgiveness, faith, and humble service. On the way between Samaria and Galilee, he heals ten lepers, and then teaches the Pharisees and his disciples about the kingdom of God and the coming day of the Son of Man.

sections.heading: The Kingdom and the Son of Man

Luke 18.overview: Jesus teaches about persistent prayer and humility through two parables, welcomes children, and tells a wealthy ruler that entering God’s kingdom requires what is impossible without God. He predicts his suffering and resurrection to the Twelve, then restores the sight of a blind man near Jericho, prompting praise to God.

sections.heading: Jesus Predicts His Death and Resurrection
A Blind Man Receives His Sight

Luke 19.overview: In Jericho, Jesus stays with Zacchaeus, whose response prompts Jesus to declare that the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost, then tells a parable about a nobleman, his servants, and his enemies. On the way to Jerusalem, Jesus enters as king, laments the city’s coming destruction, clears sellers from the temple, and teaches there while its leaders seek to kill him.

sections.heading: Teaching and Conflict in the Temple

Luke 20.overview: In the temple, Jesus answers challenges to his authority with a question about John’s baptism and tells a parable of tenants who kill the vineyard owner’s son, followed by a warning about the rejected cornerstone. He answers questions about taxes and resurrection, teaches that the Christ is David’s Lord, and warns against the scribes’ public display and exploitation of widows.

Luke 21.overview: Jesus commends a poor widow’s small offering and predicts the temple’s destruction, warning of deception, conflict, persecution, and Jerusalem’s desolation. He describes signs preceding the Son of Man’s coming, urges vigilance, and continues teaching at the temple while staying on the Mount of Olives.

sections.heading: Jerusalem’s Desolation and the Son of Man

Luke 22.overview: As the Passover approaches, Judas agrees to betray Jesus, and Jesus shares the meal with his apostles, instituting the bread and cup as signs of his body and the new covenant in his blood. Jesus teaches about service and coming trials, prays on the Mount of Olives, is arrested and taken to the high priest’s house, while Peter denies knowing him before the Sanhedrin questions Jesus and condemns his testimony.

sections.heading: Service, Peter’s Denial, and Coming Trials
Prayer and Arrest on the Mount of Olives
Peter’s Denial and Jesus Before the Council

Luke 23.overview: Jesus is brought before Pilate and Herod, who find no basis for a death sentence, but Pilate yields to the crowd’s demand to crucify him and releases Barabbas. Jesus is crucified at The Skull, promises Paradise to a repentant criminal, dies amid signs and public reactions, and is buried by Joseph of Arimathea as the women observe the tomb.

Luke 24.overview: Women find Jesus’ tomb empty, hear from two men that he has risen, and report the news to the apostles, while Peter inspects the tomb. Jesus explains the Scriptures to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, appears to the gathered disciples in Jerusalem, commissions them as witnesses, and is carried up into heaven near Bethany.

sections.heading: Jesus on the Road to Emmaus

John 1.overview: John presents the Word as God, creator, life, and light, who becomes flesh as Jesus Christ and makes the Father known; John the Baptist testifies that Jesus is the Son of God and the Lamb of God. John identifies himself as the voice preparing the Lord’s way, while Jesus gathers Andrew, Simon Peter, Philip, and Nathanael, who recognize him as Messiah, Son of God, and King of Israel.

John 2.overview: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turns water into wine as his first sign, revealing his glory to his disciples. In Jerusalem, he drives the sellers and money changers from the temple, speaks of raising the temple of his body, and remains wary of the people who believe because of his signs.

sections.heading: Jesus Knows What Is in People

John 3.overview: Nicodemus visits Jesus at night, and Jesus teaches that entry into God’s kingdom requires birth by the Spirit, then explains the Son of Man’s mission and the verdict on belief and unbelief. Jesus and John baptize in the Judean countryside, where John tells his disciples that he is not the Christ and that the Son from heaven must increase, concluding with the contrast between eternal life and God’s wrath.

sections.heading: Jesus teaches Nicodemus about new birth
The Son of Man and the verdict of belief
John explains his role beside Jesus
The Son from heaven and eternal life

John 4.overview: Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee, speaks with a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well about living water and true worship, and many Samaritans believe that he is the Savior of the world. In Cana, Jesus heals a royal official’s son from a distance, and the official and his household believe.

sections.heading: The royal official’s son is healed

John 5.overview: At the pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, Jesus heals a man who has been disabled for thirty-eight years, and the Sabbath healing leads the Jewish authorities to challenge him. Jesus explains his unity with the Father and his authority to give life and judge, then cites John, his works, the Father, Scripture, and Moses as witnesses to his identity and the authorities’ unbelief.

sections.heading: The Son’s Authority from the Father

John 6.overview: Jesus feeds five thousand people near the Sea of Galilee, walks across the sea to his disciples, and teaches in Capernaum that he is the bread of life who gives eternal life. Many disciples turn away over his teaching, while Peter affirms the Twelve’s belief, and Jesus identifies Judas as the one who will betray him.

sections.heading: Jesus Teaches About the Bread of Life

John 7.overview: Jesus goes secretly to the Feast of Tabernacles, teaches in the temple courts, and declares that his teaching comes from the Father who sent him as conflict grows over his identity and authority. On the feast’s final day, he offers living water, identified with the Spirit, and the crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Christ while the authorities fail to arrest him and Nicodemus calls for a hearing under the law.

sections.heading: Jesus and His Brothers at the Feast
Debate over Jesus’ Origin and Mission
Living Water and Division over Jesus

John 8.overview: Jesus faces a test from the scribes and Pharisees over a woman caught in adultery, then declares himself the light of the world and debates with his opponents about his testimony, origin, and relationship to the Father. He tells those who believe him that his word brings freedom from sin, identifies his opponents’ father as the devil, and declares that he existed before Abraham; they try to stone him, but he leaves the temple area.

John 9.overview: Jesus heals a man born blind by sending him to wash in the Pool of Siloam, and the man’s neighbors and the Pharisees question him and his parents about the healing on the Sabbath. After the Pharisees reject his testimony and expel him, Jesus reveals himself to the man, who believes and worships him, while Jesus declares that he brings judgment between those who see and those who are blind.

sections.heading: Healing and the Man’s First Testimony
The Pharisees Question the Man and His Parents

John 10.overview: Jesus describes the sheepfold, identifies himself as the gate and the good shepherd, and says that he lays down his life and takes it up again; his words divide his hearers. At the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem, Jesus speaks of his unity with the Father, answers accusations of blasphemy, escapes an attempt to seize him, and later receives belief from many across the Jordan.

sections.heading: The Gate and the Good Shepherd
Jesus at the Feast of Dedication

John 11.overview: Jesus delays going to Bethany, then raises Lazarus from the dead and declares himself the resurrection and the life. Many witnesses believe, while the chief priests and Pharisees plot to kill Jesus, who withdraws as Passover approaches.

John 12.overview: At Bethany, Mary anoints Jesus, while Judas objects and the chief priests plot against Lazarus; Jesus then enters Jerusalem to acclaim from the crowds. In response to Greek visitors, Jesus speaks of his death and glorification, and the chapter closes with the crowds’ unbelief, Isaiah’s words, and Jesus’ claims about his mission and the Father’s command.

John 13.overview: At the Passover meal, Jesus washes the disciples’ feet, explains the act as an example of service, and identifies Judas as the one who will betray him. After Judas leaves, Jesus speaks of his glorification and commands the disciples to love one another, then tells Peter that he will deny him three times.

John 14.overview: Jesus reassures the disciples of a place in the Father’s house, identifies himself as the way to the Father, and explains that his words and works reveal the Father. He promises the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, and peace to those who love and keep his word, then speaks of his departure and obedience to the Father.

sections.heading: A Place in the Father’s House

John 15.overview: Jesus presents himself as the true vine and the Father as the vineyard keeper, teaching that abiding in him produces fruit and that his disciples remain in his love through obedience and mutual love. He calls the disciples his friends and chosen witnesses, warns that the world will hate and persecute them as it hated him, and promises that the Spirit of truth will testify about him alongside them.

sections.heading: The Vine and Abiding in Love
The Spirit and the Disciples’ Testimony

John 16.overview: Jesus warns the disciples of persecution and explains that his departure brings the Advocate, who convicts the world and guides them in truth. He promises that their sorrow will turn to joy, speaks of asking the Father in his name, and tells the disciples they will scatter while he remains with the Father and has overcome the world.

John 17.overview: Jesus prays to the Father for the glorification that reflects their shared glory and for eternal life through knowing the Father and the Son. He asks the Father to protect and sanctify his disciples, then prays for future believers to be united in him so the world may know that the Father sent him.

sections.heading: Protection and sanctification for the disciples

John 18.overview: Jesus is arrested in a garden after identifying himself to Judas’s party and protecting his disciples, while Peter cuts off Malchus’s ear and later denies knowing Jesus three times. Annas and Caiaphas question Jesus, then Pilate interrogates him about his kingship and finds no basis for a charge, but the crowd demands Barabbas’s release.

John 19.overview: Pilate presents Jesus to the chief priests and the crowd, but under pressure he hands Him over for crucifixion. At Golgotha Jesus dies, fulfills Scripture, and is buried by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus in a nearby tomb.

John 20.overview: Mary Magdalene finds Jesus’ tomb empty, and Peter and the other disciple inspect it; Jesus then appears to Mary and commissions her to tell the disciples. He appears to the disciples, gives them the Holy Spirit, and later meets Thomas, while the chapter concludes by stating that the recorded signs testify that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

John 21.overview: At the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus appears to seven disciples, directs them to a large catch of fish, and shares breakfast with them. He charges Peter to care for his followers, foretells Peter’s death, clarifies that the beloved disciple’s fate is not Peter’s concern, and the chapter closes with testimony to Jesus and a note on the many things he did.

sections.heading: The Catch and Breakfast by the Sea
Jesus Charges Peter to Shepherd His Sheep
The Disciple’s Testimony and Closing Note

Acts 1.overview: Jesus appears to the apostles over forty days, teaches about God’s kingdom, promises the Holy Spirit, and ascends from the Mount of Olives. In Jerusalem, Peter explains Judas’s departure from the apostolic ministry, and the gathered believers choose Matthias to join the eleven apostles.

Acts 2.overview: At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit fills the disciples, who speak in other languages as Jews from many nations gather in Jerusalem and hear them declare God’s works. Peter explains the event through Joel and David, proclaims Jesus’ death, resurrection, and exaltation, and sees about three thousand people baptized as the believers form a growing community.

sections.heading: Peter Proclaims Jesus as Lord and Christ
The Crowd Responds and Is Baptized
The Believers Share a Common Life

Acts 3.overview: Peter heals a man lame from birth at the temple gate in Jesus’ name, and the crowd gathers at Solomon’s Colonnade as Peter explains that God glorifies Jesus, whom they reject and kill but raise from the dead. Peter calls the people to repent and turn back, citing Moses and the prophets as witnesses that the Christ suffers and that God appoints Jesus for the restoration and blessing of Israel.

Acts 4.overview: Peter and John are arrested for proclaiming resurrection in Jesus, then testify before the Jerusalem authorities that the healed man stands well through Jesus Christ and that salvation is found in no one else. After their release, the believers pray for boldness, are filled with the Holy Spirit, and share their possessions, including a gift from Barnabas.

Acts 5.overview: Ananias and Sapphira die after Peter exposes their deception, while the apostles perform signs and wonders and draw growing crowds in Jerusalem. After an angel releases them from jail, the apostles testify before the Sanhedrin that God raised and exalted Jesus, and Gamaliel persuades the council to release them after a flogging; they continue teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ.

Acts 6.overview: A dispute over the daily food distribution leads the Twelve to appoint seven men, including Stephen and Philip, while they focus on prayer and the ministry of the word. The Jerusalem community grows, and Stephen’s signs and disputes with members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen lead to his arrest and accusations before the Sanhedrin.

Acts 7.overview: Before the Sanhedrin, Stephen recounts God’s dealings with Abraham, Joseph, Moses, and Israel, emphasizing Israel’s repeated rejection of God’s messengers and the Most High’s presence beyond a human-built temple. He accuses his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit and betraying the Righteous One, then sees Jesus at God’s right hand as the council stones him, with Saul present.

sections.heading: The Tabernacle, the Temple, and the Accusation

Acts 8.overview: After Stephen’s death, persecution scatters the Jerusalem church, while Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria and Peter and John come to confirm the Samaritans’ reception of the Holy Spirit. An angel directs Philip to an Ethiopian official, whom he teaches from Isaiah and baptizes before continuing to preach from Azotus to Caesarea.

sections.heading: Philip in Samaria and Simon’s Offer

Acts 9.overview: Saul encounters the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, receives his sight through Ananias, and begins proclaiming Jesus before escaping plots in Damascus and Jerusalem. Peter heals Aeneas in Lydda and raises Tabitha in Joppa, leading many to believe and bringing Peter to stay with Simon the tanner.

sections.heading: Saul Encounters Jesus on the Road
Peter Heals Aeneas and Raises Tabitha

Acts 10.overview: Cornelius receives an angelic instruction to summon Peter, while Peter’s vision and the Spirit’s direction prepare him to go to Caesarea and meet the Gentile household. Peter proclaims Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection; the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentile hearers, and Peter orders them baptized in Jesus’ name.

sections.heading: The Spirit Falls on the Gentiles

Acts 11.overview: Peter recounts to the Jerusalem believers his vision in Joppa and the Spirit’s direction to visit Cornelius, explaining that the Holy Spirit came upon the Gentiles just as it had upon Jewish believers; the church accepts that God has granted Gentiles repentance unto life. In Antioch, believers proclaim Jesus to Greeks, Barnabas brings Saul to teach the growing church, and the disciples send relief to Judea after Agabus predicts a famine.

sections.heading: Famine prediction and relief for Judea

Acts 12.overview: Herod executes James and imprisons Peter, but an angel frees Peter, who joins the praying believers at Mary’s house before leaving for another place as Herod searches for him. Herod dies after a dispute with Tyre and Sidon and a public address, while God’s word spreads and Barnabas and Saul return from Jerusalem with John Mark.

sections.heading: The Word Spreads and the Mission Returns

Acts 13.overview: The Holy Spirit commissions Barnabas and Saul from Antioch, and their mission through Cyprus leads the proconsul Sergius Paulus to believe. In Pisidian Antioch, Paul recounts Israel’s history and proclaims Jesus’ resurrection and forgiveness, after which opposition drives Paul and Barnabas from the region as the message spreads among the Gentiles.

Acts 14.overview: At Iconium, Paul and Barnabas preach in the synagogue, face opposition, and flee to Lystra, where Paul heals a man and the crowd mistakes the apostles for gods. After Paul is stoned, they travel through the region strengthening churches and appointing elders, then return to Antioch and report how God opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.

sections.heading: The healing and mistaken worship at Lystra
Paul’s stoning and the return journey

Acts 15.overview: A dispute over circumcision and the law leads Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem, where Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and James address the inclusion of Gentile believers and the assembly sends a letter setting out essential requirements. The letter brings encouragement to Antioch, and Paul and Barnabas later separate over John Mark, with Barnabas sailing to Cyprus and Paul traveling with Silas through Syria and Cilicia.

sections.heading: The council’s letter goes to Antioch

Acts 16.overview: Paul recruits Timothy, delivers the Jerusalem decisions, and follows the Spirit’s direction to Macedonia, where Lydia and her household receive the gospel in Philippi. After Paul casts a spirit from a slave girl, he and Silas are beaten and imprisoned, but an earthquake leads the jailer and his household to believe and be baptized; the magistrates release them after learning they are Roman citizens.

sections.heading: The Call to Macedonia and Lydia’s Baptism

Acts 17.overview: Paul proclaims Jesus as the suffering and risen Christ in Thessalonica and Berea, where some believe and opponents drive him onward. In Athens, Paul declares the Creator God’s call to repentance and coming judgment through the appointed, risen man, prompting mixed responses.

sections.heading: Paul’s preaching and opposition in Thessalonica
Paul encounters Athens and its philosophers

Acts 18.overview: Paul works and preaches in Corinth with Aquila and Priscilla, receives the Lord’s assurance, and continues teaching despite opposition before Gallio dismisses the accusation against him.
