Paul travels through Ephesus, Caesarea, Jerusalem, and Antioch, while Apollos arrives in Ephesus, receives further instruction from Priscilla and Aquila, and later proves from Scripture that Jesus is the Christ.

Acts 19.overview: In Ephesus, Paul baptizes about twelve disciples of John in Jesus’ name, teaches in the synagogue and the hall of Tyrannus, and his ministry is accompanied by miracles, public repentance, and the spread of the Lord’s word. As Paul plans to travel through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then Rome, Demetrius incites a riot over the threat to Artemis worship and the silversmiths’ trade, but the city clerk dismisses the assembly.

sections.heading: Paul’s Travel Plans and Demetrius’s Complaint
The Ephesian Riot and Its Dismissal

Acts 20.overview: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, meets his companions in Troas, and restores Eutychus after the young man falls from an upper-room window. At Miletus, Paul tells the Ephesian elders of his coming trials, recounts his ministry, warns them about threats to the church, and bids them farewell.

sections.heading: Paul’s Address to the Ephesian Elders

Acts 21.overview: Paul travels to Jerusalem despite warnings from believers in Tyre and the prophet Agabus, and James and the elders advise him to join four men in a purification rite to counter rumors about his teaching. Jews from Asia incite a crowd against Paul in the temple, but Roman soldiers arrest him; as he is taken to the barracks, he asks permission to address the crowd.

sections.heading: Paul Meets James and the Elders
Paul Requests to Address the Crowd

Acts 22.overview: Paul addresses the Jerusalem crowd in Hebrew and recounts his Jewish upbringing, his encounter with Jesus on the road to Damascus, Ananias’s role, and his commission to witness to the Gentiles. The crowd erupts when Paul mentions the Gentiles, and the Roman commander orders him interrogated, then summons the Sanhedrin after learning Paul is a Roman citizen.

sections.heading: Paul’s encounter and commission in Damascus
The crowd’s reaction and Paul’s citizenship

Acts 23.overview: Before the Sanhedrin, Paul confronts High Priest Ananias and divides the council by declaring his hope in the resurrection, prompting the commander to remove him. After the Lord tells Paul he will testify in Rome, Paul’s nephew exposes a plot against him, and Claudius Lysias sends him under guard to Governor Felix in Caesarea.

Acts 24.overview: Ananias and Tertullus accuse Paul before Felix of stirring unrest and profaning the temple, while Paul denies the charges and identifies his faith in the Way and hope in the resurrection. Felix postpones judgment, later hears Paul speak about faith, righteousness, self-control, and judgment, and leaves him imprisoned when Festus succeeds him.

sections.heading: Felix Delays and Leaves Paul Imprisoned

Acts 25.overview: Festus hears the Jewish leaders’ charges against Paul in Caesarea, rejects their request to move the trial to Jerusalem, and sends Paul to Caesar after Paul appeals to the emperor. Later, Festus presents Paul’s case to King Agrippa and Bernice, explaining that he found no charge worthy of death but needs grounds to report to Caesar.

Acts 26.overview: Before King Agrippa, Paul recounts his Pharisaic past, his persecution of Jesus’ followers, and his encounter with the risen Jesus, who appoints him to bring Jews and Gentiles from darkness to God. Paul says his preaching fulfills the prophets’ message about the suffering and resurrection of the Christ, and after Festus and Agrippa respond, they conclude that Paul has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment but cannot release him because he has appealed to Caesar.

sections.heading: Paul’s background and hope in the resurrection
Paul’s encounter and commission from Jesus
Paul’s preaching and the prophets’ message

Acts 27.overview: Paul sails toward Italy under the guard of Julius, but worsening weather delays the voyage and the crew ignores Paul’s warning to remain in Crete. After a violent storm leaves the passengers without hope, Paul reports God’s promise that all aboard will survive, and the ship is wrecked near an island where everyone reaches land safely.

sections.heading: The voyage from Caesarea to Fair Havens
The sailors’ escape attempt and the meal

Acts 28.overview: On Malta, Paul survives a viper’s bite, heals Publius’s father and other islanders, and receives provisions before sailing on to Rome. In Rome, he meets with Jewish leaders, explains the hope of Israel, teaches about God’s kingdom and Jesus, and continues proclaiming freely for two years.

Romans 1.overview: Paul introduces himself and the gospel of God concerning Jesus Christ, greets the believers in Rome, and explains his desire to visit them and preach the gospel, which reveals God’s righteousness through faith. He argues that God’s wrath is revealed against human ungodliness: although people know God through creation, they reject and dishonor him, and God gives them over to impurity, dishonorable passions, and a depraved mind.

Romans 2.overview: Paul warns that those who judge others while practicing the same sins face God’s impartial judgment, which repays each person according to their deeds. He argues that Gentiles’ consciences testify to God’s law, exposes the hypocrisy of those who boast in the law, and defines true circumcision as a matter of the heart by the Spirit.

Romans 3.overview: Paul affirms the Jews’ advantage in receiving God’s words, yet argues that Jewish and Greek unfaithfulness cannot overturn God’s faithfulness and that all people are under sin. He explains that God’s righteousness is revealed through faith in Jesus Christ, who redeems and justifies sinners by grace, excluding boasting while upholding the law.

Romans 4.overview: Paul argues from Abraham and David that God credits righteousness through faith apart from works, and that Abraham is the father of both circumcised and uncircumcised believers. He traces Abraham’s trust in God’s promise and applies the same principle to those who believe in the God who raised Jesus, delivered over for their trespasses and raised for their justification.

Romans 5.overview: Paul says that those justified by faith have peace with God through Jesus Christ, rejoice in hope and suffering, and are assured of salvation because Christ dies for them while they are sinners and enemies. He contrasts Adam’s trespass, which brings sin and death, with Christ’s righteous act and obedience, through which grace brings justification, righteousness, and eternal life, while the law makes trespass increase.

Romans 6.overview: Paul argues that those baptized into Christ share in his death and resurrection, so their old selves are freed from sin and alive to God. He contrasts slavery to sin, which leads to death, with slavery to righteousness and God, which leads to holiness and eternal life through Christ.

sections.heading: United with Christ in Death and Life

Romans 7.overview: Paul uses the marriage bond to explain that believers die to the law through Christ and belong to the risen Christ, serving in the new way of the Spirit. He argues that the law is holy but sin uses the commandment to bring death, and he describes the struggle between delight in God’s law and sin in the body, giving thanks for rescue through Jesus Christ.

Romans 8.overview: Paul declares that those in Christ Jesus are free from condemnation through the Spirit, who gives life, marks them as God’s children, and will raise their mortal bodies. He contrasts present suffering with coming glory, describes creation and believers waiting in hope with the Spirit’s help, and affirms that God’s purpose and Christ’s intercession secure believers against every accusation and separation from God’s love.

sections.heading: God’s Love and the Believers’ Security

Romans 9.overview: Paul grieves over Israel and explains that God’s word has not failed: God’s purpose rests on his call and mercy, as shown through Isaac, Jacob, Pharaoh, and the potter’s authority. He cites Hosea and Isaiah concerning Gentiles called as God’s people, Israel’s remnant, and the stone in Zion, concluding that Gentiles attain righteousness by faith while Israel stumbles in pursuing it by works.

sections.heading: God’s purpose in election and mercy
The potter, mercy, and the remnant
Righteousness by faith and the stumbling stone

Romans 10.overview: Paul expresses his desire for Israel’s salvation, explaining that Israel’s zeal lacks knowledge of God’s righteousness and that Christ is the end of the law for everyone who believes. He describes salvation through faith in the risen Jesus and the proclamation of the word, then argues that Israel has heard the message but remains disobedient while Gentiles find God.

Romans 11.overview: Paul argues that God has preserved a remnant of Israel by grace, while Israel’s trespass brings salvation to the Gentiles. He describes the grafting of Gentiles and the future mercy shown to Israel, then praises the depth of God’s wisdom and the source of all things.

sections.heading: Gentiles Grafted into the Olive Tree

Romans 12.overview: Paul urges believers to offer themselves to God, be transformed by renewed minds, and exercise their gifts humbly as members of one body in Christ. He describes sincere love and communal conduct, including blessing persecutors, pursuing peace, and overcoming evil with good.

Romans 13.overview: Paul teaches that governing authorities are appointed by God and that submission includes paying what is owed and showing respect. He presents love of neighbor as the fulfillment of the law and urges believers to live decently in view of approaching salvation, putting on the Lord Jesus Christ.

Romans 14.overview: Paul addresses disputes over food and sacred days, telling believers not to judge or belittle one another because each belongs to the Lord and will answer to God. He urges them to avoid causing a fellow believer to stumble, emphasizing that God’s kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit and that each person should act from faith.

sections.heading: Belonging to the Lord and God’s Judgment

Romans 15.overview: Paul urges the strong to bear with the weak and calls for unity among Jews and Gentiles, grounding their shared praise in Christ and the Scriptures. He describes his ministry to the Gentiles, plans to travel to Spain after delivering aid to Jerusalem, and asks the Roman believers to pray for his safety and welcome.

sections.heading: Paul’s Travel Plans and Prayer Request

Romans 16.overview: Paul commends Phoebe to the Roman church and sends greetings to numerous believers, including Prisca and Aquila, while conveying greetings from other churches and coworkers. He warns against divisive teachers, reports greetings from his companions, and praises God for strengthening believers through the gospel and revealing the mystery of Christ to all nations.

1 Corinthians 1.overview: Paul and Sosthenes greet the Corinthian church, give thanks for its gifts and calling, and urge unity amid factions aligned with Paul, Apollos, Cephas, and Christ. Paul contrasts the world’s wisdom with the message of Christ crucified, which is God’s power and wisdom, and says that God’s choice of the lowly leaves no room for boasting except in the Lord.

sections.heading: God’s choice and the Lord’s boast

1 Corinthians 2.overview: Paul recalls proclaiming Jesus Christ crucified in weakness, relying on the Spirit’s power so the Corinthians’ faith rests on God rather than human wisdom. He contrasts the age’s wisdom with God’s hidden wisdom, revealed by the Spirit, and explains that spiritual truths are discerned by the Spirit and expressed by those who have the mind of Christ.

sections.heading: Paul’s Proclamation in the Spirit’s Power
Spiritual Discernment and the Mind of Christ

1 Corinthians 3.overview: Paul rebukes the Corinthians for their immaturity and factions, describing himself and Apollos as servants while God gives growth. He explains that Christ is the foundation on which builders’ work will be tested, warns against harming God’s temple and worldly wisdom, and concludes that all things belong to the Corinthians, who belong to Christ and God.

1 Corinthians 4.overview: Paul describes himself and Apollos as servants and stewards accountable to the Lord, who alone judges hidden motives. He contrasts the Corinthians’ pride with the apostles’ hardships, then warns them as their spiritual father and announces Timothy’s visit and his own possible return.

1 Corinthians 5.overview: Paul condemns the Corinthian church’s tolerance of a man living with his father’s wife and directs the assembled community to remove him, with the aim of his eventual salvation. He warns that sin spreads like leaven, links the church’s purity to Christ’s sacrifice as the Passover lamb, and distinguishes discipline of members from judgment of outsiders.

sections.heading: The incestuous man and church discipline

1 Corinthians 6.overview: Paul challenges the Corinthians for taking disputes between believers before unbelieving judges, arguing that they should be able to settle such matters within the church and should not wrong one another. He warns that the unrighteous will not inherit God’s kingdom, recalls the Corinthians’ transformation, and argues that their bodies belong to Christ and are temples of the Holy Spirit, so they must not be joined to sexual immorality.

sections.heading: The Unrighteous and the Corinthians’ Transformation
The Body, Christ, and Sexual Immorality

1 Corinthians 7.overview: Paul gives guidance on marital duties, separation, and marriage between believers and unbelievers, then urges each person to remain in the situation in which God called them. He discusses singleness and marriage amid the present crisis, the concerns of married and unmarried people, and decisions about betrothal and remarriage after a spouse’s death.

sections.heading: Singleness and marriage in the present crisis

1 Corinthians 8.overview: Paul addresses food sacrificed to idols, contrasting knowledge that puffs up with love that builds up and affirming that there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. He explains that eating is not inherently significant, but exercising freedom in a way that harms a believer with a weak conscience sins against Christ, so he resolves not to eat meat if it causes another to stumble.

1 Corinthians 9.overview: Paul defends his apostleship and the right of gospel workers to receive material support, while explaining that he gives up this right to avoid hindering the gospel. He describes adapting to different people to win some, then compares gospel service to athletic competition and says he disciplines himself to avoid disqualification.

sections.heading: Paul’s Apostleship and Right to Support

1 Corinthians 10.overview: Paul recalls Israel’s passage through the sea and wilderness provision, then cites their judgments as warnings against idolatry, immorality, testing Christ, and complaint, while affirming God’s faithfulness amid temptation. He argues that participation in the Lord’s table excludes fellowship with demons and instructs the Corinthians to use their freedom over food in ways that honor God and benefit others.

1 Corinthians 11.overview: Paul commends the Corinthians for keeping the traditions he delivered, then discusses head coverings in worship, grounding his instructions in headship, creation, mutual dependence, and church practice. He rebukes divisions and selfishness at the Lord’s Supper, recalls Jesus’ words over the bread and cup, and calls for self-examination, mutual waiting, and further instruction when he comes.

1 Corinthians 12.overview: Paul explains that spiritual gifts have diverse forms but come from the same Spirit and are given for the common good. He compares the church to one body with many interdependent members, then lists roles and gifts in the church and introduces the greater way he will describe next.

1 Corinthians 13.overview: Paul argues that speech, prophecy, knowledge, faith, and sacrifice have no value without love, then describes love’s qualities. He contrasts love’s permanence with the passing of partial gifts and concludes that faith, hope, and love remain, with love greatest.

1 Corinthians 14.overview: Paul contrasts tongues with prophecy, arguing that intelligible speech builds up the church and enables shared understanding. He sets rules for orderly worship, including how tongues and prophecy are used, and concludes that everything in the church must be done properly and in order.

1 Corinthians 15.overview: Paul recalls the gospel of Christ’s death and resurrection, cites its witnesses, and argues that Christ’s resurrection establishes the future resurrection of the dead. He describes the resurrection body and the final transformation in which death is defeated, then concludes that work in the Lord is not in vain.

1 Corinthians 16.overview: Paul instructs the Corinthians to set aside a weekly collection for the Jerusalem believers and outlines his travel plans, including his stay in Ephesus and possible visits from Timothy and Apollos. He gives final instructions about faithful service and love, acknowledges Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, sends greetings, and closes with his own greeting and blessing.

2 Corinthians 1.overview: Paul and Timothy greet the church in Corinth and across Achaia, and Paul describes how God comforts him in suffering, delivers him from peril, and receives the Corinthians’ prayers and thanksgiving. Paul affirms his integrity, explains his changed travel plans, grounds his message in God’s faithfulness and promises in Christ, and says he stayed away to spare the Corinthians while working with them for their joy.

2 Corinthians 2.overview: Paul explains that he delays another painful visit and writes in distress out of love, then urges the Corinthians to forgive and comfort the person who has been disciplined. After leaving Troas because Titus is absent, Paul describes God’s triumphal procession and the contrasting effects of Christ’s message, which he and his companions proclaim sincerely before God.

2 Corinthians 3.overview: Paul presents the Corinthians as a letter from Christ and says his competence comes from God, who appoints him a minister of the new covenant of the Spirit. He contrasts the fading glory of Moses’ ministry with the enduring glory of the Spirit, describing the veil over hearts as removed in Christ and believers as transformed into the Lord’s image.

sections.heading: The Greater Glory of the Spirit’s Ministry
The Veil Removed and the Lord’s Glory Reflected

2 Corinthians 4.overview: Paul describes the integrity of his ministry, the blindness that veils the gospel from unbelievers, and the light of God’s glory revealed in Christ. He portrays hardship as a means by which Jesus’ life is displayed through frail ministers, and contrasts temporary affliction with the eternal glory to come.

sections.heading: Integrity and the Light of the Gospel

2 Corinthians 5.overview: Paul contrasts the mortal body with the eternal dwelling God prepares, describes confidence in the Lord and the coming judgment seat of Christ, and says he seeks to please God. He explains that Christ’s death compels his ministry, that those in Christ are a new creation, and that God entrusts him with the message of reconciliation through Christ.

sections.heading: The Heavenly Dwelling and Christ’s Judgment

2 Corinthians 6.overview: Paul urges the Corinthians not to receive God’s grace in vain, cites the present day as the time of salvation, and describes the hardships and qualities that commend his ministry. He appeals for the Corinthians to open their hearts and calls them to separate from unbelievers, grounding the appeal in their identity as God’s temple and in God’s promises to dwell among them.

2 Corinthians 7.overview: Paul calls the Corinthians to pursue holiness and affirms that he and his companions have treated no one wrongly. He recounts his distress in Macedonia, the comfort Titus brought with news of the Corinthians’ repentance after Paul’s letter, and his renewed confidence in them.

2 Corinthians 8.overview: Paul describes the Macedonian churches’ generous contribution and urges the Corinthians to complete their gift, citing Christ’s self-giving and the principle of mutual provision. He names Titus and two other brothers as the trusted delegates who will administer the offering and asks the Corinthians to demonstrate their love before the churches.

sections.heading: The Corinthians’ gift and mutual provision

2 Corinthians 9.overview: Paul explains that he sends brothers ahead to Achaia so the Corinthians are prepared with the promised gift, which has already encouraged the Macedonians. He describes generous, willing giving as producing a harvest through God’s provision and leading the saints to thank and glorify God, then gives thanks for God’s indescribable gift.

2 Corinthians 10.overview: Paul appeals to the Corinthians in Christ’s gentleness, defends his divinely given authority, and describes spiritual weapons that demolish opposition to the knowledge of God. He rejects self-commendation, claims only the work God assigned him—including bringing the gospel to Corinth—and says that the Lord, not the person who praises himself, gives approval.

2 Corinthians 11.overview: Paul urges the Corinthians to remain devoted to Christ, warns against false apostles and a different gospel, and explains why he preaches to them without charge. He adopts foolish boasting to compare his credentials and sufferings with those of his rivals, then recounts his escape from Damascus.

sections.heading: Devotion to Christ and the Gospel

2 Corinthians 12.overview: Paul recounts a man’s ascent to Paradise and explains that a thorn in his flesh keeps him from pride; the Lord’s sufficient grace leads him to boast in weakness and Christ’s power. He defends his apostleship and conduct toward the Corinthians, then expresses concern about their conflicts and unrepented sins when he visits again.

2 Corinthians 13.overview: Paul warns the Corinthians that his third visit will bring judgment on persistent sinners, defending his authority as Christ’s messenger and urging them to examine their faith. He explains that his authority serves their strengthening, then gives final instructions for unity and peace, greetings, and a blessing invoking Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit.

Galatians 1.overview: Paul greets the Galatian churches and identifies his apostleship as coming from Jesus Christ and God the Father, then condemns their turn to a distorted gospel. He explains that his gospel came by revelation from Christ and recounts his former life, calling, travels, limited contact with the apostles, and the Judean churches’ response to his preaching.

Galatians 2.overview: Paul recounts his Jerusalem meeting with Barnabas and Titus, where the leaders recognize his mission to the Gentiles and do not require Titus to be circumcised. At Antioch, Paul confronts Cephas over separating from Gentile believers and argues that people are justified through faith in Christ, not works of the law.

Galatians 3.overview: Paul challenges the Galatians to recall that they receive the Spirit through faith, then argues from Abraham and Scripture that justification and blessing come by faith rather than works of the law. He explains that Christ redeems from the law’s curse, that the law does not annul God’s promise to Abraham, and that those united with Christ through faith are Abraham’s heirs.

Galatians 4.overview: Paul contrasts an heir’s childhood under guardians with the freedom and inheritance that come through God’s Son and the Spirit of adoption. He warns the Galatians against returning to religious observances, recalls their earlier relationship, and contrasts Hagar and the slave woman’s son with Sarah, the free woman, and the children of promise.

sections.heading: Hagar, Sarah, and the children of promise

Galatians 5.overview: Paul contrasts justification by faith in Christ with seeking righteousness through circumcision and the law, urging the Galatians to stand firm in their freedom. He calls them to serve one another in love and contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit.

sections.heading: Freedom from justification by the law
The works of the flesh and fruit of the Spirit

Galatians 6.overview: Paul instructs the Galatians to restore those caught in trespass, bear one another’s burdens, assess their own work, support their instructors, and persist in doing good. He contrasts sowing to the flesh with sowing to the Spirit, rejects circumcision as grounds for boasting, and concludes by boasting in Christ’s cross and identifying new creation as what matters.

Ephesians 1.overview: Paul greets the saints in Ephesus and praises God for choosing, adopting, redeeming, and sealing believers in Christ as part of his plan to unite all things under Christ. He prays that they will know their calling, inheritance, and God’s power, shown in Christ’s resurrection, exaltation, and headship over the church.

Ephesians 2.overview: Paul contrasts humanity’s former death in sin with God’s action in making people alive with Christ, raising them with him, and saving them by grace through faith rather than works, for a life of good works. He describes how Christ brings Gentiles near, makes Jews and Gentiles one through the cross, and builds them together into God’s household and dwelling place.

Ephesians 3.overview: Paul describes his commission by God’s grace to reveal that Gentiles share in the promise of Christ, and explains that the church displays God’s wisdom to the heavenly powers. He prays that the Father will strengthen believers through the Spirit so they can know Christ’s love and be filled with God’s fullness, then gives glory to God in Christ.

sections.heading: Paul’s Commission and the Revealed Mystery
The Mystery Made Known Through the Church

Ephesians 4.overview: Paul urges the Ephesians to live in unity, grounded in one body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, and God, and describes Christ’s gifts and leaders as equipping the church to grow into maturity. He contrasts the Gentiles’ former way of life with the new self in Christ and calls for truthful, constructive, forgiving conduct shaped by the Holy Spirit.

Ephesians 5.overview: Paul calls the Ephesians to imitate God through love, reject impurity and corrupt speech, and live as children of light with wisdom and Spirit-filled worship. He then describes mutual submission and the distinct responsibilities of wives and husbands, grounding marital love in Christ’s relationship with the church.

sections.heading: Marriage and Christ’s relationship with the church

Ephesians 6.overview: Paul instructs children and parents, then slaves and masters, on their conduct within household relationships. He calls believers to stand against spiritual powers with God’s armor and persistent prayer, asks for prayer for his gospel proclamation, sends Tychicus with news, and closes with greetings and a blessing.

Philippians 1.overview: Paul and Timothy greet the believers and leaders in Philippi, and Paul gives thanks for their partnership in the gospel, expressing confidence in God’s work and praying for their growth in love and discernment. He explains how his imprisonment advances the gospel, weighs life and death in service to Christ, and urges the Philippians to stand together without fear amid opposition and suffering.

sections.heading: Paul’s Hope for Life or Death

Philippians 2.overview: Paul urges the Philippians to unity and humility, presenting Christ’s self-emptying, obedience to death, and exaltation as the pattern and ground of their shared mindset. He calls them to live faithfully as God works in them, describes his own joy and hopes for Timothy and Epaphroditus, and commends both men’s service to the gospel.

sections.heading: Unity and Christ’s Humility and Exaltation

Philippians 3.overview: Paul warns the Philippians against those who rely on circumcision and the flesh, contrasting their claims with worship by the Spirit and faith in Christ. He recounts his own credentials as loss compared with knowing Christ, describes pressing toward the heavenly calling, and contrasts enemies of the cross with the believers’ heavenly citizenship and the promised transformation of their bodies.

sections.heading: Warning Against Confidence in the Flesh

Philippians 4.overview: Paul urges the Philippians to stand firm, calls Euodia and Syntyche to unity, and commends rejoicing, prayer, peace, and disciplined thought and practice. He describes his contentment in every circumstance, thanks the Philippians for their support through Epaphroditus, and closes with greetings and a blessing.

Colossians 1.overview: Paul and Timothy address the believers at Colossae, and Paul gives thanks for their faith, love, and hope while praying for their knowledge, strength, and fruitful conduct. Paul presents the Son as creator and head of all things who reconciles them to God, then describes his commission to proclaim the mystery of Christ and his labor for the church.

Colossians 2.overview: Paul describes his struggle for the Colossians, the Laodiceans, and others, urging them to remain rooted in Christ and warning against deceptive teaching. He argues that believers are complete in Christ, who defeats hostile powers, and rejects judgments, angel worship, and human regulations as grounds for spiritual standing.

sections.heading: Paul’s Concern and Their Walk in Christ
Warnings Against Judgment and Angel Worship

Colossians 3.overview: Paul grounds a call to seek the things above in believers’ life hidden with Christ, then contrasts the old self with the renewed self and describes the virtues, unity, worship, and gratitude that characterize it. He gives instructions for wives and husbands, children and fathers, and slaves, framing their conduct and work in relation to the Lord and stating that wrongdoing receives just recompense.

Colossians 4.overview: Paul instructs masters to act justly and urges prayer, wise conduct toward outsiders, and gracious speech. He names Tychicus and Onesimus as messengers, sends greetings from fellow workers, directs the exchange of letters with Laodicea and a message to Archippus, and closes with his own greeting from prison.

1 Thessalonians 1.overview: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greet the Thessalonian church and give thanks for its work of faith, labor of love, and enduring hope, noting the gospel’s arrival in power and the believers’ welcome of it amid suffering. The Thessalonians become examples across Macedonia and Achaia as they turn from idols to serve the living God and await Jesus, raised from the dead and their deliverer from coming wrath.

1 Thessalonians 2.overview: Paul describes his bold, sincere ministry in Thessalonica, marked by gentle care, hard work, and encouragement toward a life worthy of God. He thanks God for the Thessalonians’ reception of the word and their endurance of persecution, then expresses his desire to see them and calls them his hope, joy, and crown at Jesus’ coming.

1 Thessalonians 3.overview: Paul sends Timothy from Athens to strengthen the Thessalonians in their faith amid persecution and to learn how they are holding up. Timothy returns with good news of their faith and love, and Paul expresses his joy, prays to visit them, and asks God to establish them in love, holiness, and blamelessness at Jesus’ coming.

sections.heading: Timothy sent to strengthen the church

1 Thessalonians 4.overview: Paul urges the Thessalonians to pursue holiness, sexual integrity, brotherly love, quiet living, and honest work. He teaches that the dead in Christ rise before living believers are gathered with them to meet the Lord at his coming.

1 Thessalonians 5.overview: Paul describes the sudden coming of the Day of the Lord and calls the Thessalonians, as people of the day, to stay alert in faith, love, and hope because God appoints them to salvation through Jesus Christ. He gives instructions for community life and worship, then prays for their sanctification and closes with requests, a charge to read the letter, and a blessing.

sections.heading: The Day of the Lord and readiness

2 Thessalonians 1.overview: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greet the Thessalonian church and thank God for its growing faith, love, and perseverance amid persecution. Paul describes God’s judgment at Jesus’ revelation, when the afflicted receive relief, their persecutors face destruction, and Jesus is glorified in believers, then records a prayer for their calling and faithful work.

2 Thessalonians 2.overview: Paul rejects reports that the Day of the Lord has already come, describing the rebellion, the revealing and eventual destruction of the lawless one, and the deception accompanying his coming. He thanks God for the Thessalonians’ calling to salvation and glory, urges them to stand firm in the teachings they received, and prays that God and Christ will strengthen them.

sections.heading: The Day of the Lord and the Lawless One

2 Thessalonians 3.overview: Paul asks the Thessalonians to pray for the spread of the Lord’s word and for his deliverance, and expresses confidence that the Lord will strengthen and guide them. He instructs them to distance themselves from undisciplined believers who refuse to work while admonishing them as brothers, then gives a blessing of peace and identifies his handwritten greeting.

sections.heading: Prayer and confidence in the Lord

1 Timothy 1.overview: Paul greets Timothy and directs him to stop false teaching in Ephesus, explaining that the law is properly used in service of sound teaching and the gospel. Paul describes the mercy and commission he receives through Christ, then charges Timothy to hold to faith and a good conscience, naming Hymenaeus and Alexander as examples of those who have rejected them.

sections.heading: False teaching and the lawful use of the law

1 Timothy 2.overview: Paul urges prayer for all people, especially rulers, so believers may live peacefully, and grounds this practice in God's desire for salvation through the one mediator, Christ Jesus, whose ransom Paul proclaims to the Gentiles. He directs men to pray without conflict and women to dress modestly and learn quietly, citing Adam and Eve before describing salvation through childbearing with continued faith, love, holiness, and self-control.

sections.heading: Prayer for All and Christ the Mediator

1 Timothy 3.overview: Paul outlines the qualifications for overseers and deacons, including their character, household management, reputation, and faithfulness. He explains that he writes so Timothy will know how people should conduct themselves in God’s household, and concludes with a confession about the mystery of godliness and Christ’s appearance, proclamation, reception, and glory.

1 Timothy 4.overview: Paul warns that some will abandon the faith for deceptive teachings that forbid marriage and restrict foods, while affirming that God’s creation is good and made holy through the word and prayer. He instructs Timothy to teach sound doctrine, pursue godliness, set an example, devote himself to Scripture and teaching, use his gift, and persevere in life and doctrine.

sections.heading: False Teaching and God’s Good Creation

1 Timothy 5.overview: Paul instructs Timothy to treat people in the congregation with familial respect and purity, and sets out how families and the church should support widows according to their need, age, conduct, and household circumstances. He describes honor and discipline for elders, charges Timothy to act impartially and cautiously in appointments, addresses his health, and notes that sins and good deeds eventually become evident.

1 Timothy 6.overview: Paul addresses the conduct of enslaved people, condemns false teachers who treat godliness as a means of gain, and contrasts the desire for wealth with contentment. He charges Timothy to pursue faithfulness until Christ’s appearing, instructs the rich to trust God and share their resources, and closes by urging Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him.

sections.heading: False Teaching and the Desire for Wealth
Instructions to the Rich and Final Charge

2 Timothy 1.overview: Paul greets Timothy, recalls his prayers and longing to see him, and affirms the sincere faith Timothy shares with Lois and Eunice. He urges Timothy to rekindle God’s gift and remain unashamed of the gospel amid suffering, then contrasts those who desert him in Asia with Onesiphorus’s support in Rome and Ephesus.

sections.heading: God’s gift and the gospel charge

2 Timothy 2.overview: Paul instructs Timothy to pass on sound teaching, endure hardship, and remember Jesus Christ’s resurrection, while affirming that God’s word remains unbound and that faithfulness leads to life with Christ. He warns against quarrels and false teaching by Hymenaeus and Philetus, then describes those fit for service and the Lord’s servant’s patient response to opponents.

sections.heading: Vessels for Service and Gentle Correction

2 Timothy 3.overview: Paul describes the moral corruption of the last days and false teachers who oppose the truth, comparing them to Jannes and Jambres and predicting that their folly will become evident. He contrasts them with Timothy’s knowledge of Paul’s teaching and persecutions, then affirms the Scriptures’ role in making the man of God complete and equipped for every good work.

2 Timothy 4.overview: Paul charges Timothy to preach and teach patiently amid coming rejection of sound doctrine, and he describes his approaching death and confidence in the Lord’s reward. He requests Timothy’s visit and supplies, reports on his companions, opponents, and defense, and sends final greetings.

Titus 1.overview: Paul describes his apostolic mission as proclaiming the hope of eternal life and greets Titus, his child in the shared faith. He charges Titus to appoint qualified elders in Crete and confront deceptive teachers whose conduct and teaching contradict their claims to know God.

sections.heading: Paul’s Mission and Greeting to Titus

Titus 2.overview: Paul directs Titus to teach sound doctrine through instructions for older men and women, younger women and men, and slaves. He grounds these instructions in God’s saving grace and Christ’s self-giving redemption, then charges Titus to teach, encourage, and rebuke with authority.

Titus 3.overview: Paul urges believers to respect authorities and act peaceably, then recalls that God saves through mercy, new birth, and the Holy Spirit, making them heirs of eternal life and calling for good works. He warns against pointless disputes and divisive people, gives travel and support instructions involving Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas, Apollos, and Nicopolis, and closes with greetings and a blessing of grace.

sections.heading: Salvation by Mercy and Its Fruit

Philemon 1.overview: Paul and Timothy greet Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church meeting in Philemon’s house, and Paul gives thanks for Philemon’s faith and love. Paul appeals for Onesimus to be received as a beloved brother, offers to repay any debt, and closes with travel plans, greetings, and a blessing.

Hebrews 1.overview: God, who formerly spoke through the prophets, now speaks through His Son, the heir and creator of all things, who sustains creation, purifies sins, and sits at God’s right hand. Citing Scripture, the chapter establishes the Son’s superiority to angels and contrasts His eternal rule with the angels’ role as servants to those who inherit salvation.

Hebrews 2.overview: The chapter warns that neglecting the salvation announced by the Lord and confirmed by eyewitnesses and God’s signs brings judgment, and it argues that the world to come is not subjected to angels. It presents Jesus, through suffering and death, as crowned with glory, united with those he sanctifies, and made a merciful and faithful high priest who frees Abraham’s descendants from death’s power and helps those who are tempted.

Hebrews 3.overview: The chapter presents Jesus as the faithful Son over God’s house, greater in honor than Moses, who served within it. Citing Israel’s wilderness rebellion, it warns against unbelief and hard-heartedness, urges daily mutual encouragement, and concludes that the generation led by Moses fails to enter God’s rest because of disobedience and unbelief.

Hebrews 4.overview: The chapter argues that God’s promised rest remains open, drawing on creation, Israel’s disobedience, and the later call in David’s words to show that a Sabbath rest remains for God’s people. It declares that God’s word exposes every person before him and presents Jesus, the sinless and sympathetic high priest, as the basis for approaching God’s throne of grace.

Hebrews 5.overview: The chapter describes the high priest’s human appointment and duties, then presents Christ as called by God as Son and high priest in the order of Melchizedek. Christ’s suffering and obedience make him the source of eternal salvation, while the author rebukes the hearers for needing basic instruction instead of solid food.

sections.heading: The High Priest’s Duties and Calling

Hebrews 6.overview: The writer calls the community to move beyond foundational teachings toward maturity, warns that those who fall away after sharing in spiritual gifts cannot be restored to repentance, and contrasts fruitful land with land producing thorns. He expresses confidence in their work and love, urges diligence and patience, and grounds their hope in God’s oath to Abraham and Jesus’ entry into the inner sanctuary as high priest forever.

sections.heading: Falling Away and the Land Illustration

Hebrews 7.overview: The chapter presents Melchizedek’s encounter with Abraham and uses Abraham’s tithe and Melchizedek’s blessing to establish the superiority of his priesthood over the Levitical priesthood. It argues that Jesus, from Judah and appointed by oath as a priest forever, brings a better covenant through his permanent priesthood and once-for-all sacrifice.

sections.heading: A Change of Priesthood and Law

Hebrews 8.overview: Jesus serves as high priest in the true heavenly sanctuary, with a ministry and covenant superior to the earthly priesthood and the first covenant. The chapter quotes God’s promise of a new covenant with the houses of Israel and Judah, in which God’s laws are written on hearts, all know God, and sins are forgiven, making the first covenant obsolete.

Hebrews 9.overview: Hebrews describes the first covenant’s earthly sanctuary, its furnishings, and the restricted access maintained by repeated sacrifices, which could not cleanse the worshiper’s conscience. Christ enters the heavenly sanctuary once by his own blood, establishing the new covenant through his death and offering himself once to bear sins before he appears again to bring salvation.

sections.heading: The earthly sanctuary and its limits
Christ’s sacrifice and the new covenant

Hebrews 10.overview: Hebrews contrasts the law’s repeated sacrifices, which cannot remove sins, with Christ’s single offering, which sanctifies and perfects those who are being sanctified; Christ sits at God’s right hand, and the promised new covenant makes further offerings for sin unnecessary. The chapter sets out the confidence and mutual encouragement made possible by Jesus’ priesthood, warns of judgment for deliberate rejection, and recalls the community’s endurance as it urges them to persevere in faith until the promised coming.

Hebrews 11.overview: The chapter defines faith as confidence in what is hoped for and unseen, then recounts how Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Rahab, and others act or endure by faith. These figures are commended without receiving all that was promised, as God prepares a better outcome in which they are made perfect together with the present community.

Hebrews 12.overview: The author presents Jesus as the model and completion of faith, explains suffering as God’s discipline that yields holiness, and calls for peace and holiness while warning through Esau’s example. The chapter contrasts the fearsome mountain of Sinai with Mount Zion and its heavenly assembly, then warns against rejecting God’s voice and describes the unshakable kingdom and worship due to God.

sections.heading: Endurance and the Example of Jesus

Hebrews 13.overview: The chapter gives closing instructions on brotherly love, hospitality, solidarity with the mistreated, marriage, contentment, and respect for leaders. It grounds resistance to strange teachings and communal worship in Jesus Christ and his sacrifice, then closes with prayer, a blessing, and greetings.

James 1.overview: James addresses the twelve tribes of the Dispersion and argues that trials test faith and develop perseverance, wisdom comes from God, and the circumstances of the humble and the rich are temporary. He distinguishes temptation from God from desire that gives birth to sin and death, and presents God’s word as the source of new birth and the basis for active, undefiled religion.

James 2.overview: James condemns favoritism toward the wealthy, contrasting it with God’s choice of the poor and the royal law of love, and he warns that the law calls for mercy. He argues that faith without deeds is dead, citing Abraham’s offering of Isaac and Rahab’s welcome of the spies as examples of faith expressed through action.

James 3.overview: James warns that teachers face stricter judgment and describes the tongue as a small but powerful force that can direct, corrupt, and contradict itself. He contrasts earthly wisdom marked by jealousy and selfish ambition with wisdom from above, which is pure and peaceable and yields righteousness.

sections.heading: The Power and Inconsistency of the Tongue

James 4.overview: James attributes conflicts and ineffective prayer to selfish desires, warns that friendship with the world is hostility toward God, and contrasts pride with the grace given to the humble. He rejects slanderous judgment and presumptuous plans, affirming God as the sole Judge and calling attention to life’s uncertainty and the sin of failing to do what is right.

James 5.overview: James condemns rich oppressors for hoarding wealth, withholding workers’ wages, and persecuting the righteous, and urges believers to endure patiently until the Lord’s coming. He addresses speech, prayer, sickness, confession, and restoration, citing the prophets, Job, and Elijah as examples of endurance and effective prayer.

1 Peter 1.overview: Peter addresses the chosen exiles across several regions of Asia Minor, praising God for new birth, living hope, and an imperishable inheritance through Jesus Christ. He describes faith tested by trials and salvation announced by the prophets, then calls for holiness, reverent conduct, and sincere love grounded in Christ’s redemption and the enduring word of God.

sections.heading: Sincere Love and the Enduring Word

1 Peter 2.overview: Peter urges believers to reject malice and seek spiritual growth, then describes them as living stones built around Christ, the cornerstone, and as God’s chosen people. He calls them to honorable conduct among the Gentiles, submission to human authorities and masters, and patient endurance of unjust suffering, following Christ’s example and returning to him as Shepherd and Overseer.

sections.heading: Christ the cornerstone and God’s people
Conduct among the Gentiles and authorities

1 Peter 3.overview: Peter instructs wives and husbands in their conduct toward one another, then calls all believers to unity, blessing rather than retaliation, and a respectful defense of their hope amid suffering. He grounds this teaching in Christ’s suffering and resurrection, the spirits from Noah’s time, baptism, and Christ’s authority in heaven.

sections.heading: Blessing Others and Suffering for Good

1 Peter 4.overview: Peter connects Christ’s bodily suffering with leaving past sins behind, living for God, and facing God’s judgment, while noting that the gospel is preached to the dead. He calls believers to prayer, mutual service, and endurance of trials, concluding that those who suffer according to God’s will entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and continue doing good.

sections.heading: Living for God and Facing Judgment

1 Peter 5.overview: Peter urges the elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly and humbly, and calls the community to humility under God’s care. He warns believers to resist the devil and stand firm through suffering, promises God’s restoration, and closes with greetings sent through Silvanus and from the church in Babylon and Mark.

2 Peter 1.overview: Peter says God’s power and promises provide what believers need for godly life, and he urges growth in faith and related qualities. He explains his resolve to preserve these teachings and supports the promised coming of Jesus Christ with eyewitness testimony and the prophetic word, spoken by people carried along by the Holy Spirit.

2 Peter 2.overview: Peter warns that false teachers introduce destructive heresies, exploit others, and bring disgrace, while examples from the angels, Noah, and Lot show that the Lord judges the unrighteous and rescues the godly. He describes the teachers’ arrogance, greed, and deception, recounts Balaam’s rebuke, and says those who turn back from righteousness face a worse end.

2 Peter 3.overview: Peter recalls the words of the prophets and apostles, answers scoffers who deny the Lord’s coming with the examples of creation and the flood, and explains the Lord’s patience and the coming day of judgment. He describes the promised new heaven and new earth, calls for holy conduct, and closes by warning about distorted Scripture and urging growth in Christ’s grace and knowledge.

sections.heading: A reminder of prophetic and apostolic teaching
Scoffers and the coming day of the Lord
Holy conduct and the promised new creation
Peace, Scripture, and growth in Christ

1 John 1.overview: John presents the apostles’ testimony to the Word of life, the eternal life revealed from the Father in Jesus Christ, and its purpose of fellowship and complete joy. He declares that God is light and contrasts walking in the light with claims that deny sin, affirming cleansing through Jesus and forgiveness for those who confess their sins.

sections.heading: The Word of Life and Fellowship

1 John 2.overview: John presents Jesus Christ as the believer’s advocate and atoning sacrifice, and describes obedience, love for fellow believers, and conduct like Jesus as marks of knowing and abiding in God. He warns against love of the world and antichrists who deny Jesus, then urges the community to remain in the truth and in Christ, whose coming and righteousness frame the chapter’s conclusion.

sections.heading: Warning Against Love of the World

1 John 3.overview: John describes believers as God’s children, whose hope of seeing Christ leads to purity, and contrasts those who practice righteousness with those who persist in sin. He presents love for fellow believers, modeled on Jesus’ self-giving, as evidence of life in God, and connects obedience with confidence before God and the Spirit’s presence.

1 John 4.overview: John identifies confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh as the mark of the Spirit of God, contrasts those from God with worldly voices, and warns against the spirit of antichrist. He grounds love for one another in God’s love shown through the sending of his Son, linking love with the Spirit, confession of Jesus, abiding in God, confidence on the day of judgment, and love for a brother.

sections.heading: Perfect Love and Love of a Brother

1 John 5.overview: John links belief in Jesus as the Son of God with birth from God, love for God’s children, obedience, and victory over the world. He presents the Spirit, water, and blood as witnesses to God’s testimony of eternal life in the Son, then describes confidence in prayer, the distinction between sin leading to death and other sin, believers’ protection, and the warning against idols.

sections.heading: Witnesses to the Son and Eternal Life

2 John 1.overview: The elder addresses the chosen lady and her children, expressing joy that some of them walk in truth and urging them to love one another by keeping the commandments. He warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, explains the need to remain in Christ’s teaching, and closes with plans for a visit and greetings from the chosen sister’s children.

sections.heading: Greeting and joy in the truth
The command to walk in love
Warnings about deceivers and false teaching
Plans to visit and closing greetings

3 John 1.overview: The elder greets Gaius, rejoices in his faithfulness to the truth, and commends his hospitality toward traveling brothers who serve the Name. He condemns Diotrephes’ rejection of the elder’s authority and refusal to welcome the brothers, commends Demetrius, and closes with plans to meet Gaius and greetings.

sections.heading: Greeting and Joy in Gaius’s Faithfulness

Jude 1.overview: Jude urges his audience to contend for the faith against intruders who misuse God’s grace and deny Jesus Christ, recalling examples of judgment and describing their conduct and fate. He recalls the apostles’ warnings, calls for faith-building, prayer, perseverance, and mercy toward others, and closes with praise to God, who can keep them from stumbling.

sections.heading: Greeting and the call to contend

Revelation 1.overview: John presents the revelation as a message from God through Jesus Christ and an angel, introduces Jesus’ titles and coming, and addresses the seven churches of Asia. On Patmos, John sees the risen Christ among seven lampstands, receives a command to write, and learns that the stars and lampstands represent the churches’ angels and the churches.

sections.heading: John’s Vision of the Risen Christ

Revelation 2.overview: The risen Christ addresses Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira, commending their deeds and endurance while identifying failures involving lost love, coming persecution, false teaching, and tolerance of Jezebel. He calls the churches to repentance or perseverance and promises the tree of life, protection from the second death, hidden manna and a new name, and authority over the nations with the morning star.

Revelation 3.overview: Christ addresses Sardis, warning that its reputation for life masks spiritual death, calling it to wake, remember, and repent, and promising white garments and names retained in the Book of Life to the faithful. He commends Philadelphia for keeping his word and promises protection and honor, then condemns Laodicea’s lukewarmness and self-sufficiency, calling it to repent and promising fellowship and a place on his throne to the one who overcomes.

Revelation 4.overview: John is called through an open door into heaven, where he sees the throne, the twenty-four elders, and four living creatures amid signs of divine power. The creatures proclaim the holiness of the Lord God Almighty, and the elders worship the enthroned One, casting down their crowns and declaring that all things exist by his will.

Revelation 5.overview: John sees a sealed scroll in the hand of the One on the throne, and an elder identifies the triumphant Lion of Judah, the Root of David, as worthy to open it. The slain Lamb takes the scroll, and the living creatures, elders, angels, and all creation praise the Lamb and the One on the throne.

sections.heading: The Sealed Scroll and the Worthy One
Praise from Heaven and All Creation

Revelation 6.overview: The Lamb opens the first four seals, revealing horsemen associated with conquest, the removal of peace, scarcity, and death across the earth. At the fifth seal, slain witnesses call for justice and are told to wait; at the sixth, cosmic upheaval drives people of every rank to hide from the wrath of the One on the throne and the Lamb.

Revelation 7.overview: John sees four angels hold back the winds until God’s servants are sealed, and he hears the number of the sealed from Israel’s tribes. He then sees an uncountable multitude from every nation worshiping before the throne and the Lamb, and an elder identifies them as those who come through the great tribulation and receive God’s care.

Revelation 8.overview: When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, silence falls in heaven as an angel presents the prayers of the saints before God and casts altar fire to earth. Seven angels prepare their trumpets, and the first four bring judgments on the earth, sea, waters, and heavenly lights before an eagle announces three woes for the remaining blasts.

sections.heading: The Seventh Seal and the Altar

Revelation 9.overview: At the fifth trumpet, a star opens the Abyss, releasing locusts that torment those without God’s seal for five months under the rule of Abaddon, or Apollyon. At the sixth trumpet, four angels bound at the Euphrates lead a vast mounted force that kills a third of humanity, while the survivors persist in idolatry and other sins.

sections.heading: The Four Angels and the Mounted Force

Revelation 10.overview: John sees a mighty angel standing over sea and land, hears seven thunders whose words he is forbidden to write, and hears the angel swear that God’s mystery will be fulfilled when the seventh angel sounds. At heaven’s command, John takes and eats the angel’s open scroll, which tastes sweet but turns bitter, and receives a commission to prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.

sections.heading: The Angel and the Seven Thunders

Revelation 11.overview: John is told to measure God’s temple while the nations trample the holy city, and the two witnesses prophesy, are killed by the beast, and are raised and taken to heaven. At the seventh trumpet, heavenly voices announce the Lord and Christ’s reign, the elders proclaim judgment and reward, and the heavenly temple opens with the ark visible.

sections.heading: The Temple and Holy City Measured
The Two Witnesses and Their Vindication
The Seventh Trumpet and Heavenly Reign

Revelation 12.overview: A woman gives birth to a son destined to rule the nations, while a dragon seeks to destroy him; the child is taken to God’s throne, and the woman finds refuge in the wilderness. Michael and his angels drive the dragon, identified as the devil and Satan, from heaven, and a heavenly voice declares the Lamb’s victory before the dragon pursues the woman and makes war on her other children.

sections.heading: The Woman, the Child, and the Dragon
War in Heaven and the Dragon’s Defeat

Revelation 13.overview: A beast rises from the sea, receives authority from the dragon, and is worshiped as it blasphemes God and wages war against the saints. A second beast rises from the earth, deceives the earth’s inhabitants into worshiping the first beast and its image, and imposes a mark associated with buying and selling and the number 666.

sections.heading: The Beast’s Authority and the Saints

Revelation 14.overview: The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who sing a new song and are described as redeemed and blameless. Three angels announce judgment and warn against worshiping the beast, while a heavenly voice blesses the dead who die in the Lord; the chapter closes with images of the earth’s harvest and the winepress of God’s wrath.

Revelation 15.overview: John sees seven angels carrying the final plagues and the victors over the beast standing beside a glassy sea, singing of God’s mighty works, holiness, and just ways. The heavenly temple opens, the angels receive golden bowls of God’s wrath, and smoke fills the temple until the plagues are completed.

Revelation 16.overview: A voice from the temple sends seven angels to pour out God’s bowls of wrath, bringing sores, blood, scorching heat, darkness, and judgments that prompt curses but no repentance. The sixth bowl dries the Euphrates and gathers the kings at Armageddon through demonic spirits, while the seventh brings a great earthquake, Babylon’s judgment, and devastating hail.

sections.heading: The Seventh Bowl and Final Plagues

Revelation 17.overview: One of the seven bowl angels shows John the great prostitute, identified as Babylon the Great, seated on a scarlet beast and drunk with the blood of the saints. The angel interprets the beast, its seven heads and ten horns, and the woman, describing the kings’ war against the Lamb, their destruction of the prostitute, and her identity as the great city ruling the earth’s kings.

Revelation 18.overview: A glorious angel declares Babylon fallen, and a voice from heaven calls God’s people out of the city while announcing judgment for its sins. Kings, merchants, and seafarers mourn Babylon’s destruction, while heaven and the saints are called to rejoice as an angel depicts the city’s irreversible fall and blood guilt.

Revelation 19.overview: Heavenly voices praise God for judging the great prostitute and announce the Almighty’s reign and the Lamb’s marriage; an angel tells John to worship God. Heaven opens to reveal the rider called Faithful and True and the Word of God, who defeats the beast, the false prophet, and the assembled kings and armies.

sections.heading: The Lamb’s Marriage and the Angel
The Rider Called Faithful and True
The Beast and Its Armies Defeated

Revelation 20.overview: An angel binds Satan in the Abyss for a thousand years, while those who remained faithful to Jesus come to life and reign with Christ. After Satan’s release, his forces are destroyed and he is thrown into the lake of fire; the dead then stand before the great white throne and are judged, and Death and Hades are also cast into the lake of fire.

Revelation 21.overview: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, the New Jerusalem descending from God, and hears that God dwells with his people, ends death and sorrow, and gives life and inheritance to those who overcome while the wicked face the second death. An angel shows John the city’s dimensions, gates, foundations, and precious materials, while God and the Lamb serve as its temple and light, and only those in the Lamb’s Book of Life enter.

sections.heading: The New Creation and Its People
The City’s Light and Its People

Revelation 22.overview: The angel shows John the river of life and the tree of life in the city, where God’s servants see his face and reign without curse or night. The angel and Jesus affirm the prophecy, announce Christ’s coming and reward, warn against altering the book, and close with an invitation to the water of life, John’s prayer, and a blessing.

sections.heading: The River and Tree of Life
The Angel’s Words and John’s Response
